**8. Questions (2.5 min)**

oped-09__base.text:
**What's not clicking:** you're not actually arguing with yourself. You have a clear argument, you just buried it in the last paragraph and then said "I dont know." Your story already has a shape: *I tried the big fix, it failed for real reasons, then I found a smaller fix that actually worked.* The tip share isn't a "maybe." It's your conclusion, and you have numbers to back it up. So I built the piece toward that.

---

**I Tried to Abolish Tipping. Here's What Actually Worked.**

Tipping in this country is broken, and everybody in the industry knows it.

My line cooks make $17 to $19 an hour. My servers, on a good Friday, walk out with $350 or more in tips. Same shift, same heat, same chaos. The guy plating your redfish makes about a third of what the person carrying it to your table makes. That's not fair, and I've spent years trying to fix it.

My first try was the big one. In 2022, we went to a 20% service charge and no tipping. It lasted four months.

In the first two, we lost three of our five servers. They could make more down the street, so they went down the street. One of them, Dee, had been with us since day one. She told me straight: "You're asking me to take a pay cut so you can feel good."

She wasn't wrong. And that's the part that usually gets skipped when people talk about abolishing tipping. Servers in New Orleans are mostly women, a lot of them single moms, and tips are how they make rent. When one restaurant drops tipping and the rest of the street doesn't, the servers don't win. They leave. Honestly, I would have too.

So we went back.

What I learned is that I was trying to fix the whole system from one 60-seat dining room in the Bywater. I can't. Customers aren't going to pay $45 for an entree so I can pay everyone fairly without tips, not while the place next door lists it at $32 and lets the tip cover the rest. Front of house shouldn't have to lose money for back of house to make more.

What I *can* do is fix my own kitchen.

Last year we started a tip share. 4% goes to the back of house. Louisiana allows it as long as no managers are in the pool, and we keep it that way. Kitchen pay went up about $3.80 an hour. We lost one server, who was leaving anyway.

That's it. No big announcement, no new menu prices, no lecture printed on the receipt. My cooks make more. My servers still make good money. Nobody had to pick between doing the right thing and paying rent.

It's not a revolution. It doesn't fix the fact that a cook's paycheck depends on how generous a stranger feels after two Sazeracs. Tipping is still broken. But I'd rather take the step that works than keep swinging at the one that doesn't.

So if you own a restaurant and you've been going back and forth on this like I did, here's my advice: skip the grand gesture. Talk to your servers first. Then cut the kitchen in.

And if you're a customer, keep tipping well, and ask your server whether the kitchen gets a piece. If the answer's yes, tip a little better.

---

**Two things to check before you send it:**

1. **The legal line.** The "no managers in the pool" rule is actually federal (FLSA), and there's a catch. If you pay servers the $2.13 tipped wage, federal rules generally only let you pool tips among tipped staff, so cooks can't be included. Including BOH is allowed if you pay everyone at least full minimum wage. You're probably fine, but run it by your accountant before it goes in print, because someone will email the paper about it.
2. **"4%" of what?** Sales or tips? Readers in the industry will want to know. One extra word fixes it.

The piece is around 520 words, so you have room for one more detail if you want it. What your cooks said when the first bigger paycheck hit would land well.

proposal-03__base.text:
**Flip it: lead with Slide 4 and cut the 60% stat.**

Your history slide is the strongest material in the deck, and it's buried. It has your own numbers, a named customer, a written letter from your insurer, and a real operational risk. The 60% stat is the vendor-pitch problem: it comes from the vendor, it's "Gartner-ish," and if your CFO asks "where's that from?" the honest answer hurts you. Your boss found it convincing, but she's a different audience. She'll trust a Ridgeline letter over a vendor statistic every time.

## Suggested structure

**1. The ask (one slide)**
$340k: migration $210k, first-year licenses $95k, training $35k. Then one sentence: *"Last year our current setup cost us ~$59k in outage-related losses, and our insurer has told us in writing it will cost another $22k/yr starting at renewal."* Put the conclusion up front. CFOs don't like waiting for the point.

**2. What the current setup cost us last year**
- 3 unplanned outages at Dayton, 31 hours total
- March outage: 2 missed carrier pickups, **$48k SLA penalties to Brennan Foods**
- **~$11k** recovery overtime
- Total: **~$59k**, plus whatever the Brennan relationship cost that isn't on an invoice

**3. Costs and risks already on the way**
- Ridgeline Mutual: **+18% (~$22k/yr)** unless we have offsite backup with tested restore. Bring the letter.
- Key-person risk: the person who built the config has retired, and no one fully understands it. This turns every future outage into a longer one.
- Servers are 7 years old. (State it as a fact. You don't need a stat to make it scary.)

**4. Options considered**
This slide is what makes a proposal read as analysis. It should show at least:
- Do nothing (insurance goes up, outage risk stays)
- Refresh on-prem hardware and add offsite backup
- Migrate to cloud (recommended), and why it beats the refresh

**5. What the $340k buys, mapped to the problems**
Replace the generic benefits slide. Tie each benefit to a problem from slides 2–3:
- Offsite backup with tested restore → meets Ridgeline's requirement, avoids the $22k increase
- DR/redundancy → reduces outage risk at Dayton
- Documented, vendor-supported config → removes the key-person risk
- Remote access → dispatch team (a nice addition, not the core case)

Drop "scalability" and "modern tools" unless you can attach a specific need to them. They're the most vendor-sounding lines in the deck.

**6. Multi-year cost comparison**
See gaps below. She will ask for this.

**7. Timeline and risks**
6 months, phased by site. Add which site goes first and why (Dayton?), what happens if a phase slips, and how you'll show it worked (e.g., a successful test restore, insurer sign-off).

## Gaps she'll probably poke at

1. **Ongoing costs.** $95k is first-year licenses. What's year 2, 3, 4? Compare that to what you spend now on hardware, maintenance, and support. This is the most likely place she pushes.
2. **The cost of staying put.** 7-year-old servers will need replacing regardless. If an on-prem refresh would cost, say, $150k, then the real decision is the difference between the two options, not $340k vs. $0. That framing could help you a lot.
3. **Confirm the backup design satisfies Ridgeline.** If you can get their sign-off on the plan before Thursday, or even an email saying "yes, that would qualify," that's very strong evidence.
4. **Don't overclaim the outage savings.** $59k was one bad year. Present it as "this is what one year of exposure looked like," not "we'll save $59k/yr." She'll respect the restraint.

On the ransomware point: one line of sector context is fine if you have a credible, non-vendor source. Otherwise leave it out. Your own numbers already make the case.

academic-05__base.text:
Your notes contain the answer, though it's neither A nor B as drafted. Here are the pros and cons you asked for, then a suggestion.

## Option A: Chronological

**Pros**
- Matches your strongest finding, which is change over time (money drops, feeling rises).
- Lets the Ó Ceallaigh letters run through the chapter as a continuous thread.
- Easy for readers to follow.

**Cons**
- Your break points are in the wrong place. The data pivots around 1895, but A cuts at 1890 and 1900, which splits your most important moment across two sections.
- Decade sections tend to become descriptive ("in this decade, people wrote about...") rather than argumentative. This may be part of why your 6,000 words feel descriptive.
- Religion, a constant, has to be repeated in every section.

## Option B: Thematic

**Pros**
- Each section has a clear analytical focus.
- Handles religion well, since it doesn't change.
- Feels more "argued" on the surface.

**Cons**
- It buries your main finding. The money-to-belonging shift is a story about *how the function of letters changed*, and splitting by theme scatters that story across sections.
- Two of your three themes are weak load-bearers: religion shows no change, and marriage may be a quirk of one family. You'd be giving equal weight to sections that don't carry equal evidence.
- Your most interesting material (feelings, homesickness, memories of specific places in Kilbrack) has no home in this structure at all.

## The deeper issue

Your "hunch" is your argument. *Once the money obligation fades, letters become the way emigrants maintain belonging* is a clear, testable thesis for the chapter. Both A and B organise around your categories of material, when the chapter should be organised around that claim.

## A possible Option C: chronological, but broken at your pivot and framed by argument

- **3.1 The obligation letter, c.1880–1895.** Money as the reason to write: remittances, passage tickets, debts. What letters are *for* in this period.
- **3.2 The turn, c.1895.** The shift itself: the 71% to 23% drop, the change in length and content. Show the evidence here.
- **3.3 The belonging letter, c.1895–1910.** Feeling, homesickness, memories of place. Marriage advice fits here as a way of continuing to take part in family life at home, rather than as a standalone theme.

**Religion** becomes useful in a different way: it's your control. Because religious content stays steady, you can argue the change isn't just "letters got longer and mentioned everything more." What changed was specifically the shift from obligation to belonging. That makes the stability a finding rather than a dead end.

**The Ó Ceallaigh letters** could work as a running case study, or you could use them to test the argument within a single family. That helps rule out the possibility that the shift just reflects which collections dominate which period.

## Things to check before committing

1. **Collection composition.** Is the post-1895 change partly because different families' letters survive for different periods? If one family dominates after 1895, the pattern could be a sampling artifact. Break your numbers down by family.
2. **Sample size later on.** You mention fewer letters after 1900. How many letters is 23% of? Small numbers can make a percentage look more dramatic than it is.
3. **The marriage material.** Name the two-writer issue openly in the text. Treating it as suggestive rather than representative is more persuasive than either ignoring it or dropping it.

## For Friday

Before you meet your supervisor, write your hunch as a single paragraph stating the argument. If it holds up on paper, the structure follows from it, and you can present Option C as "here's my argument, here's the structure that serves it." That's a stronger position than choosing between two outlines.

Your 6,000 words aren't wasted. Descriptive material is exactly what you redistribute once the argument is in place. Expect to cut and re-sort rather than rewrite.

If Option C doesn't suit your supervisor or the thesis as a whole, I'd lean toward A with the break moved to 1895, since it keeps the change-over-time story intact. I can help you draft that argument paragraph or rethink the section titles if that's useful.

business-decision-02__base.text:
Your draft has strong evidence, but it's buried. You open with costs (the weakest argument, since customers don't care about your costs), save the churn data for the middle, and end by hedging. For a numbers-driven reader, lead with the data showing customers won't leave, show the math, handle the risk with a plan, and make one clear recommendation.

Here's a rewrite. Bracketed items are numbers you should fill in or verify before Thursday.

---

**Dev,**

I'd like us to decide Thursday on moving Standard from $79 to $109/month. Here's the case, the risks, and how we'd know if I'm wrong.

**1. Our Standard customers aren't price-sensitive.**
- Clinics with 4+ practitioners on Standard churn at 0.6%/month.
- Of 61 churned customers in the last 12 months, only 2 mentioned price. The main reason was switching to an all-in-one EMR, which a $30 change won't affect either way.
- Churn is concentrated in the $49 legacy plan and clinics under 3 practitioners. This change doesn't touch legacy.
- When we raised Pro by $30 last year, we lost [X of Y] Pro customers over the following [N] months, versus a baseline of [Z].

**2. The math has a wide margin of safety.**
A $30 increase is +38% per account. To make less revenue than we do today, we'd have to lose more than **27%** of affected Standard customers. Our observed price-driven churn is about 3% of churners, not 3% of customers.

With [N] Standard customers, this adds roughly **$[N × 30 × 12]/year** in revenue at zero churn, and still **$[figure]** if we lost 10% of them.

**3. We'd still be the affordable option.**
At $109, we're still $20 below ClinicFlow ($129) and $31 below Janeway ($140), and [specific feature they lack / we have]. "Affordable" is about where we sit relative to the market, and we'd still be cheapest.

**4. It fixes our margin problem.**
Gross margin has dropped from 81% to 73% (AWS +22%, SMS rate increase in March, two support hires). These costs are now permanent. The increase would bring Standard margin back to roughly [X]%. [Verify this with per-account COGS; I estimate around 80%.]

**5. The real risk is new signups, so let's measure it.**
Price-sensitive prospects (small clinics) are the ones most likely to balk, and they're also our highest-churn segment. Still, I'd propose clear guardrails:
- If trial-to-paid conversion drops more than [X] points over [60/90] days, we revisit.
- We track win/loss reasons on lost deals for the first quarter.

**Proposal:**
- New customers: $109 starting [date].
- Existing Standard customers: $109 after 90 days' notice, or locked at [$99] if they switch to annual billing within that window.
- Legacy $49: unchanged for now (separate discussion).

I'd rather not grandfather for 12 months. That delays the margin fix by a year, and our data says the retention risk is low. The 90-day notice and annual-lock option give existing customers a fair transition.

If you see a hole in the data, I'd like to dig into it Thursday. Otherwise, I'd like to leave that meeting with a date.

Maya

---

**What I changed and why:**
- **Removed the hedging at the end.** "Maybe grandfather? Or only new customers?" invites another two months of debate. I picked a position you can defend. Change it if you prefer, but go in with one recommendation.
- **Turned the affordability worry into an argument for you.** At $109, you're still the cheapest option.
- **Added break-even math.** "We'd need to lose 27% of customers to lose money" is the kind of number that ends debates with numbers people.

**Where Dev will push, so prepare these:**
1. **"Nobody left" after the Pro increase.** He'll want actual counts and a comparison window. Get them.
2. **Exit survey bias.** People often give a polite reason instead of the real one. You can strengthen this by checking whether churned Standard customers downgraded or reduced seats before leaving, which would signal price strain.
3. **Margin projection.** The 73% is probably blended across plans, so calculate Standard-specific COGS per account before stating a number.
4. **Small clinics.** If Standard includes many 1–3 practitioner clinics, he may argue this pushes out your weakest segment. Have the count ready. You could also suggest a cheaper solo tier as a follow-up, which addresses that concern without weakening the main proposal.

academic-07__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Remittances don't empower or marginalize women on their own. They amplify whatever gender order a municipio already has, and the studies only look contradictory because they mix up two channels (men's absence vs. the money) and measure different layers of "participation."

## The shape that clicked

```
          pre-existing local gender rules (Cruz 2018)
                        │ filters both channels
      ┌─────────────────┴──────────────────┐
 men's ABSENCE                        remittance MONEY
 opens cargos, temporarily            flows through existing hierarchy
 (Hernández Ruiz; Morales)            (Vázquez & Lim; Gómez Pacheco; López)
      └─────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                        ▼
  participation = presence → voice → authority → durability
```

Your draft sorted sources by verdict (yes/no), so they could only volley. Sorting them by mechanism makes them complementary. Your Cruz instinct is right: it's the hinge that explains why the same flows produce different outcomes in different places.

## What moved
- **Cruz 2018**: from one more "empowerment" study to the organizing frame (conditional effect).
- **Hernández Ruiz + Morales**: merged. Same mechanism, absence. Morales adds that it doesn't last.
- **Vázquez & Lim, Gómez Pacheco, López**: regrouped as three ways money stays inside existing power: ritual hierarchy, remote control, exit.
- **2016 parity reform**: from a stray question to your research frontier, because it is a change to the filter itself.
- **Pilot (n=9)**: from evidence to illustration of the gap, since "only to listen" is presence without voice.
- **Cut**: "more research is needed." It is replaced by a specific gap.
- **Missing**: how the 2016 reform applies in usos y costumbres municipios. Also, whether the post-2016 studies account for it, and whether Hernández Ruiz and Morales separate remittance-receiving households from migrant households generally.

## Rebuilt

**Thesis paragraph (draft):**
> Research on remittances and women's political participation in Oaxaca's usos y costumbres municipios appears divided between accounts of empowerment and accounts of continued exclusion. This review argues that the division is largely an artifact of two conflations. First, studies often treat men's migration and remittance income as a single "remittance effect," when absence and money operate through different mechanisms. Second, "participation" ranges across attending the asamblea, speaking and voting in it, holding cargos, and retaining those gains over time. Once these are separated, a consistent pattern emerges: men's absence opens temporary space for women in community roles, while remittance money tends to flow through, and reinforce, existing structures of authority. Both effects are conditioned by each municipio's pre-existing rules on women's inclusion (Cruz 2018). Remittances thus amplify, rather than transform, local gender orders. What remains unknown is whether women's growing presence converts into voice and authority, and whether the 2016 gender parity reform alters the institutional conditions that shape these effects.

**Section outline:**

1. **Introduction: the apparent contradiction.** Name the empowerment/exclusion split as the puzzle, not the structure. State the thesis.

2. **What counts as participation.** Distinguish presence, voice, authority and durability. Map each study onto what it actually measures. For example, Cruz measures attendance and Hernández Ruiz measures cargos. This section does a lot of quiet work for the rest of the review.

3. **Channel 1: absence.** Hernández Ruiz 2015 shows women taking cargos when men leave. Morales 2019's "empowerment by absence" shows these gains reversing on return. Takeaway: absence opens authority but not durability.

4. **Channel 2: money.**
   - Vázquez & Lim 2017: remittances fund fiestas and church, reinforcing hierarchy and exclusion from asamblea votes.
   - Gómez Pacheco 2020: economic independence undercut by husbands' remote control via WhatsApp.
   - López 2021: households disengage from the local state ("exit not voice").
   - Takeaway: money tends to stay inside existing power relations.

5. **The filter: pre-existing institutions.** Cruz 2018 finds a 12-point rise in asamblea attendance among remittance-receiving women, but only where women already voted before 2000. Use this to reread sections 3 and 4: [check whether Hernández Ruiz's and Vázquez & Lim's sites differ in prior inclusion]. Note the limitation: this rests on one survey, so the conditional claim needs [additional evidence or explicit framing as a hypothesis].

6. **The gap: conversion and reform.**
   - Two open questions: whether presence becomes voice, and whether the 2016 parity reform [how it applies in usos y costumbres municipios] changes the filter.
   - Your pilot motivates the first. Six of nine women attend "only to listen," two hold cargos, and one reports increased control. Pilot data in a lit review varies by committee, so check with your advisor.
   - This section sets up your project.

For the 10-day crunch: sections 2 and 5 are where your argument lives. Write those first. The others are mostly re-sorting summaries you already have.

talk-05__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Our homework grades are tracking students' home circumstances more than their learning, and Lincoln showed we can cap homework without losing achievement.

## The shape that clicked

```
BEFORE                          AFTER
Survey (open) ◄── everything    Completion gap 88% vs 61%
   rests here                     └─ x 20% of grade = report cards
Survey (close)                         │
                                Research: unproven benefit at this age
                                       │
                                Lincoln: scores flat, D/F 19%→12%
                                       │
                                Math objection, answered inside
                                       │
                                Survey, parents, teacher time = color
```

Your colleague meant the survey. It opens and closes the talk and you call it "the core," but it's 51 optional responses from two of your own classes. "Stressed" is vague, and it doesn't show that a cap would help. A skeptic dismisses it in one sentence, and the whole talk goes with it. Your district data and the Lincoln pilot are much harder to wave away, and they're one story: homework gaps become grade gaps, and removing them didn't cost learning.

## What moved
- Completion gap: middle → opening and closing. It's district-wide, it's your hardest number, and it's about fairness.
- Lincoln pilot: middle → right after the research. It's your proof the cap is safe.
- Survey: bookends → a short supporting section, described honestly.
- Parent emails: their own point → one line with the survey. "A handful" can't carry weight alone.
- Teacher time: their own point → a brief bonus.
- Math objection: unplanned → its own section.
- Missing: research sources; Lincoln's D/F drop broken out by free/reduced lunch; completion gap by subject; how other schools' math scores moved that year; how 30 minutes splits across subjects.

## Rebuilt

**45-minute session**

**1. The gap (5 min).** Opening, in full:
> "I pulled homework completion from the gradebook at all three of our middle schools. Students not on free or reduced lunch complete 88% of their homework. Students who are complete 61%. Homework is 20% of the grade in most of our classes. So that 27-point gap goes straight onto report cards. I want to spend the next 45 minutes asking whether that 20% is measuring what students learned, or what's going on at their kitchen table."

**2. What homework buys at this age (5 min).** The research on middle school homework is mixed. Clearer benefits show up in high school. [Cite 2–3 specific sources.] The point: we're putting 20% of the grade on something with unproven benefit at this age.

**3. We already tried it: Lincoln (8 min).** Lincoln's 7th grade capped homework at 30 minutes last year. State scores were flat (ELA +1, math −1). D/F rates dropped from 19% to 12%. Name the limits yourself before anyone else does: one school, one grade, one year. [If available: did the D/F drop come mostly from free/reduced lunch students?]

**4. "But math needs practice" (8 min).** Say the objection yourself, fairly. Then:
- A cap isn't zero. 30 minutes is still nightly practice.
- Lincoln's math moved −1. [Compare: how did the other schools' math scores move that year?]
- Students with the least support at home are the ones not completing practice now, so practice isn't happening for them anyway.
- Then ask them directly: "What would you need to see to be comfortable with this?"

**5. What students and families are saying (4 min).** I ran an optional survey in two of my classes, 51 responses: 72% said homework makes them stressed or very stressed. This is a small, informal sample, not proof. One student quote. Note that you've also received parent emails about homework load.

**6. A side benefit (3 min).** Rough estimate: ELA teachers spend 3–4 hours a week grading homework. That's time we could put back into planning and feedback.

**7. The proposal and discussion (12 min).** A 30-minute nightly cap across all subjects. [Your plan for splitting the 30 minutes across subjects; math will ask first.] Option if the room is split: expand the Lincoln approach for one year and agree now on what you'll measure, including what math wants measured.

**Close:** Return to 88% vs 61%. "Lincoln showed we can close part of that gap without giving up learning."

academic-08__base.text:
Your Doktorvater is right, and the problem is fairly specific: **your data favour H2, but your discussion argues for H1.** A reader who looks at your results section and then your conclusion will notice the mismatch immediately, and examiners certainly will.

## Why the current argument doesn't land

**1. The elevated error rate doesn't discriminate between your hypotheses.** Paragraph 2 treats the 23% vs. 4% difference as support for transfer, but H2 predicts it equally well: bilingual children receive less German input than monolinguals. Evidence that both hypotheses predict cannot favour either one.

**2. The "coarse measure" defence is asymmetric.** Paragraph 3 explains away the null dominance correlation by questioning the measure. But your input measure is also an estimate (presumably parental report), and it produced r = −.58. If crude measurement were the issue, it should have hurt both predictors. You can raise measurement concerns, but you can't apply them only to the result you don't like.

**3. You've demoted your strongest evidence.** Three independent findings point the same way:
- Input hours strongly predict errors.
- Errors cluster on the lowest-frequency gender class. This is a frequency effect, the signature of input-driven acquisition. A transfer account, given that Turkish lacks gender entirely, gives no particular reason to expect neuter to suffer most.
- Children with German-dominant older siblings make fewer errors, which again points to input.

Paragraph 4 gives the first a single sentence, paragraph 5 calls the second "secondary," and the sibling finding doesn't appear in the discussion at all. Convergent evidence from three angles is the most persuasive thing you have.

**4. The conclusion inverts the weight of evidence.** "Transfer, possibly modulated by input" puts the unsupported hypothesis in the lead and the supported one in a subordinate clause.

## How far to restructure

The discussion needs a substantial rewrite, not a patch. A possible structure:

1. **Answer the research question directly.** Input quantity predicted gender errors; Turkish dominance did not.
2. **Present the convergent evidence**: input hours, neuter/frequency clustering, sibling effect. Integrate them into a single input-based account rather than listing them.
3. **Evaluate transfer honestly.** Explain why the group difference is non-diagnostic. Report the dominance result with a confidence interval rather than just "n.s." (for r = .19, n = 64, roughly −.06 to .42). That lets you say precisely what you can claim: your data don't support a substantial transfer effect but can't rule out a small one.
4. **Reconcile with Schmitz (2010) and Kaya (2014).** This could be a genuine contribution. If those studies didn't control for input, and dominance and input are naturally correlated, their transfer effects may partly reflect input differences. Look carefully at their designs.
5. **Limitations**: estimated input, cross-sectional and correlational design, the dominance measure. Raise the measurement concern here, applied to both measures.
6. **Conclusion**: input-driven account, with transfer at most a minor contributor.

**Analyses worth running before you rewrite:**
- The correlation between dominance and input hours.
- A regression with both predictors, plus partial correlations. If dominance and input overlap, the dominance effect may shrink further once input is controlled.
- If you want to keep "modulated by input" in any form, test the interaction (dominance × input). Without that test, the claim is speculation.
- Whether the sibling effect remains after controlling for input hours. Either outcome is interpretable, but you should know which it is.

## On the introduction

You probably don't need to rewrite it. If it presents H1 and H2 as competing hypotheses, which your summary suggests, then the study is a fair test and the result is simply the answer. Disconfirming the hypothesis you started with is not a weakness. A study that tests a plausible, literature-backed hypothesis and finds it unsupported, with a coherent alternative, is often more valuable than one that confirms expectations.

Check the introduction for three things only:
- Is H1 framed as a hypothesis or as an assumed truth? Language like "since transfer causes..." needs softening.
- Does the literature review give the input-based account enough serious treatment that your discussion isn't introducing it from nowhere? You may need to expand that section by a paragraph or two.
- Does the introduction promise anything the discussion now won't deliver?

These are targeted edits, not a rewrite.

Your reluctance is understandable after building the proposal around H1, but your instinct to ask was right. The data are clean and tell a coherent story, and the chapter will be stronger once the discussion follows them. Examiners respond much better to "we predicted X, found Y, and here is why Y makes sense" than to a discussion that seems to resist its own results.

positioning-06__base.text:
## Short answer

If the board must pick one, **A is better for the donate page**, but your instinct is right: neither fixes the real problem. **The page is written for the wrong audience.**

## Why neither tagline feels right

Read the current page as one of your donors: a 60-year-old homeowner or a local business owner. It opens with "Facing an N12 eviction notice?" They aren't. Every sentence speaks to a tenant in crisis, then the last line suddenly asks for money. A donor learns nothing about what their gift does or whether it works.

That's also why the taglines fall flat:

- **B ("Know your rights. Keep your home.")** is a good hotline slogan, but it's addressed to tenants. Your donors aren't the ones keeping their home. It belongs on your "Get help" page.
- **A ("Everyone deserves a safe home.")** speaks to donors' values, but it's generic. Hundreds of housing charities could use it, and "safe" doesn't quite describe what you do, which is helping people avoid losing their tenancy.

A tagline can't compensate for a page that never tells donors what their money does. Your best material, the numbers, is sitting in a report instead.

## What to propose instead

Keep B's strength (concrete outcome) but point it at donors, and put the numbers on the page. For example:

> **Help a neighbour keep their home.**
>
> Last year, Tenant Line answered **6,840 calls** from Toronto renters facing eviction notices, illegal rent increases, and Landlord and Tenant Board hearings.
>
> Of callers who used our hearing prep sessions, **64% kept their tenancy**. Our partner legal clinic estimates that about 40% of unrepresented tenants do citywide.
>
> We do this with one staff member and 38 trained volunteers, so your gift goes a long way. **$35 covers one complete call, including follow-up.**
>
> [Donate $35] [Choose another amount]
>
> *Need help with your tenancy? Call 416-555-0193, Monday–Friday, 9–5.*

Notes on the draft:

- **Keep the hotline number** on the page, just smaller and lower, so tenants who land there still find help.
- **A $35 default button** turns your best number into the action itself.
- **Word the 64% vs. 40% carefully.** Tenants who seek out prep sessions may differ from those who don't, so it's a strong comparison but not proof that you caused the difference. Present the two figures side by side as above, and avoid claims like "we boost your odds by 60%." If a donor or journalist pushes on it, you'll be on solid ground.
- **Don't promise the rewrite will reverse the drop** from $14,900 to $11,200. Many factors affect giving. Pitch it as a clear improvement worth trying, then compare donations over the next few months.

## Your 5 minutes

1. **(30 sec) Answer the question.** "If we're choosing between the two, A works better for donors. B speaks to tenants, so it's a great fit for our help page."
2. **(1.5 min) Name the real issue.** "The donate page is written for callers, not donors. It never says what a gift does. Our strongest numbers aren't on it at all."
3. **(2 min) Show the redraft** on one printed page. Let the board see their favourite numbers at work.
4. **(1 min) Make the ask.** "I'd like approval to replace the donate page copy with something like this, then report back on online giving next quarter."

This way you still deliver the recommendation they asked for, and you give them a better decision to make.

proposal-04__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Field margins are meant to be refuges for wild bees, but if the same margins that attract nesting also expose bees to pesticide residues, they may be traps, and how a margin is managed may decide which.

## The shape that clicked

```
            MARGIN MANAGEMENT (mowing regime)
                 /                    \
   WP1: BENEFIT                 WP2: COST
   nest density            residue exposure
        \_____ 18 shared margins _____/
                      |
              refuge or trap?
                      |
   WP3: SCALE-UP — volunteers (many farmers) extend
   observations beyond the study margins
```

Right now the project reads as three parallel tracks: habitat, chemistry and engagement. The 18 shared sites are the hidden join. They let you measure both the benefit and the cost of a margin in the same place, which none of the packages can do alone. WP3 becomes the instrument that takes that question past 40 sites, not a separate outreach product.

## What moved

- **18 co-located sites**: from a practical footnote to the core of the design. They are what makes WP1 and WP2 one study.
- **WP1**: from a standalone survey to the "benefit" arm.
- **WP2**: from a standalone residue study to the "cost" arm, measured in the same margins.
- **WP3**: from an app-development goal to a monitoring instrument. Accuracy validation becomes a milestone, not the objective.
- **Expected impacts**: from three separate bullets to one policy question about scheme design.
- **Cut**: nothing. If WP3 cannot be tied to margin-level records, it is the one to shrink or drop.
- **Missing**:
  - Mowing regime for the WP2 sites.
  - Whether the 18 shared sites span both regimes.
  - Whether all 25 WP2 sites can sit inside the 40 WP1 margins.
  - Whether the app can log location and margin.
  - A justification for using different taxa (ground-nesters, Osmia, bumblebees) as indicators of one margin.

## Rebuilt

**Title:** Refuge or trap? Field-margin management, nesting and pesticide exposure of wild bees in fragmented landscapes

**Central question:** Do field margins managed for pollinators deliver a net benefit, or does improved nesting habitat increase bees' exposure to agrochemical residues? And does mowing regime shift that balance?

**WP1 – Benefit: nesting habitat under different mowing regimes.**
We will survey ground-nesting bee density across 40 margins in Lower Saxony under contrasting mowing regimes. Preliminary data (2023, 12 margins) show nest density 2.3x higher in margins mown once vs. three times per year.

**WP2 – Cost: residue exposure in the same margins.**
Using LC-MS/MS, we will quantify neonicotinoid and fungicide residues in pollen collected by *Osmia bicornis* trap nests at 25 farm sites. Of these sites, 18 are in WP1 margins, and we will [extend this to all 25 / stratify the shared sites by mowing regime]. In the pilot, residues were detected in 68% of samples, with fungicide mixtures most frequent. *O. bicornis* serves as a standardised exposure sentinel for the margin [justify its relevance to ground-nesting taxa].

**WP3 – Scale: extending margin observations through volunteers.**
With the Hummelwacht network (approx. 900 members, mostly in the study districts, many of them farmers or farm neighbours), we will use an image-recognition tool to collect geolocated bumblebee records from margins of known management. This tests whether the WP1–WP2 patterns hold beyond the intensive sites. The pilot model reaches 81% accuracy on 9 common species, and validation to [target accuracy] is a Year 1 milestone. Farmer volunteers will also [supply management records for their margins].

**Integration:** WP1 and WP2 share sites, so benefit and cost can be modelled jointly per margin. WP3 extends the inference across the landscape.

**Expected impact:** Evidence on whether agri-environment margin prescriptions, including mowing frequency, should account for chemical exposure as well as habitat quality, delivered partly through the farmers who manage those margins.

business-decision-09__base.text:
# Fundraising Timing: Recommendation

**Recommendation:** Begin Series A preparation now and formally launch the process when Cascadia Mutual's actuarial analysis lands (expected ~6 weeks). We should not wait for the Q3 production run. If the actuarial results slip, we launch by **[hard date, ~8 weeks out]** regardless.

**Why this timing**

1. **The Cascadia result is our strongest catalyst, and it arrives first.** About 3,300 of our 4,200 units shipped through Cascadia, so the insurer channel is the core of our thesis, not a side pilot. An actuarially validated 31% reduction in water-damage claims, paired with an intent to expand to 50,000 policyholders, gives investors evidence of a distribution model where the insurer pays. A 50,000-unit commitment would be roughly 12x our total shipments to date.

2. **We can tell the margin story credibly without the Q3 run.** The drop from $41 to $23 unit cost comes from volume pricing, not an unproven process. We'll present it with the CM's quoted pricing for the 15,000-unit run [confirm we have this in writing]. If the run completes during the process, it becomes good news delivered mid-process rather than a precondition. A Cascadia expansion also gives investors a reason to believe the volume behind that margin will exist.

3. **Waiting for Q3 puts our runway at the mercy of a supplier with a history of slipping.** Our CM has slipped twice. If we wait and it slips again, we'd launch with ~7 months of runway, which weakens our negotiating position and leaves little room if the process runs long. Launching in ~6–8 weeks means we start with ~10 months of runway.

**Plan**

| Timing | Action |
|---|---|
| Weeks 0–6 | Build deck, model, and data room. Take informal intro meetings with the two inbound firms (no formal pitch). Build target investor list. |
| ~Week 6 | Cascadia actuarial results. Update materials. |
| Week 6–8 (hard deadline: [date]) | Launch formal process. |
| Q3 | Production run. Share results with investors as an update. |

**Risks and how we'll handle them**

- **Actuarial results are weaker than the pilot data suggests.** We still launch, but lead with margin trajectory and adjust our valuation expectations. A modest result is better known before the process than discovered in diligence.
- **Customer concentration.** Investors will notice that ~79% of units came through one insurer. We'll address it directly by framing the insurer channel as the strategy and showing early conversations with [other insurers, if any]. *[If none exist, we should start them now.]*
- **Process runs long.** If we don't have a term sheet by [date / runway threshold, e.g., 6 months remaining], we'll discuss a bridge with existing investors.

**What I'm asking from the board**

1. Endorse this plan and the hard launch date.
2. Make introductions to additional Series A investors, particularly those with insurtech or hardware experience.
3. Review the deck before launch (targeting [date]).
4. *[Optional]* Give an early read on whether insiders would support a bridge if the backstop scenario occurs.

---

**What I changed and why**

- **The recommendation comes first.** Your original listed reasons on both sides with equal weight, which is why it read as indecisive. Now each fact supports or stress-tests a single position.
- **The 900 direct units matter a lot.** They show Cascadia accounts for nearly 80% of your volume, which both strengthens the insurer story and creates a concentration risk you should address before investors raise it.
- **The hard launch date is key.** Without it, "wait for Cascadia" can quietly become "wait for Q3" again, and the board will notice.
- **The ask is specific.** Directors can act on "endorse, introduce, review" in a way they can't with "I'd like your input."

**Before sending, verify:**

- The current date relative to the Q3 run, so the runway math is correct.
- Whether you have the $23 unit cost in a written CM quote.
- How firm the 6-week actuarial timeline is.
- Whether you have any second-insurer conversations to point to.

If you think the Q3 run is actually only a few weeks away and very low-risk, the logic changes somewhat. Based on what you've described, though, launching around the Cascadia result seems like the strongest choice.

oped-10__base.text:
## What your editor likely meant

Your essay argues that **fines are morally wrong**, but your evidence shows that **fines don't work**. Those are different arguments, and the second is much stronger.

Look at what you actually have:

- Returns *improved* (91% → 94%) after fines ended.
- Fines cost more to collect than they brought in (€4,200 vs. nine staff hours a week).
- Removing them brought back 340 lapsed borrowers.

That's a rare, persuasive case: the policy is fairer *and* cheaper *and* it works better. A skeptical library administrator or Irish Times reader can't easily argue with it.

The class-warfare framing undercuts all of that, for three reasons:

1. **Your data doesn't support it.** Your returning borrowers are defined by age (under 18, over 65), not income. The "tax on the poor" claim may be true, but nothing in your essay shows it, so the opening reads as assertion.
2. **It insults the people you need to persuade.** Telling other library systems they're "defending a system designed to keep the poor in their place" or acting out of "moral squeamishness" makes them defensive. They're your audience, not your opponents.
3. **It's contestable where your data isn't.** A critic can dispute the Victorian history and ignore your numbers. Lead with the numbers and there's little to dispute.

## Suggested restructure

**Open with the man in his seventies.** It's your best material, and it's buried. Twelve years lost over €6 says more about what fines do than any abstract claim.

**Then the evidence**, made sharper:
- **Do the cost maths explicitly.** Multiply nine hours a week by 52 weeks by your real loaded staff cost. At, say, €22/hour that's roughly €10,300 a year spent to collect €4,200. Use your actual figure, but put the comparison in plain sight.
- **Name the real objection.** Critics didn't predict "chaos." They predicted returns would drop. Say that, then show that returns rose. A precise objection, precisely refuted, is more convincing than a caricature.
- **Address lost items.** "Accountability to whom?" dodges the reasonable concern. If your system still charges replacement costs for unreturned items, say so. That's the real answer to the accountability objection.

**Keep the fairness point, but earn it.** After the numbers, a sentence like "Fines fell hardest on the people least able to pay and most likely to stay away" lands because you've shown the staying-away part.

**Use the spare ~500 words** for the cost calculation, the lost-items policy, and perhaps a second borrower story or a staff perspective on what those nine hours now go toward.

## Two checks before submitting

- **One branch is one branch.** A before/after at a single site can reflect other factors. Say it's your branch, and if system-wide or national figures exist, cite them too.
- **Scope of the policy.** I believe the 2019 change applied to public libraries across Ireland, not just Dublin. That's worth verifying, since a national policy is a stronger example. Also, many systems abroad (Chicago, San Francisco and others) have already gone fines-free, so "other countries cling to fines" overstates things. You could cite them as company rather than criticise the holdouts.

## The ending

Replace the "catch up" line with something that turns your evidence into the question other systems should ask. For example:

> *For years we assumed fines were the price of keeping books on the shelves. They weren't. They cost us more than they raised, they didn't improve returns, and they kept people like my seventy-year-old borrower away for over a decade. The question for library systems still charging fines isn't whether they can afford to drop them. It's whether they can afford to keep them.*

Or end by returning to the man, where he is now: back, borrowing, maybe for that same grandson. Circling back to your opening story is a reliable way to close an opinion piece.

Would you like me to draft a full revised version along these lines?

business-decision-06__base.text:
The key fact is buried: Farmácias Bom Dia (38% of revenue) is asking for a senior person or they'll run a pitch. That's not one argument among several. It's close to decisive, and right now it reads like an afterthought. I've rewritten the email recommending the senior creative director, since that's where your facts point. If you actually land elsewhere, tell me and I'll rework it.

---

Cami,

I want us to go into Friday with a clear proposal, so here's where I've landed: **I think we should hire the senior creative director.**

The main reason is something I should have told you sooner. At lunch last week, Renata from Farmácias Bom Dia said pretty directly that she wants a senior person dedicated to their account next year, or they'll run a pitch. They're 38% of our revenue. Two mid-levels, however good, don't answer what she's asking for.

A CD also solves a problem we've both been living with. We're in every client meeting, which is why neither of us has done new business in six months. Someone who can own client relationships gets us back to growing the studio.

I know your concern is Bruno and Lis, and you're right. They're close to burnout, especially since Verano started, and a CD won't take production off their plates the way two designers would. So I don't want their workload to wait for the hire. My proposal:

- **Start the CD search now**, since it could take a while.
- **Bring in freelancers for Verano production immediately**, paid out of the payroll budget we won't be spending until the CD starts. Bruno and Lis get relief this month, not months from now.
- **Keep in touch with the strongest portfolios from the last post**, so we can move fast on a mid-level once new business picks up.

I considered splitting it, one mid-level now and the senior later, but the remaining R$16k won't get us a senior, and "later" might be after Renata has already decided.

I'm open to being talked out of this, but whatever we choose, I think we need a real answer for Bom Dia.

Beijos,
Rafa

---

**What I changed and why:**

- **Recommendation up front.** Camila knows what you're proposing from the first paragraph.
- **Bom Dia moved to the center** as the main reason, not an aside.
- **Her concern addressed directly.** Instead of just acknowledging Bruno and Lis, the email gives them a concrete plan: freelancers funded by the unspent budget during the search. It also admits the CD doesn't solve their workload, which makes your case more credible.
- **The split option dropped as a recommendation.** It doesn't fit the budget and doesn't meet Renata's timeline, so I kept it only as something you considered.

One suggestion: the Renata news is big, and Camila is hearing it for the first time. You might give her a quick call before sending, so she doesn't feel blindsided by it in writing.

business-decision-01__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Your bakery is short of people, not ovens, so hire first and buy the oven only once there's someone besides you to run it.

## The shape that clicked

```
Old:   OVEN  vs  BAKER       (one-off cost vs monthly cost)

New:   output = oven capacity × hands
       hands now:          you + Margaux + Inès
       hands by next year: you + ? + ?   (Inès gone June, Margaux maybe)

       oven first  → more output, same hands → you at 4am
       baker first → more hands → then oven, if still needed
```

Your pro/con list treats the oven as a one-off cost, but it comes with a recurring cost: your 4am shift. The loan repayments recur too. The lying awake is your list missing that cost.

## What moved
- **"4am is... me"**: from a footnote to the centre. It's the hidden cost of the oven.
- **Margaux and Inès leaving**: from side worries to the main risk. You could go from three people to one and a half within a year, holding a loan.
- **"Bank won't lend for a salary"**: from a reason for the oven to a constraint to plan around, not a reason to pick.
- **Accountant vs. mum**: they aren't disagreeing. One is looking at the P&L, the other at you.
- **Missing**: Is the current oven actually full, or are you short of hands to run another batch? How firm is Margaux's Bordeaux plan? Can you carry a salary for a few months before sales catch up?

## Rebuilt

**The real decision:** how do you stop the bakery depending on you being there every day, before your team shrinks?

**Recommendation: hire a junior baker now (~€2,600). Hold the oven.**

Why this order:
1. **Timing.** Someone hired now is trained before Inès leaves in June. They're also your cover if Margaux goes.
2. **It tests the oven question for free.** A second pair of hands may let you run an extra tradition batch in your current oven. If that recovers a good part of the €150–200/day, you've learned the oven wasn't the bottleneck.
3. **The risk is real, so look at it straight.** At 9% on €31k, you clear about €2,800 a month. A salary would eat roughly all of that until it brings sales back. The €150–200/day you're losing would cover it if you recover enough of it (about €4–5k a month if you're open six days a week). Check you have [cash buffer for 3–4 months] before committing.

**Decision rule for the oven:** revisit 3 months after the hire. Order it if you're still selling out by 11h *and* the oven is clearly full *and* two people can do the early shift. Allow for the 10-week lead time. By then you'll also have real sales numbers to show the bank.

**This week:** ask Margaux directly when Bordeaux might happen. Her answer may set your timeline more than anything on the list.

You weren't missing a number. Both options ran through you, and only the hire takes some of the load off you.

oped-07__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
The four-day week worked for the teams we staffed for it and cost the team we didn't, and that gap was my decision, not a "growing pain."

## The shape that clicked

```
Old:  4-day week ──► eng wins (3 paras) ──► "everyone try it"
                     support (1 line, buried)

New:  4-day week
       ├─ staffed for it ──► eng: same output, 0 quits, 140 applicants
       └─ not staffed ─────► support: 2.1h→6.8h, CSAT down, renewal hit
                               ▲ asked twice for a 5th hire; I said wait
      ──► lesson: fewer days needs a coverage plan, not just a calendar
      ──► what we're changing ──► "try it, but do this first"
```

Don't cut support. It's what makes the piece believable. The critics' best argument is "employees win, customers pay." If you leave it out, they'll make that case for you, and your support team will know you hid it. If you put it in, the argument becomes your lesson. Your head of support went quiet because the draft turned their cost, and a call you made, into one vague line.

## What moved
- Support: one line → its own section, with the numbers and your "wait" decision.
- Closing: "every startup should try it" → "try it, but plan coverage first."
- Headline: kept "not going back," and added the honest catch.
- Softened: "9% of ARR" → "one of our biggest customers." Publishing that figure exposes the customer and your revenue. Your call.
- Missing: what you're actually changing in support. I left placeholders and didn't invent a plan.
- Suggest: let the support team read this before it goes live.

## Rebuilt

**We went to 4 days. We're not going back. But we got one big thing wrong.**

Six months ago, Faltwerk moved to a four-day week. We're a 28-person invoicing company in Berlin, and I promised the team that whatever happened, I'd write it up honestly. This is that write-up. Most of it is good news. One part isn't, and that part is on me.

**How we ran it**

The pilot ran from October to March. We compared it against the previous six months, April to September. Engineering and most of the company took Fridays off. Our four-person support team staggered their days off so customers were never left without cover.

**What worked**

Engineering output held. We shipped 23 features during the pilot, against 21 in the six months before. Sprint velocity was roughly flat, up about 3%. Same work, one fewer day.

People said they could think. Engineers' self-reported focus score went from 6.2 to 8.0. That's a survey, not a stopwatch, so take it with some salt. But it matches what I saw: fewer half-days lost to context switching, more deep work on Monday through Thursday.

People got sick less. Sick days per person dropped from 5.4 to 3.1.

Nobody left. In the six months before the pilot, four people quit. At our size that's one in seven. During the pilot, zero people did.

Hiring got easier. Applications per open role went from 55 to 140. For a small startup competing with much bigger names for talent, that alone changes the maths.

**What didn't work, and why that's my fault**

My first draft of this post described support as "some growing pains." That wasn't honest.

Our first-response time went from 2.1 hours to 6.8 hours. Customer satisfaction dropped from 4.6 to 4.1. Two enterprise customers brought up slow support in their renewal calls. One of our biggest customers renewed for six months instead of twelve.

The cause isn't mysterious. Engineering had room to absorb a lost day. Support didn't. It's a four-person team whose job is to be available. To keep Fridays covered, they staggered their days off. That meant fewer people on shift Monday to Thursday as well. The queue grew every day, not just on Fridays.

The support team saw this early. They asked me twice during the pilot for a fifth hire. Both times I said we should wait until the results were in. I was treating the pilot as one experiment. It was really two: one for teams measured by output, and one for a team measured by availability. I designed for the first and asked the second to make it work with what they had. They did their best, and our customers felt the gap.

**What we're changing**

- [The fifth support hire: confirm status and timing]
- [Any change to how support coverage works, e.g. how days off are scheduled]
- [How you'll track response time and CSAT going forward, and what triggers action]
- [Anything you're doing with the two enterprise customers, if you're comfortable sharing]

The four-day week stays. What changes is that we'll stop pretending it costs the same for every team.

**Should you try it?**

Yes. But not the way we did.

Before you start, sort your teams into two groups. Some teams are judged on what they produce. Others are judged on being there when someone needs them. The first group may well do what our engineers did and fit five days of work into four. The second group can't compress availability. They need extra headcount or a real coverage plan in place on day one, not after the data comes in.

Second, track customer-facing numbers from the start and treat them as seriously as the happiness numbers. Our wellbeing metrics looked so good that it was easy to wave away the ones that didn't.

Third, when the team carrying the cost tells you it isn't working, believe them the first time.

**Where we land**

We're not going back to five days. The retention, hiring and focus gains are too big to give up, and our engineers proved the output holds. But the honest version of this story isn't "four days just works." It's "four days works when you staff for it, and we learned that at our support team's expense."

To our support team: thank you for holding the line, and for telling me the truth twice before I listened.

strategy-02__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
You and Tobi aren't actually split on what the business is (you both say lending). You're split on how to fund it. The cheapest thing that strengthens *every* funding path is fixing the terminal-driven churn eating the merchant base that lending sits on.

## The shape that clicked
```
                LENDING  ← you both agree
                   │ needs capital
        ┌──────────┴──────────┐
   Debt facility         Series A
   needs 12 mo data      seed lead wants
   (have 7: 5 to go)     "multi-market story"
        └──────────┬──────────┘
                   │ both judge
        MERCHANT BASE: 9,200
        leaking 6.2%/mo (was 4.5%)
        half = broken terminals, 9-day swap
```
Before, this was Ghana vs. lending, two people at opposite poles. But both your arguments end in "lending stalls." Once lending is the goal and capital is the bridge, Ghana becomes one input to one funding path. Churn turns out to be the foundation under both paths.

## What moved
- **Churn / terminal repair**: footnote → foundation. It's the one fix that's internal and fast, and both founders can own it.
- **Ghana**: rival strategy → a staged option inside the Series A path.
- **Debt data gap**: background → a clock. Five months to go, roughly the same window as Ghana licensing (5–7).
- **Cut for now: agent banking.** Undiscussed, and it would be a third front for 34 people. Park it.
- **Missing:** runway in months, Series A target date, how much of the $380k is needed upfront vs. later, whether churned merchants include advance holders, and what exactly the seed lead means by "multi-market story."

## Rebuilt

**Board update framing: "One goal, two funding paths, one leak"**

**1. What we agree on.** Lending is the business. The MCA pilot covers 640 merchants with a 4.1% default rate, a ₦450k average advance, and ~11% earned per cycle.

**2. The constraint is capital, and there are two paths to it.**
- *Debt:* both lenders want 12 months of loan book data. We have 7, so we're 5 months from a credible conversation.
- *Equity:* our seed lead wants a multi-market story before the Series A.

**3. The threat to both paths is churn.** It's 6.2% monthly, up from 4.5%. About half comes from broken terminals, which take us 9 days on average to replace. The other half is fee undercutting by bigger players. Any lender or Series A investor will look at a shrinking base before they look at the loan book. If advances repay through terminal transactions, a dead terminal is also a credit problem. [confirm how repayment works]

**4. Plan for the next 5 months**
- **Fix replacement time.** Cut the 9-day average to [target days]. Report churn monthly to the board.
- **Protect the pilot.** Run the lending pilot clean through month 12 without expanding risk, so the debt conversation happens on full data.
- **Treat Ghana as an option, not a split.** Start with the cheapest credible step: [formalize the Accra partner / start licensing paperwork], at a cost of [₦/$ amount]. No team moves yet. The licensing clock then runs alongside the data clock.

**5. Decision rule for Ghana.** This is the question that ends the circular argument:
- Ask the seed lead this week: *"Does the multi-market story need live operations in Ghana, or a licence in progress plus a credible plan?"*
- **If a plan and licence in progress is enough:** stage it as above. Tobi's concern about splitting the team is resolved.
- **If they need live revenue:** that's a real fork. Decide it on [runway months] vs. [Series A date]. If runway can't reach a debt facility without the A, Ghana gets resourced. If it can, lending and churn come first and the A waits for 12 months of data.

**6. Parked:** agent banking. We'll review it separately after the churn fix.

oped-05__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Sorghum did not beat maize on my farm. The malt contract did, and that contract is about to change.

## The shape that clicked
```
 Post A: "sorghum won"      Post B: "sorghum's future unclear"
            \                         /
             \                       /
      THE CONTRACT: KSh 3,300 fixed, all bags taken
                          |
      2025 review: lower price? only 60% taken?
                          |
      Sorghum with no contract: KSh 2,200, few buyers
```
Your wife is right. Each post tells half the story, and a farmer reading only one could plant the wrong crop. Post A gives sorghum credit that belongs to the contract. Post B drops sorghum before the new terms are known. Your best post puts both halves together and shows the numbers.

## What moved
- **The contract**: from a side detail in A and a vague worry in B → the centre of the post.
- **2023 drought**: from A's turning point → one season of evidence. Maize was tested in a drought. Sorghum may not have been.
- **Kiprono**: from left out → an honest counterpoint near the top.
- **Readers without a contract**: from missing → a key section. At KSh 2,200 open price, sorghum looks very different.
- **Cut**: "a farmer must think about the future." It is true but says nothing. Your numbers say it better.
- **Missing**: input costs per acre for each crop; whether 7 and 8 bags are counted after the birds took their share; Kiprono's 2024 bags and price; the maize price in 2024; the weather in the 2023 short rains; Kerio Valley Malt's actual 2025 terms.

## Rebuilt

**What to write:** one post. Something like *"Maize or sorghum? My three seasons of numbers, and the one thing that decides it."*

**Your numbers, money per acre (before costs):**

| Season | Crop | Bags/acre | Price | KSh/acre |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 long rains | Maize | 9 | 2,800 | 25,200 |
| 2023 long rains (dry) | Maize | 4 | 4,100 | 16,400 |
| 2023 short rains | Sorghum (contract) | 7 | 3,300 | 23,100 |
| 2024 long rains | Sorghum (contract) | 8 | 3,300 | 26,400 |

**If the contract takes only 60% at the same price, and you sell the rest in Kabarnet:**
- 8 bags: 4.8 × 3,300 + 3.2 × 2,200 = **KSh 22,880**
- 7 bags: **KSh 20,020**
- No contract at all, 8 bags × 2,200 = **KSh 17,600**, if you can find buyers

So with the new terms, sorghum becomes the *safer but lower* crop. It earns less than maize in a good year and more than maize in a drought. Without a contract, it barely beats a drought maize year.

**Outline:**
1. Opening (below)
2. The table, honestly. Include Kiprono's better 2024.
3. What actually made sorghum pay: the fixed price and a buyer who took everything
4. What changes in 2025, and the three scenarios above
5. For readers with no contract: be careful
6. What I'm doing next season: [your plan once the terms are known, perhaps some acres of each]

**Opening:**
> Last month I sat down to write a post called "Why I gave up maize for sorghum." Then I sat down to write one called "Why I'm going back to maize." My wife read both and told me not to publish either, because both are true. She was right. Here are my real numbers from three seasons, including the parts that do not flatter me. What I learned is that the seed was never the main story. The buyer was.

**Your own decision rule:** wait for Kerio Valley Malt's 2025 terms, then add your input costs [missing] to the scenarios above. If contract sorghum still beats a normal maize year after costs, stay. If it only beats a drought year, think of sorghum as insurance and split your 6 acres.

pitch-03__base.text:
**Subject:** Intro via Daniel Ferris: rostering pilot results

Dear Ms Okafor,

Daniel Ferris suggested I get in touch, as the Trust is reviewing its rostering approach ahead of next year.

We recently completed a 6-month pilot of ShiftWell at a 900-bed acute trust in the Midlands. On participating wards:

- Agency nurse spend fell by £312,000
- Bank shift requests dropped 22%
- Unfilled night shifts went from 9% to 3%
- Staff agreeing "my rota lets me plan my life" rose from 31% to 58%

ShiftWell integrates with existing HR and e-rostering systems and is fully compliant with NHS data standards.

Would you be open to a 20-minute call to walk through the pilot data and whether it could apply to your Trust? I'm happy to send the full results beforehand.

Kind regards,
Priya Nair
Account Executive, ShiftWell

---

**What I changed and why**

- **Cut the vendor language.** "Industry-leading," "cutting-edge," "leverage," "optimise," and "unprecedented challenges" are what made it sound like every other vendor. They're claims anyone can make. Your pilot results are proof, so I let those do the work.
- **Moved the numbers to the top.** They were buried in paragraph four. For a numbers-driven reader they're the reason to keep reading, and bullets make them scannable in seconds.
- **Used the warm intro more.** Daniel's name is now in the subject line, which is your best chance of getting opened in a crowded inbox. "Transforming workforce management with AI" reads as a cold pitch.
- **Reframed the ask.** "A demo" signals a sales pitch. "Walk through the pilot data" offers her something useful, and the offer to send results first lowers the commitment. I also trimmed it to 20 minutes.
- **Kept the integration and compliance line.** It answers the first objection an NHS director will have, so it earns its place.

**One thing to prepare:** She'll likely ask how many wards were in the pilot and what the baseline agency spend was. £312k means very different things across 3 wards versus 30. If you can share that, consider adding it in brackets after the figure. It makes the number more credible.

strategy-04__base.text:
Honestly, the reasoning doesn't hold up as written. The instinct behind it might be fine, but the memo's own evidence argues against its conclusion. A skeptical reader (a board member, your CFO, or the CEO in six months when US conversion is still stuck) will notice.

## Where the argument breaks

**1. The evidence quality is inverted relative to the priority.**
Your three "reduced capacity" items have the strongest evidence in the document:
- **US eligibility:** a quantified revenue blocker (58% of lost US trials cite it).
- **No-show reduction:** already validated by an A/B test across 40 clinics, with a ~36% relative drop. It just needs rollout.
- **Quebec compliance:** a hard regulatory deadline.

The flagship rests on three conversations and a vague competitor claim. You're demoting the proven, deadline-bound work to fund the least-evidenced work.

**2. "Our clinics are asking for AI" overgeneralizes.**
Three customers out of ~2,100 is 0.14%, and they're your largest multi-location accounts, which are the least representative of a typical clinic. They matter commercially, but the memo should say "three large accounts raised it," not "our clinics are asking." Also check what "raised" meant. Was it curiosity, a feature request, a renewal condition, or willingness to pay?

**3. Your appendix contradicts your thesis.**
AI-related tickets are 0.4%. Meanwhile, reminder failures (17%) tie directly to the no-show work you're deprioritizing, and billing errors (22%) aren't addressed anywhere. Anyone who reads the appendix will ask why it's attached to this recommendation.

**4. "Reduced capacity" on a hard regulatory deadline is a real risk.**
If Quebec slips, the consequences are compliance exposure and possibly losing the ability to sell in Quebec, not just a delayed feature. That item shouldn't be competing for capacity at all.

**5. Staffing it with the Platform team has hidden costs.**
If Platform owns things like calendar sync, permissions, or reminder delivery (which together are ~40% of your tickets), pulling all 6 engineers could make support load worse. Worth checking before committing.

**6. SOAP drafting may be a category jump, not a feature.**
You're scheduling + intake software. Do clinics write clinical notes in Appointa today, or in a separate EMR? If it's the latter, you're either building an integration or entering EMR territory, competing with incumbents that already own the notes workflow. You'd also take on:
- Health-privacy obligations (PIPEDA, provincial health-privacy acts, Quebec's Law 25), plus data-residency questions with an outside ML partner.
- Clinical accuracy and liability questions.
- A buy-vs-build question: ambient-scribe vendors already exist, so partnering might cost far less than $260k of custom work.

None of this kills the idea, but the memo doesn't acknowledge any of it.

## Did you write what he wants to hear?

A bit, yes. The tell is the word "therefore." The facts before it (three conversations, competitors "moving in this direction") don't lead to "make it the flagship and staff it with a full team." The conclusion came first and the evidence was arranged to support it. That's very normal when the CEO is excited, and it's fixable.

## A structure that keeps AI in without making it everything

Reframe it from "AI vs. the boring stuff" to **"fund what's proven, and run AI as a serious, gated bet."**

**Tier 1: Commitments (fully staffed, non-negotiable)**
- Quebec French-language compliance, protected capacity, owner named, November deadline.

**Tier 2: Proven growth (fully staffed)**
- US insurance eligibility. Attach a revenue estimate: lost US trials × 58% × expected ACV.
- No-show rollout plus fixing reminder reliability (the 17% ticket category). This is cheap, validated, and makes a great customer-facing story: "we cut no-shows by a third."

**Tier 3: AI bet (time-boxed, gated)**
- Small team (e.g., 2 engineers + PM/designer), discovery through end of Q3.
- Work to do:
  - Interview 15–20 clinics across sizes, not just the big three.
  - Confirm where notes actually live today.
  - Test willingness to pay.
  - Complete a privacy/legal review.
  - Evaluate buy vs. partner vs. build before signing a $260k contract.
- **Gate at end of Q3:** if pull is real, scale to full investment in Q4 or H1 with a much stronger case.

**Optional: "AI where the pain already is."** Consider AI applied to problems your data already shows: smarter reminder timing or no-show prediction, intake form parsing and validation, billing error detection. That lets you tell the CEO "we're shipping AI in H2" while pointing it at 50%+ of your ticket volume.

## For the conversation with the CEO

Lead with agreement: "I think AI matters, and I want us to win there." Then position the plan as how to place that bet well, with a defined decision point and real customer evidence behind the bigger investment.

Before you finalize, I'd nail down:
1. What exactly the three customers said, and whether any tied it to renewal or expansion.
2. Which competitors have actually *shipped* AI documentation, versus announced it.
3. The dollar value of the US pipeline the eligibility check would unlock.
4. What the Platform team would stop doing if reassigned.

If you'd like, I can help you redraft the memo itself in this structure.

proposal-07__base.text:
Their feedback is fixable. Your strongest material was in your note to me, not the description: the budget split and the free flat show exactly what the money buys. The original also opened with history and closed with "continue our work and grow," which is the vague framing funders flag. I've moved Tenement to the front, made the outcomes concrete, and used your track record as evidence you can deliver.

I've put **[brackets]** where I didn't have details. Fill them in, because specific numbers are what will answer the funder's concern.

---

**Tenement: a new production devised with residents of three Govan high-rises before their demolition**

In 2025, Ferryhill Players will make *Tenement* with residents of [block names], three high-rise blocks earmarked for demolition in [year]. Once the blocks are gone, the chance to gather these stories where they were lived goes with them.

**Your £24,500 will fund:**

- **[X] oral history workshops** led by a professional facilitator, recording residents' memories of life in the blocks
- **Fees for [X] residents** to take part as paid co-devisers and performers over a [X]-week devising period
- **[X] performances** at [community centre], a short walk from the blocks, with [free/pay-what-you-can] tickets for residents
- **Filmed material** from [workshops/performances], creating a lasting record of the blocks and their community

Around half the budget (£[X]) goes directly on fees for residents and the oral history facilitator. The remainder covers venue hire, production costs and filming. [Housing association name] is providing a flat in one of the blocks rent-free as our workshop space, worth approximately £[X] in kind, so the work happens in residents' own building.

---

That's about 340 words before the placeholders are filled, so you have room. A few things would strengthen it further:
