academic-03__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

The floor didn't destroy jobs. It moved workers from formal into informal employment, and it raised pay in the informal sector they moved into. So informality is not an escape from the minimum wage. It is another channel through which the minimum wage operates.

## The shape that clicked

```
OLD:  Q1 disemployment? ── −1.8%
      Q2 lighthouse?    ── +4.2%        (stapled together in para 3)

NEW:  Floor +14%
        ├─ formal jobs   −1.8% ─┐
        │                       ├─ total ≈ 0  → reallocation, not job loss
        └─ informal jobs +3.1% ─┘
                 └─ informal pay +4.2% → the floor follows workers out
```

The intro reads as two papers because the findings are presented as two answers to two questions. They are one sequence. Your co-author is right that the employment question is the door referees recognise. You are right that the wage result is the contribution. Lead with the employment question, then let the wage result overturn the standard answer to it. Neither finding is subordinated: one sets up the other.

## What moved

- **Total employment unchanged**: from a final bullet to the hinge of the argument. It turns "−1.8%" into "reallocation."
- **Lighthouse literature**: from a parallel paragraph to the explanation of the twist. The citations stay attached to it.
- **"Contributes to both literatures"**: cut. It announces the staple.
- **Conclusion**: should restate the spine, not the two findings.
- **Missing**:
  - Significance or precision for the +3.1%, +4.2% and total-employment results.
  - Evidence that +4.2% is a spillover, not composition. Displaced formal workers may simply earn more. This is the referee objection you most need to answer, e.g. using incumbent informal workers.
  - Citations for the "masked by informality" claim.

## Rebuilt

**¶1** A central question in labour economics is whether minimum wages reduce employment. In developing economies with large informal sectors, the standard answer has two parts [cite]. First, formal disemployment may be masked by movement into informality. Second, informality acts as an escape valve: it preserves jobs, but it places displaced workers beyond the minimum's reach. We study a regional wage floor introduced in 2017 in three northeastern states, which raised the minimum 14% above the national level. We find that the first part of this account holds but the second does not.

**¶2** Using a synthetic control design with RAIS and PNAD data, we find that formal employment among workers earning under 1.5 times the floor fell 1.8%. Informal employment in the same occupations rose 3.1%, leaving total employment essentially unchanged. The floor reallocated workers rather than eliminating jobs. Yet the informal sector did not stand outside the floor: average earnings of informal workers in affected occupations rose 4.2%, though no law required it [precision; composition test]. This is consistent with a "lighthouse effect", whereby statutory minimums act as a reference point for informal wages (Souza 2011; Neri et al. 2015). Movement into informality is therefore not only how disemployment is hidden. It is also how the minimum wage reaches workers the law does not cover.

**¶3 (sketch)** One-sentence contribution built on the spine → identification → [composition result] → roadmap.

proposal-06__base.text:
Your team lead is right, and the problem is specific: **your strongest finding doesn't make it into your recommendation.**

## What's off

**1. Point 6 is your headline, and it's buried.** Recovering commercial losses gets you to 48% with no tariff change. A 20% hike gets you to 37%. That's the most important fact in the note, and it sits at point 6 of 8.

**2. Your options ignore your own evidence.** Points 3, 4 and 6 all point toward fixing losses and supply, but none of your options (a, b, c) addresses that. The analysis builds toward one conclusion and the recommendation picks another.

**3. Option (c) isn't quantified.** You give cost-recovery numbers for the hike and for loss reduction, but not for the option you recommend. The PS will ask.

**4. Point 4 suggests a sequence you haven't drawn out.** Residents will pay more *if supply improves*. So revising tariffs on 1.5 hours of supply on alternate days risks backlash and low collection. Fixing losses and supply first makes a later tariff revision easier to sell.

**5. The PS won't reach the recommendation.** If they read half a page, they'll see background and case studies, then stop.

## Suggested fix

Put the conclusion first and make the options reflect the evidence. Something like:

> **Recommendation:** Prioritise recovery of commercial losses (illegal connections, unmetered supply, billing errors), followed by a shift to telescopic tariffs with a lifeline slab once supply regularity improves.
>
> **Why:** O&M cost recovery is 31%. A 20% across-the-board hike would raise it to only ~37%. Recovering commercial losses alone would raise it to ~48% with no tariff change. Consultations also show residents are willing to pay more if supply becomes regular (currently 1.5 hrs on alternate days). A tariff revision is therefore more effective and more acceptable *after* loss reduction and service improvement.
>
> **Decision sought:** Approval to [launch a commercial loss reduction drive / prepare a phased plan / etc.].

Then revise the options to something like:
- (a) Status quo
- (b) 20% across-the-board hike: ~37%
- (c) Telescopic tariff alone: [add figure]
- (d) Commercial loss reduction, then telescopic tariff: ~48% from losses, plus [X] after tariff revision

Move background, case studies and NRW detail below as supporting material. Keep the case studies, but use them to support the telescopic tariff in phase 2, not as the lead.

**Before you submit:** calculate the cost-recovery figure for telescopic tariffs, and if you can, add a rough timeline or cost for the loss-reduction drive. The PS will likely ask how long it takes and what it needs.

positioning-01__base.text:
The good news is that your copy doesn't need inventing. It needs reordering. The most distinctive material is buried in the third section, and the generic lines at the top are doing the hard work.

**What's going on now**

- **Your best facts are hidden.** "Same three farms since our first order," "fixed $4.10/lb," "2.3x market," and "farmers' names on every bag" are things almost no roaster can say. Right now a visitor has to scroll past "crafted with care" to find them.
- **The sub contradicts you.** "The finest single-origin coffees from around the world" is the opposite of what you do. You buy from three farms in one region. That's a stronger story, and the current line hides it.
- **Vague words are standing in for specifics you already have.** "Ethically sourced" is a claim; "$4.10 a pound, fixed, regardless of market" is proof. "Passion for coffee and community" could be anyone's; "we still buy from the same families" is only yours.

**Suggested order**

1. Hero + sub (the farms, the price, the names)
2. The farms (the sourcing detail, plus no blends)
3. Freshness (Tuesday/Wednesday)
4. Our story (short, tied to the farms)
5. Subscriptions (with the 19-month stat)

---

**HERO** (pick one)

- *Three farms. One fixed price. Every bag since 2019.*
- *We know exactly who grew your coffee. Soon you will too.*
- *Same three farms since our very first bag.*

**SUB**

Every bean we roast comes from three family farms in Huila, Colombia. We've bought from them since day one, we pay them the same fixed price whatever the market does, and their names are printed on every bag.

---

**THE FARMS**

**$4.10 a pound. Fixed.**

Coffee prices swing with the commodity market, and farmers usually wear the risk. We don't play that game. We pay [Farmer 1], [Farmer 2] and [Farmer 3] $4.10 USD per pound, every harvest, no matter what the market is doing. In [year], that was about 2.3 times the market price.

We visit every harvest. We know their families, their plots and what each lot tastes like before it's roasted.

**No blends. Ever.**

Blending is a good way to smooth out a coffee and a good way to hide where it came from. We'd rather you taste each farm for what it is. Now and then we bring in a guest lot when something too good to pass up comes along, and we'll tell you exactly where it's from.

---

**FRESHNESS**

**Roasted Tuesday. On its way Wednesday.**

We roast once a week and ship the next morning, so your beans leave us within 24 hours of roasting.

---

**OUR STORY**

Ridgeline started in a Brunswick garage in 2019, two mates and a roaster that barely fit. Our very first green coffee order came from three families in Huila.

We've grown since then and now roast for cafes and home brewers across Melbourne. The farms haven't changed.

---

**SUBSCRIPTIONS**

**Our subscribers stay for 19 months on average.**

Most of them found us because a friend handed them a bag. Choose your roast, choose how often, and pause anytime.

---

**A few notes before you publish**

- **Farmer names:** Check the farmers are happy to be named (and photographed, if you add photos) on the website, not just the bag. Real names and faces in the farms section would be the strongest thing on the page.
- **The 2.3x figure:** Put the year next to it and update it annually. If the market spikes one year, the multiple drops, and an undated claim can go stale.
- **The 19-month stat:** I left out your supplier's "wildly high for the category" because it's hearsay you can't source. The number is strong on its own.
- **Word of mouth:** 60% is "most," so the subscriptions line is accurate. If you have permission, a short testimonial there would fit well.
- **Subscription options:** Since you only roast three farms, consider letting people "choose your farm" instead of "choose your roast." It reinforces everything above it.

If you'd like, send me the bottom half of the page and I'll keep it in the same voice.

team-02__base.text:
Your manager's right, but you're closer than you think. The facts are all here. What's missing is the **analysis**: *why* each thing happened and what in the *system* allowed it. That's also how you avoid blaming the reviewer.

## The blame concern

Blameless doesn't mean leaving out what happened. It means asking "why did the process make this easy to miss?" instead of "why did this person miss it?"

The reviewer checking only YAML syntax isn't a personal failure. It's evidence that:
- Nothing in the PR made it obvious the change would hit prod
- There's no expectation (or tooling) for semantic review of config changes
- One approval from a teammate was enough to change prod config on sale day

Write it that way and nobody's named. Honestly, a reviewer in that situation would almost always miss it, which is exactly the point.

## The freeze delay is highly relevant

25 of the 93 minutes, roughly a quarter of the outage, was spent waiting for permission to *fix* the problem. And it raises a sharp question you should check before Wednesday: **did the 17:05 config change go through the freeze process?** If config changes bypassed the freeze but the revert didn't, the freeze blocked the fix and not the cause. The CTO will care about that a lot.

## What to add: contributing factors

Something like this, framed as a chain:

1. **Root cause:** staging and prod share a values file, so a staging change was applied to prod. This is the real fix target.
2. **Review didn't catch it:** the PR diff didn't show which environments were affected; no rendered per-env diff; no required owner review for prod config.
3. **Latent until peak load:** pool size 20 was fine for ~2.5 hours, then failed when sale traffic ramped. Nothing alerted on pool saturation *before* users were affected.
4. **Slow diagnosis (49 min to find the change):** "check recent changes" isn't an early runbook step, and config changes may not be visible in a deploy log/channel. You found it because someone happened to ask. That's luck, not process.
5. **Restart was ineffective:** the bad config persisted across restarts, so it only bought temporary relief.
6. **Slow mitigation (25 min):** reverts required the same freeze exception approval as new changes.

## Better action items

Each should have an **owner, a due date, and a type** (prevent / detect / mitigate). Examples:

| Action | Type | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| Split staging/prod values files (or enforce env overlays) so one change can't hit both | Prevent | | |
| CI posts rendered per-env diff on config PRs; flag changes to prod | Prevent | | |
| Require CODEOWNERS approval for prod config changes | Prevent | | |
| Clarify whether config changes are covered by sale-day freeze; close the gap if not | Prevent | | |
| Alert on DB connection pool utilization >80% for orders-svc (and other critical svcs) | Detect | | |
| Post all deploys *and config changes* to a #deploys channel | Detect | | |
| Runbook: "check changes in last 24h" as step 1-2 for any error spike | Detect | | |
| Pre-approve rollbacks/reverts during freezes; no exception process needed | Mitigate | | |

Drop "add more dashboards." It's not tied to anything that went wrong.

## Restructure

1. **Summary** (3–4 sentences: what broke, why, impact, duration). The CTO may only read this.
2. **Impact** (you have this; add duration and maybe peak error rate)
3. **Root cause & contributing factors** (the list above)
4. **Response analysis:** time to detect, to diagnose, and to mitigate. Break the 93 min down: ~49 min to find cause, ~10 min to start the revert, ~25 min waiting on approval, ~10 min to deploy and recover.
5. **What went well:** be specific. "Rohan identified pool exhaustion within 30 min" beats "team jumped in fast."
6. **What went wrong / where we got lucky:** "found the config change because someone asked in channel" belongs here.
7. **Action items** (table)
8. **Appendix: timeline** (your current doc, nearly as-is)

One more thing: as the on-call, don't let the doc read as self-criticism about the gateway red herring. Checking the gateway first was reasonable. The fix is a runbook that points people at recent changes sooner, not "I should have known."

business-decision-10__base.text:
Here's a layout built to keep Sunday calm. Before the numbers, one suggestion that might matter more than any of them:

## Change the question

Right now the argument is "shop or trade." Your dad hears "abandon the shop" and digs in. Your numbers don't actually support abandoning anything: retail is still two-thirds of turnover. So reframe it as:

**"Keep the shop exactly as it is. Grow the trade side alongside it. Trial it for six months and let the numbers decide."**

Also worth saying out loud: those 23 trade accounts are mostly *dad's* relationships. The trade plan is built on what he created, not a rejection of it.

## The sums

### Step 1: Gross profit (the bit that makes trade look weak)

| | Turnover | Margin | Gross profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail | £410k | 31% | **£127k** |
| Trade | £190k | 24% | **£46k** |

Get this on the table first, before your dad does. It shows you're not hiding anything.

### Step 2: What each side costs to serve (the bit you haven't proven yet)

Retail has costs trade mostly doesn't. Trade has a few of its own. **I've used made-up placeholder figures below. Your sister needs to fill in the real ones before Sunday.**

| | Retail | Trade |
|---|---|---|
| Gross profit | £127k | £46k |
| Floor staff time | –£40k *(guess)* | – |
| Shrinkage (often 1–2% of sales) | –£6k *(guess)* | – |
| Returns / damaged stock | –£3k *(guess)* | ~£0 |
| Credit terms, chasing invoices, bad debt | – | –£2k *(guess)* |
| **What's left** | **~£78k (19p per £1 sold)** | **~£44k (23p per £1 sold)** |

If the real numbers look anything like this, your instinct is right: **each pound of trade sales is worth slightly more than a pound of retail, once you count everything.** But it's a modest edge, not a landslide. Don't oversell it on Sunday, because if dad catches one inflated number he'll dismiss the rest.

One honest caveat: floor staff cost doesn't disappear if trade grows. You're keeping the shop open. So the argument isn't "trade saves us staff costs." It's "**new** trade sales don't **add** staff costs the way new retail sales would."

### Step 3: The number nobody's said yet

Running costs per year if you do it the full way:

- Van (£14k spread over ~5 years): ~£3k
- Insurance, fuel, servicing: ~£5–6k
- Driver: £13k
- Website (say £6k spread over 3 years): ~£2k
- **Total: roughly £23–24k a year**

At 24% margin, **you need about £100k of extra trade sales a year just to cover that.** That's trade turnover growing by more than half before it makes you a penny.

This isn't a reason not to do it, but you need to know it before dad or your sister works it out. It's also why I'd push for a smaller start.

## Ways to make the maths easier

- **Charge for delivery**, or deliver free only above a minimum order (e.g. £150). Trades expect this.
- **Driver does shop shifts** between runs. That's part of £13k you're not paying someone else.
- **Start cheap on the website.** You don't need £18k. A basic B2B order form, or even WhatsApp Business with a product list, proves whether trades will use it. Your customers are already texting you orders; formalise that first.
- **Test delivery before buying a van.** Hire one for a couple of days a week, or use your own vehicle for small drops, to see if the 6 who asked actually order.
- **Count the defensive value.** If those trades start getting next-day delivery from a big merchant, some of that £190k drifts away. Delivery may be partly about keeping what you have.

## A proposal for Sunday

1. **Nothing changes in the shop.** Same hours, same staff, same stock.
2. **Six-month trade trial:** delivery to the 6 who asked, cheap ordering system, delivery fee or minimum order.
3. **Track three numbers monthly:** trade turnover, number of delivery orders, delivery cost per order.
4. **Agree now what success looks like**, e.g. "if trade is up 25% by month six, we buy the van." Then nobody has to argue about it later.

## The one-pager for dad

Print this. Keep it to one sheet:

> **The shop isn't going anywhere.**
>
> - Shop sales are down £58k since 2021. That's about £18k less profit a year, mostly since the warehouse opened.
> - Trade customers already bring in £190k, and they're people Dad brought in.
> - Six of them have asked us to deliver.
> - After costs like staff time and shoplifting, a pound from trade is worth about the same as a pound from the shop, maybe a bit more.
> - A van and driver costs about £24k a year, so we'd test it small first.
>
> **Proposal:** try delivery for 6 months with the trades who asked. Check the numbers together every month. Decide on the van in the summer.

## Before Sunday

- **Ask your sister for the real figures for Step 2 this week.** Floor staff hours, stock write-offs, unpaid trade invoices. Bringing her in early gets her invested in the numbers instead of stuck between you and dad.
- **Ask dad what he's worried about** before the meeting, not during it. If it's "the shop closing," step 1 of the proposal answers that. If it's something else, like losing touch with the community or the shop being his legacy, better to know now.
- **Let him suggest something.** If he wants a condition ("the shop gets new signage too" or "we check in after three months"), take it. A plan he helped shape is one he'll back.

If you send over the real figures from your sister, I can redo the tables with them.

business-decision-07__base.text:
## Why the current draft feels like begging

- **It justifies the increase with your costs.** Insurance, certification and software are your business expenses, not reasons for a client to pay more. They make the email about your needs.
- **It apologises in advance.** "I completely understand budgets are tight," "after a lot of reflection," and "thank you so much for understanding" all signal that you expect them to be upset.
- **"Slightly" works against you.** This is a 33% increase. Calling it slight invites them to do the maths and feel misled. It's better not to characterise it at all.
- **"Happy to discuss if it causes any difficulty" invites negotiation.** It reads as "this is my opening offer."
- **Your strongest point is buried.** Cutting turnaround on long contracts by 30% is a real benefit *to them*, but it's presented as one of your costs.

## Rewrite (for most clients)

**Subject:** Updated rates from 1 March

Dear [name],

Thank you for another year of working together. I particularly enjoyed [project] last autumn.

I'm writing to let you know that from 1 March my rates will be:

- Standard: €0.12 per word
- Urgent: €0.16 per word

This is my first rate change since 2021. Since then I've expanded what I offer: I now regularly handle certified translations for court proceedings, and my specialised EU competition law terminology resources have reduced turnaround on long contracts by around 30%.

Any project already under way, or quoted before 1 March, will be invoiced at my current rates.

I look forward to continuing to work with you, and I'm happy to talk if you have any questions.

Best regards,
Lucía

One practical point: give at least 4–6 weeks' notice. If 1 March is closer than that, move the date to 1 April rather than squeezing it.

## Should all 11 get the same email?

**The 9 smaller clients (including the notaries):** Yes, send the same email, personalised with the name and a project reference.

**The two big firms:** No. Treat them differently. Here's what I'd suggest:

1. **Call or meet before you email.** A short conversation ("I wanted to tell you personally before I send anything in writing") shows they matter to you. It also lets you gauge their reaction. Then send a written confirmation.
2. **Consider a loyalty arrangement, framed as a thank-you rather than a concession.** For example, you could add this paragraph to their version:

   > *Because of the volume and continuity of our work together, I'd like to offer [Firm] a preferential rate of €0.11 standard / €0.15 urgent until 31 December, with my standard rates applying from 1 January.*

   Or you could simply give them a later start date (for example 1 June). Either way, you raise your rates, and they get a reason to feel valued instead of squeezed.
3. **Decide your floor before the conversation.** If they push back, know in advance what you'll accept (perhaps €0.11 permanently) and what you won't. That way you're not deciding under pressure.

## Some perspective on the fear

At €0.12 instead of €0.09, you earn the same total income even if your volume drops by **25%**, and you'd be working fewer hours for it. Law firms are used to periodic rate increases from their suppliers; many raise their own fees every year. After more than three years at the same rate, an increase is expected and normal.

You've drafted this six times over two months. The email is ready. The best thing now is to pick a send date, schedule the two calls, and send it.

positioning-07__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Foreign companies hire Mendes & Prado for its results, and the founders' experience is the reason those results exist.

## The shape that clicked

```
NOW:   Tradition → Partners → Values → Practice areas → Results
       (asks for admiration first, gives proof last)

NEW:   The reader's problem: "a claim just arrived"
               ↓
       Results: what this firm does about it
               ↓
       Partners: the people who make those results possible
               ↓
       Practice areas → Values (shown, not just listed)
```

The current page treats the founders and the results as two separate things. They are one thing: the numbers are the proof of the founders' seniority. Once you see that, the partners don't move down. They become the answer to the question the results create: *who does this?*

## What moved

- **Results**: last → first section. This is what the reader came for.
- **24-hour response in English, Spanish or German**: from the results list → subheadline. It answers the first, most anxious question.
- **Partners**: second → right after results, introduced as "the people behind these numbers." Full bios go on their own page.
- **Values**: a list of words → proof. The 24-hour response *is* Proximity, and publishing the numbers *is* Transparency.
- **Cut from the top**: "tradition, excellence and commitment." Every firm says this. "Since 1998" says it with a fact.
- **Missing**:
  - Please ask the firm to confirm that publishing these statistics follows OAB advertising rules, and whether they want a "past results do not guarantee future outcomes" note. They will know the rules better than anyone.
  - The contact method for the call to action.
  - The medal's English name, plus one line explaining it for foreign readers.

## Rebuilt

### Homepage top

**Headline** (choose one)
- A. *Brazilian labour law surprises foreign companies. It doesn't surprise us.*
- B. *Labour claims in Brazil, resolved before they reach trial.*

I recommend A. It speaks to the reader's real experience, and it quietly honours the firm's long history, which may help with Dr. Ricardo.

**Subheadline**
Mendes & Prado defends the Brazilian subsidiaries of foreign companies in labour disputes. When a new claim arrives, you hear from us within 24 hours, in English, Spanish or German.

**[Button: Received a claim? Talk to us → [contact method]]**

**First section: What we achieve for our clients**

| | |
|---|---|
| **400+** | labour claims defended for foreign subsidiaries since 2015 |
| **82%** | resolved by settlement or dismissal before reaching trial |
| **67%** | average reduction between the amount claimed and the amount paid |
| **24 hours** | maximum response time to every new claim notification, in English, Spanish or German |

*Behind these numbers are the two partners who founded the firm in 1998.*
→ leads straight into **Dr. Ricardo Albuquerque Mendes** and **Dr. Helena Vasconcelos Prado** (photo, two or three lines each, and "Read full profile").

### Arguments for Dr. Ricardo

You could open the conversation with: *"I want the partners to be the reason clients believe the results, not a page they scroll past."*

1. **"You would never open a defence with your CV."** In court, he leads with his strongest argument and lets his credentials support it. A homepage works the same way. This analogy comes from his own profession, so he will likely respect it.

2. **Your reader arrives worried, not curious.** A US or European HR director has just received a claim they don't understand. Their first question is "can you help me, and how fast?" Prestige matters a lot, but it confirms the decision. It doesn't start it.

3. **The partners are promoted, not hidden.** Today they are introduced with general words. In the new version, they are introduced as the people responsible for 82% and 67%. That is a stronger tribute.

4. **Foreign readers can't judge Brazilian prestige alone.** They may not recognise the universities or the state bar medal. They do recognise "67% less paid." The results translate the partners' reputation for an international reader.

5. **The values become believable.** English-speaking readers often skip lists of values because every firm has them. A 24-hour response in three languages *proves* Proximity in a way the word alone cannot.

6. **A compromise if he resists:** keep "Since 1998" and both partners' names in the subheadline, and place the partner section immediately after the numbers, with photos.

(Your English is excellent, by the way.)

team-01__base.text:
The main issue is that the actual news doesn't appear until paragraph four. Readers wade through context without knowing what it's context *for*, which is why your co-founder had to reread it. The fix is to lead with the change and follow with the reasons.

---

**Subject:** Platform is moving into the product domains on 1 November

Team,

Starting 1 November, the Platform team will no longer be a standalone group. Its engineers are joining the four product domains, and each domain will own its own infrastructure. **Nobody is losing their job.**

Here's what that looks like:

- **Platform's 14 engineers** will join Payments, Lending, Onboarding and Risk, three or four per domain.
- **A Developer Experience group of 3**, led by Joost, will keep looking after shared tooling and CI.
- **If you're on Platform**, your manager will reach out this week to talk through where you're headed.

**Why we're doing this**

In eighteen months we've gone from 60 to 140 engineers. Some of how we work has scaled well, and some hasn't. In the last two engagement surveys, you told us that ownership of shared infrastructure feels unclear, and that product teams often wait on Platform for things they could do themselves.

The numbers back that up. The average Platform ticket now takes 11 working days, up from 4 a year ago. That's not on the Platform team. It's what happens when one team of 14 sits between 140 engineers and their infrastructure. The structure is the bottleneck, not the people.

We spent Q3 talking to leads across the org and looking at how other companies handled this stage. There's no perfect answer, but moving infrastructure ownership into the domains came up again and again.

**Questions**

Change like this is hard, and you'll have questions. We're running an AMA on Thursday at [time / link]. Bring anything.

Finally, I'm proud of what we've built: two new markets and a new payments ledger. Thank you, especially, to everyone who made the ledger migration happen.

Marieke

---

**On the 11-days stat:** I'd keep it. It's your clearest evidence that this isn't arbitrary. But in your draft it comes right after "teams wait on platform," so it does read like a scorecard for Platform. The fix is to frame it explicitly as a structural problem, which I've done above. If Platform did heavy lifting on the ledger or the Belgium/Germany launches, naming that specifically would help too.

**A few other things to check before Monday:**

1. **The numbers might confuse people.** Your draft says all 14 Platform engineers join domains *and* a DX group of 3 remains. Are those 3 part of the 14 (so 11 move), or separate? Readers will notice, so make it explicit.
2. **Platform should hear first.** If those 14 people learn this from an org-wide email, it will land badly no matter how it's written. Ideally they get a team meeting or individual conversations before Monday.
3. **"Managers will reach out this week"** was ambiguous in the original. I assumed you meant Platform engineers. If domain teams are also getting conversations, say so.
4. **Fill in the AMA time and link.** Otherwise "Thursday" just generates a pile of DMs.

team-09__base.text:
Your COO is right, and the fix is mostly reordering. You already have the material for a strong case. It's just arranged in the order you *discovered* things rather than the order the committee needs to *decide* things.

## The core problem

Your paper currently builds toward the recommendation: background, features, costs, evidence, options, and then the answer on the last line. That's a research narrative. A decision paper should work the other way: **answer first, then the reasons, then the detail.**

There's also a second issue. The feature table sits in position 2, so the first substantive thing the committee reads is "LexVault scores highest on 9 of 14." That frames the whole decision as "which software is nicer?" Partners attached to DocuNest can easily argue with that, and cost-sensitive partners will reasonably ask why nicer software is worth SGD 155k more.

Your strongest material is buried in sections 4 and 5: **the firm is losing roughly SGD 9–10M a year in non-billable time and has had two near-misses on outdated precedents.** That's the story. The software choice is just the solution to it.

## Suggested structure

**1. Recommendation and decision required (one short paragraph)**
State the ask up front: approve Option A, consolidating on LexVault, at a net incremental cost of X, over 18 months. If they read nothing else, they know what you want.

**2. The problem: what our current setup costs us**
- Time study: 4.6 hrs/week average, 6.1 in Bangkok and Jakarta, 31% failure rate on cross-office matters
- The SGD 9–10M figure, with the arithmetic shown in one line
- The two near-misses, framed as professional risk (PI exposure, client trust)

Fold your Background section in here as a single sentence, e.g. "We currently run three systems that don't talk to each other, and this is what that costs us." The background matters only because it causes the problem.

**3. Options considered**
Assess A, B and C against **3–4 criteria that matter to this decision**, not all 14. For example:
- Does it fix cross-office findability?
- Does it give a single authoritative version of precedents? (This addresses the near-miss risk.)
- Total cost
- Implementation risk and disruption

This is where you show why B and C fall short. C doesn't address the cross-office problem at all. B's federated search is likely to leave the version-control risk in place, because two systems can still hold divergent copies of a precedent. That point does more work than any feature score.

**4. Cost and return**
Make this its own short section, because it's what the cost-sensitive partners will go straight to. See the numbers notes below.

**5. Risks and how we'll manage them**
Your implementation, change management and timeline material goes here, framed as "here's what could go wrong and how we'll handle it." That reads as competence rather than caveats.

**6. Next steps**
What happens in the first 90 days if they approve.

**Appendices:** full 14-criteria feature table, time study methodology, detailed timeline. Keep the table. It's evidence you did the work. It just shouldn't lead.

## On the numbers

**Lead with net cost, not gross.** If Option A retires DocuNest, the licence increase isn't SGD 155k. It's roughly 465k − 310k − 95k = **about SGD 60k/yr**. Please verify that the 465k full-rollout estimate actually covers Jakarta. If it does, that is a very different headline for a cost-sensitive committee.

**Gaps to fill before this goes to committee:**
- **One-off costs** for Option A: migration, implementation, training, any backfill for lost productivity during transition. The committee will ask, and their absence will undermine you.
- **Option B's cost.** Federated search isn't free, and if it's expensive, that strengthens your case.

**Don't claim SGD 9–10M as a saving.** That figure measures the problem, not the benefit. Recovered time won't all become billable, and a sceptical partner will say so. Instead, use a conservative return case, something like: "If consolidation recovers even one hour per associate per week, that's worth roughly SGD 2M a year, many times the incremental cost." A deliberately cautious number that still clears the bar easily is more persuasive than a large one that invites argument.

**Be upfront about the time study's limits.** It covered 36 associates over two weeks. Say so in a line, and note that even at half the measured figure the case holds. Pre-empting the challenge is better than having it raised.

## Handling the DocuNest partners

This is as much about process as about the paper.

- **In the paper:** acknowledge what DocuNest does well, and make clear the problem is fragmentation across three systems, not DocuNest itself. Be careful with the Jakarta near-misses. Present them as a consequence of having no single authoritative version across the firm, not as a Jakarta failing, or you'll put those partners on the defensive in front of their colleagues.
- **Before the meeting:** talk to both partners individually. Walk them through the time study, ask what they'd need to see in a transition, and offer a role in shaping the Jakarta rollout (e.g. preserving workflows they value, sequencing, a Jakarta champion). Partners who've been consulted in advance are far less likely to oppose in the room, and you may learn about objections you can address in the paper.

## A possible opening paragraph

> *I recommend we consolidate all offices onto LexVault over 18 months, at a net incremental licence cost of approximately SGD 60k per year plus one-off implementation costs of SGD [X]. Our three disconnected systems are costing us significantly: an August time study found associates spend 4.6 hours a week searching for or recreating precedents, rising to 6.1 hours in Bangkok and Jakarta, and on cross-office matters fail to find the document they need almost a third of the time. We have also had two near-misses this year involving outdated precedent versions. Consolidation is the only option that addresses both the lost time and the version-control risk.*

That paragraph does the work your current page and a half of build-up is trying to do. Everything after it is supporting evidence.

talk-07__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Your best collection was invisible, three different methods each found the same reason, and making it visible raised second-floor visits from about 36% to 59% in six weeks.

## The shape that clicked

```
        THE MYSTERY: 64% never see the second floor
                          |
     ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
  TRACKING            INTERVIEWS              APP
  what they did      what they knew      what the tool showed
  64% never up       58% didn't know      7% reached 2nd floor;
                     "staff-only" door    map hides 2nd floor
     └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
        ONE CAUSE: physical + digital invisibility
                          |
        THE FIX → 36% → 59%  → limits & next questions
```

Right now the talk is organised by method, so each part is a small fact with no question attached. If you organise it by the question, each method becomes a clue, and the methods become the most interesting part. Your three studies are not three findings. They are one finding seen three ways, and for an academic audience that is triangulation, a strength you should show.

## What moved

- **The 64% figure**: from inside Part 1 → the opening, as the question.
- **Methods**: from separate parts → three "clues," each with its method in one slide. The detail stays, but now it has a purpose.
- **Fix and results**: from the reward at the end → the answer to the question, around minute 12.
- **Satisfaction 4.3/5**: kept as a twist. Visitors were happy and didn't know what they missed.
- **Cut or moved to backup slide**: café prices, 38 seconds per artwork, temporary-room dwell time, the entrance-hall audio stop. They are true but off the spine.
- **Missing**:
  - What your limitations actually are.
  - How the 59% was measured (same method as the 36%?).
  - Whether the summer season affects the comparison.
  - Whether the tracking result is why you added the azulejo question to the interviews. That would be a great detail to include.

## Rebuilt

**1. The mystery (0–2 min).** Opening, in full:

> "Our museum has a collection of 18th-century azulejos that we are very proud of. Last spring we discovered that most of our visitors never see it. 64% never go to the second floor. More than half don't know the collection exists. Today I want to show you how three different methods led us to the same, surprisingly simple, reason, what we changed, and what happened next."

**2. Three methods, one question (2–3 min).** One slide shows the timeline: tracking (Feb–Mar, 212 visitors), exit interviews (April, 180 interviews), and app analytics (Jan–June, 9,400 sessions). Say what each method can and cannot see.

**3. Clue 1, what visitors did (3–6 min).** Tracking results. Median visit 47 minutes. 64% never reached the second floor. Briefly explain your method: observers, sampling, [how routes were recorded].

**4. Clue 2, what visitors knew (6–9 min).** Satisfaction was 4.3/5, and still 58% didn't know the azulejos existed. Then the quotes: they thought the staircase was "for staff" because of the heavy wooden door and the small sign. This is your emotional centre, so slow down here.

**5. Clue 3, what the app showed (9–11 min).** Only 7% of sessions reached a second-floor stop. The map was used in 31% of sessions, but it hid the second floor by default. The building and the app made the same mistake.

**6. The fix (11–15 min).** In July you replaced the door with glass, added an "Azulejos ↑" sign, and changed the map to show both floors. Visits to the second floor went from about 36% to 59% in 6 weeks. [Measurement method] [any app data after the change].

**7. Limitations and what's next (15–19 min).** [Your limitations]: only six weeks of data, [season], [which change did what], [next study].

**8. Close (19–20 min).** Come back to the opening: "Our visitors were satisfied. They just didn't know what they were missing. Sometimes the barrier is a door."

talk-03__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
For these teens, heritage-language words do social work rather than informational work: they mean "this is just us," and every finding shows it from a different angle.

## The shape that clicked

```
            CLAIM: heritage words = an in-group marker
                    ("when it's just us")
                 /            |              \
     WHAT gets switched   WHEN it appears    WHO uses it, and HOW
     food, family,        falls ~70% when    non-speakers (7/15)
     teasing, excl.       an adult joins     cross-borrowing
     teasing: 3.1 vs 1.2  2.3x after 11pm    no fixed spelling
```

Your list was a row of findings with no center. "Performance vs actual communication" is a false split, and a room of sociolinguists will attack it, because performance *is* communication. Put "in-group marker" at the center instead, and the findings sort into three questions: what, when, who. Late night now fits as one of the "just us" moments, alongside "no adults present."

## What moved
- **Late night**: orphan → paired with the adult-added finding, under "when." It is supporting evidence, not load-bearing, because time of night may be confounded with who is online and what they are talking about.
- **"Can't really speak it" (7/15)**: buried → the opening hook.
- **Cross-borrowing**: trivia → strongest evidence. If this were about heritage, Punjabi-background kids wouldn't use "aiyah."
- **Spelling**: trivia → under "how." No written standard is needed when the word works as a signal.
- **82% English matrix**: context slide. It shows heritage words are inserted into English, not used as the main language of the chat.
- **Cut**: anonymization methods. Keep one line in the talk and move the rest to backup slides for Q&A. It's a separate paper.
- **Missing**:
  - Do teasing messages in English also get high reacts? Without that comparison, the 3.1 figure could just mean teasing gets reactions.
  - Your theoretical framing. Check the work on "crossing" (Rampton) and emblematic language use.
  - A so-what for the field.

## Rebuilt (20 min)

1. **Hook (2 min).** "7 of 15 said they can't really speak their heritage language. They use it in chat constantly." Pose the question: what is it doing?
2. **Data (2 min).** 11 chats, ~38k messages, ages 14–17, Toronto, three language pairs. 82% of mixed messages have English as the matrix language. One line on anonymization.
3. **Claim (1 min).** The spine sentence, plus your interview quote: "when it's just us."
4. **What gets switched (3 min).** Food, family terms, teasing, exclamations. Teasing switches get 3.1 reacts vs 1.2 baseline. [English-teasing comparison]
5. **When it appears (3 min).** Switching falls ~70% for two weeks after an aunt is added. It runs 2.3x higher after 11pm. Both are moments where the audience is only peers.
6. **Who uses it, and how (3 min).** Non-speakers use it. Kids borrow each other's heritage words. "kain/kaen/kayn" all appear in one chat.
7. **Objection (3 min).** "Isn't this just low proficiency?" Proficiency explains *which* words kids have. It doesn't explain *when* they use them or why kids from other backgrounds borrow them. Be upfront about the limits: the adult finding comes from 2 chats, and the event-planning topic also changed.
8. **So what (2 min).** [Implication, e.g. for how heritage-language maintenance is measured beyond proficiency]
9. **Backup slides.** Anonymization methods.

proposal-05__base.text:
## The short answer

I'd recommend neither A nor B as the primary option. The items your committee set aside could cover most or all of the $96,000 without eliminating either program. Before the 15th, I'd verify those numbers and lead with a third option, keeping A vs. B as the fallback.

## Why A vs. B is a weak choice

- **Option B doesn't solve the problem.** It leaves a $35k gap, so you'd still need more cuts.
- **Option B may cost more than it saves.** If several families move kids to Kindersley, the enrollment-based funding you lose could eat into the $61k. That's worth raising explicitly.
- **Option A hits the number but costs the most.** It removes a program for 74 students (about a quarter of your school) and a major community event. It's hard to reverse; rebuilding a band program after instruments and kids scatter takes years.

## The numbers on the set-aside items

| Item | Potential savings | Status |
|---|---|---|
| New bus carrier | ~$40,000 | Informal quote only |
| Reading software | Up to $27,000 | Could cancel or renegotiate |
| Shared music teacher with Eston | Maybe $30–45k (if 0.8 FTE → ~0.4 FTE) | Floated, never pursued |
| **Total** | **~$97,000–112,000** | |

That reaches the target on paper. Each item needs a reality check:

1. **Bus contract.** Confirm whether you actually control it. In many Saskatchewan divisions, transportation is a division-level contract, and savings might not flow to your school's budget. If it is yours, get a formal written quote this week and check the new carrier's safety record, route coverage, and winter reliability. A $40k saving means nothing if kids are stranded in January.
2. **Reading software.** Be careful here. "Only grades 1–3 use it" may mean it's doing exactly its job, since early literacy is where intervention matters most. Rather than cutting it, ask the vendor about a K–3-only license, which might save $10–15k while keeping what works. Talk to your primary teachers before proposing anything.
3. **Shared music teacher.** Call the Eston principal now. Even an "we're open to exploring it" gives the board a credible path. This keeps band alive in reduced form instead of killing it.

If the verified numbers come up short, you can close a smaller gap with a partial version of B, such as trimming travel instead of eliminating it. That's far less contentious than a full cut.

## Before you send anything

Loop in your staff committee. They narrowed it to A and B, and if you go to the board with something different, they should hear it from you first. Ask why these items were excluded; there may be a reason you don't know, like the bus contract being out of your hands. Framing it as "following up on ideas we raised" keeps them on side.

## Writing it so it doesn't blow up

The board is split "along the usual lines," probably arts vs. athletics. Your memo's main job is to keep it from becoming that fight.

**Suggested structure:**

1. **The shared goal (1 paragraph).** "We need $96,000 in savings while protecting as many student opportunities as possible."
2. **What we examined.** List all five items, including A and B, so no one feels their program was singled out or ignored.
3. **Recommendation: operational savings first.** Present the bus, software, and shared-staffing package with verified numbers and honest caveats. Lead with the dollars, not the programs.
4. **Fallback if those don't materialize.** State plainly that if the operational savings fall short, the committee's original options remain, and lay out the trade-offs neutrally, including B's funding gap and enrollment risk.
5. **Next steps and timeline.** Formal bus quote by X, Eston conversation by Y, vendor response by Z.

**Tone tips:**
- Don't call either program "less important." Talk about students affected and dollars saved.
- Acknowledge the community side of both: the Regina trip *and* the role of senior sports in a small town.
- Be upfront that some numbers are preliminary. Overstating them will hurt your credibility if they slip later.
- If you can, brief the board chair, or one member from each "side," before the meeting so no one is blindsided.

## If you truly must pick A or B

On the numbers alone, A is the only one that meets the target. But given how much is sitting in that "didn't include" list, I'd push hard not to be in that position. A few phone calls this week could change the whole conversation.

If you'd like, I can help draft the memo or the talking points for the meeting.

talk-08__base.text:
## The thread: same ocean, two outcomes

Your strongest result isn't a loss or a hope. It's a **comparison**. The co-managed sites went through the same heatwaves as everywhere else and came out differently. That's close to a natural experiment, and it gives you a story with tension and a reveal. So instead of building up losses and appending the good news, set up two paths from the very first minute and follow both.

This also places the fishers at the centre of the result rather than in a closing "what you can do" slide. The message becomes: *we can't turn down the ocean's temperature from Valparaíso, but the things within local reach (harvesting, urchins) turned out to decide whether a forest survived the heat.*

## Proposed structure (15 minutes)

**1. Opening: two dives, one week (0:00–2:00)**
Two sites during the 2023 heatwave: one a forest, one a barren. Don't explain why yet. Pose the question the talk will answer.

**2. What we'd lose (2:00–4:00)**
Make the kelp forest vivid rather than listing functions. Ask who has seen *huiro* washed up on the beach. Pick two or three relatable residents: a fish people eat, juveniles sheltering in the canopy. Nursery habitat is your best concept here, because it connects to tomorrow's catch.

**3. The heat hit everyone (4:00–5:30)**
Methods in one sentence: "For eight years, twice a year, we dove the same 14 places and counted." Then the heatwaves. A 0.4°C average will sound trivial to a general audience, so lead with the heatwaves as events, and if the fishers noticed the 2023 warm water, say so. Establish clearly that *every site* experienced them. That sets up the reveal.

**4. Path one: the open-access coast (5:30–8:30)**
Tell it as a chain of events, not a list of results. Export prices rose, harvesting increased, the forest thinned, urchins moved in, and then the heatwaves hit a forest that was already weakened. Use three numbers at most: about half the kelp gone, urchins tripled, fish species from 21 to 13. Show one barren photo and let it sit.

**5. Path two: the caleta (8:30–12:00)**
This is the heart of the talk, so give it the most time. Explain what the fishers actually do: restrict harvest, dive to remove urchins. Show photos of them at work if you can. Then the results (kelp up 18%, fish steady at about 20 species) and the reveal: *same heatwaves*. If they agree, name them, invite them to stand, or play a short recorded comment from one of them.

**6. Why keeping beats replanting (12:00–13:30)**
The restoration trial fits here and strengthens the argument. Even with care, only about 30% of transplanted kelp survived a year. Restoration is slow, hard, and worth pursuing, but an existing forest is far easier to keep than a new one is to grow. That's exactly what the caleta has been doing.

**7. What you can do (13:30–15:00)**
Keep it short and concrete. Buy from local caletas, support management areas, report illegal harvesting (with a number or channel to do so). End by returning to the two dive sites from your opening.

## Draft opening (about 2 minutes spoken)

> In the autumn of 2023, the sea off this coast was warmer than almost anyone could remember. And in the space of one week, I made two dives.
>
> The first was at [site]. I went down expecting what I'd seen there for years: a forest. Kelp, *huiro*, taller than a person, swaying in the current, with fish weaving between the stalks. Instead I found rock. Bare, pale rock, covered in black sea urchins. Hundreds of them. No forest, almost no fish. Just urchins, and silence.
>
> A few days later I dove at [site], [not far away / a short distance up the coast]. Same ocean. Same heatwave. Same warm water. And I swam into a forest so thick I had to push my way through it. Fish everywhere. Young ones hiding in the kelp, the way they're supposed to.
>
> Two places. Same sea, same heat. One forest gone, one forest thriving.
>
> For eight years, my team and I have been diving fourteen sites along this coast, counting kelp, counting urchins, counting fish. And for a lot of that time, the story we were recording was a sad one. I'll tell you that story, because it matters.
>
> But the real question of this talk is about the difference between those two dives. Why did one forest survive the heat when the other didn't?
>
> The answer isn't something we found in a laboratory. It's something people from a caleta not far from here have been doing with their own hands, underwater, for years. Some of them might be in this room tonight.
>
> So let's start with what a kelp forest actually is, and why it's worth fighting for.

## A few notes

- **Check causation framing.** Three co-managed sites against eleven open-access ones is compelling but observational. Phrasing like "the forests that held were the ones being looked after" is honest and still powerful. Acknowledging that the fishers may know things about their sites that your transects don't capture is both accurate and respectful.
- **Ask the fishers beforehand** whether they'd like to be named, shown in photos, or invited to speak. Their own words about removing urchins will land harder with the audience than any graph.
- **Language.** If you give the talk in Spanish, use the terms people actually say: *huiro*, *erizo negro*, and the formal name of the area if it's an AMERB. "Urchin barren" might work better as *blanquizal* or simply "desierto de erizos."
- **Cut the slides to match.** One image per idea, almost no graphs. If you keep one chart, make it the two-line comparison of kelp density, open-access versus co-managed, across the same heatwave years. That single image tells the whole talk.

academic-07__base.text:
Your notes are much less of a mess than you think. The tennis match happens because you're sorting studies by **verdict** (empowers vs. doesn't). If you sort them by **what they're actually measuring and under what conditions**, the contradictions mostly dissolve, and that dissolution *is* your argument.

## The core insight: your sources aren't disagreeing as much as it looks

There are three things your literature keeps conflating.

**1. Two different "treatments": migration vs. remittances**
- Hernández Ruiz (2015) and Morales (2019) are really about **male absence**: men leave, so cargos open up.
- Vázquez & Lim (2017) and Gómez Pacheco (2020) are about **money**: what remittances fund and who controls them.
- These can push in *opposite directions in the same community*. Absence opens space for women while money reinforces the fiesta/church hierarchy. That's a real analytical contribution, not just a summary.

**2. Different "outcomes" all called "participation"**
- **Presence**: attending the asamblea (Cruz 2018)
- **Voice**: speaking or voting in it (Vázquez & Lim; your pilot's "solo a escuchar")
- **Authority**: holding cargos (Hernández Ruiz)
- **Engagement with the municipal state vs. the community**: López (2021) is about exit from the *local state*, which is a different arena from the asamblea.

Your pilot data illustrate this beautifully: 6 of 9 women now attend, but "only to listen." That's presence without voice.

**3. Conditions that moderate the effect**
- **Pre-existing institutions**: Cruz's finding that the effect only appears where women already voted before 2000 is huge. Remittances seem to *amplify* existing openings rather than create new ones. Your instinct is right; this is probably your most important source.
- **Temporality**: Morales shows gains may be contingent on men staying away.
- **Transnational control**: Gómez Pacheco (and your 1 interviewee) show male authority can be reconstituted remotely. Absence isn't the same as loss of control.
- **Formal reform**: the parity reform is a top-down institutional change that might interact with all of this. Does it create the "pre-existing openings" Cruz identifies, or does it clash with usos y costumbres?

## Possible thesis statements

**Version A (conditional framing):**
> Existing scholarship frames remittances as either empowering or reinforcing women's exclusion in Oaxaca's usos y costumbres municipios. I argue this debate is largely an artifact of conflating migration with remittances, and attendance with political voice. Read together, the evidence suggests that migration and remittances expand women's *presence* in community politics, but this converts into *voice and authority* only where institutional openings already exist, and these gains remain vulnerable to men's return and to transnational forms of control.

**Version B (shorter, punchier):**
> Remittances do not create women's political participation in Oaxaca's indigenous municipios so much as amplify, or constrain, the institutional openings already present. The key question is therefore not *whether* remittances empower women, but *under what conditions* women's increased presence becomes political voice.

Version B then sets up your gap: we don't know much about that *conversion mechanism* from presence to voice, or how formal parity reform changes the conditions. That's where your project fits.

## Suggested structure

1. **Introduction**: the empowerment vs. reinforcement debate and why it seems stuck. State your thesis.
2. **Disaggregating the cause: absence vs. money.** Hernández Ruiz and Morales on absence; Vázquez & Lim and Gómez Pacheco on money.
3. **Disaggregating the outcome: presence, voice, authority.** Cruz, Hernández Ruiz, Vázquez & Lim, and López (with the community vs. municipal state distinction).
4. **Conditions and mechanisms**
   - Institutional preconditions (Cruz)
   - Temporality (Morales)
   - Transnational control (Gómez Pacheco)
   - Formal reform: the parity requirement and sistemas normativos internos
5. **Gaps and your contribution.** How presence converts to voice; interaction with parity reform. Your pilot data can briefly motivate this ("preliminary interviews suggest...").

## What a synthesis sentence looks like (vs. tennis)

*Tennis:* "Hernández Ruiz (2015) finds that remittances increase participation. However, Vázquez & Lim (2017) find they reinforce hierarchy."

*Synthesis:* "Hernández Ruiz (2015) and Vázquez & Lim (2017) appear to reach opposite conclusions, but they trace different mechanisms: the former examines how male absence opens cargos to women, the latter how remittance money sustains ritual hierarchies. Read together, they suggest migration and remittances may exert countervailing pressures within the same community."

The trick is that every paragraph should be *about an idea*, with sources as evidence, not about a source.

## Two quick flags
- **Double-check the reform details.** Pin down exactly which reform you mean (state vs. federal, the year, and whether it applies to usos y costumbres municipios). There were several parity reforms at different levels around that period, including the 2019 federal "paridad en todo," and your comité will want precision.
- **Don't over-lean on n=9.** Use the pilot to *illustrate* the presence/voice distinction, not to prove it.

## A rough 10-day plan
- **Days 1–2:** Lock the thesis; re-sort your notes under the three disaggregations.
- **Days 3–6:** Draft sections 2–4 (write the hardest one first).
- **Day 7:** Intro + gaps section (easier once the body exists).
- **Days 8–9:** Revise for synthesis. Check that each paragraph starts with *your* claim, not an author's name.
- **Day 10:** Polish and citations.

If you want, paste in one of your current tennis-match paragraphs and I'll show you how to rework it in this structure.

strategy-02__base.text:
You're not actually stuck on "lending vs. Ghana." Two of the things in your notes break the dichotomy.

## 1. Terminal replacement is the most urgent item

Half your churn is merchants whose terminals break and wait 9 days for a replacement. That's not a competitive problem. It's an operations problem you can fix in weeks.

- **It's the cheapest fix available.** If half of 6.2% monthly churn is terminal-related, getting replacement time down to 1–2 days could plausibly bring churn back toward 4% or below. 6.2% monthly means losing about 54% of merchants a year; 4% means about 39%.
- **It directly threatens the lending business.** MCAs usually collect from a share of POS transaction flow. A merchant with a dead terminal for 9 days has no collections, and a merchant who churns because of it is likely to become a default. Your 4.1% default rate may already include some of this, and it will get worse as the book grows.
- **It's the metric Series A investors will look at first.** Rising churn undercuts both your lending story and your expansion story. "We found the cause and fixed it" is a strong board slide.

A spare terminal pool, swap-first-repair-later, and a 48-hour SLA probably costs a small fraction of the Ghana budget. Do this regardless of everything else.

## 2. Ghana doesn't have to be all-or-nothing

You're both arguing about a $380k, team-splitting expansion. But your seed lead asked for a multi-market *story*, not necessarily a live second market.

Look at the timelines:
- Lenders want 12 months of data. You have 7, so that's **5 more months.**
- Ghana licensing takes **5–7 months.**

These line up. A staged option could look like this:
- **Now:** Sign with the Accra partner and file for licensing. Spend only on licensing and legal, with the partner doing the legwork. No team split.
- **Months 1–5:** The core team fixes churn and grows the loan book carefully toward 12 months of data and a debt facility.
- **Decision gate (~month 5–6):** If the license is near and the A is in motion, commit the operating budget. If not, you've lost a fraction of $380k.

That lets you tell investors "licensing underway in Ghana, launching post-raise," which may be enough. Tobi's concern about splitting the team is addressed because you don't split it yet.

## 3. Turn the core disagreement into a question you can answer

You and Tobi are partly arguing about something neither of you knows: **how much do Series A investors actually require a second market?** Find out:
- Ask your seed lead directly: "Is a second market a must-have for the A, or would a strong lending business in Nigeria with Ghana licensing in progress work?" Their "multi-market story" may mean "show us the TAM is bigger than Nigeria," which strong revenue-per-merchant growth from lending could also answer.
- Have informal conversations with 2–3 target Series A investors before the board meeting if possible.

Also note that equity and debt are different pools. The debt facility depends mostly on loan book data, not on the A. Lenders may want an equity cushion, so ask both lenders how they think about that.

## 4. Pressure-test the lending numbers before calling it "the business"

The pilot looks promising, but check:
- **Is 4.1% per cycle or cumulative?** And how long is a cycle? 11% per cycle means very different things if a cycle is 2 months versus 6.
- **Selection bias.** Were the 640 pilot merchants your best ones? Defaults usually rise when you expand to the broader base.
- **Seasoning.** Seven months is early. Look at defaults by cohort over time, not one blended number.
- **Unit economics with debt.** Naira debt is expensive. Run 11% yield minus defaults minus cost of capital minus ops cost per cycle and confirm the margin holds at scale.

## 5. Agent banking: defer it explicitly

Tell your ops lead it's parked until after the raise, with a date to revisit. Leaving it undiscussed lets it linger, and you don't have the capacity for a third initiative.

## For the board update

Don't present two positions. Present one sequenced plan with decision gates:

1. **Honest state of the business:** churn is up, here's why, here's the fix and target.
2. **Lending as the core thesis:** pilot results, the 12-month milestone, debt facility status.
3. **Ghana as a staged option:** licensing starts now at low cost, operating spend contingent on [gate].
4. **What we need from the board:** their read on investor expectations, intros to Series A investors and lenders.

## What I'm missing

My suggestions depend on a few things you didn't mention:
- **Runway.** If you have under 9–10 months, the A timing dominates everything and the plan changes.
- **Target date for the A.**
- **How the $380k breaks down** between licensing and operating costs.

If you share those, I can help you tighten the plan or draft the board slides.

## What moved

business-decision-07__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
You're announcing a decision, not asking permission. Lead with the new rate, then show what clients get for it.

## The shape that clicked
```
BEFORE                                 AFTER
thanks                                 new rate + date (fact)
my costs went up                         ↓
sorry, budgets are tight               what you get from me now
"slightly" → new rate (para 3)           ↓
"happy to discuss if difficult"        ongoing work stays at old rate
thank you for understanding              ↓

```
Your draft buried the rate under justifications and wrapped it in apologies, which is why it reads as begging. Your strongest material was framed as *your costs* when it is really *their benefit*: 30% faster turnaround, sworn certification and court work.

## What moved
- **Rate and date:** paragraph 3 → opening line. It's news, so state it first.
- **Software, terminology database, certification:** "my costs" → "what you now get."
- **"Held my rates for over three years":** kept, but as a plain fact, not a sacrifice.
- **Old rate for ongoing projects:** kept and moved up. It's real, concrete goodwill.
- **Cut: "slightly."** €0.09 → €0.12 is a 33% increase. Lawyers will do the maths, and "slightly" costs you credibility.
- **Cut: insurance increase.** That's your overhead, not their concern, and it reads as a plea.
- **Cut: "budgets are tight," "after a lot of reflection," "thank you for understanding."** These are apologies.
- **Replaced: "happy to discuss if it causes difficulty."** This invites them to negotiate the rate. Swapped for an offer to talk about upcoming work.
- **Missing:** your answer if one of the two big firms pushes back. That is probably why this has sat unsent for two months. See below.

## Rebuilt

**Subject:** My rates from 1 March

Dear [name],

I'm writing to let you know that from 1 March my rates will be €0.12 per word for standard translations and €0.16 per word for urgent work. My rates have been unchanged since 2021, and any project already underway on that date will be completed at the current rate.

Over that time I've renewed my sworn translator certification and invested in new CAT software and a specialised terminology database for EU competition law, which has cut my turnaround on long contracts by around 30%. I'm also handling more certified translations for court.

It has been a pleasure working with you, most recently on [project], and I look forward to continuing. If it would help to talk through any upcoming work, I'm always happy to.

Warm regards,
Lucía

**Should all 11 get the same email?** Give everyone the same rates and the same core message, but tailor it in two ways:

1. **Personalise the middle paragraph.** Mention the competition-law database only to firms that do that work. For the notaries, lead with sworn certification.
2. **Call the two big firms first, then send the email as written confirmation.** Before you call, decide two things:
   - one concession you'd offer if they push back, such as a later start date for them;
   - whether you'd stay at €0.09 if they refuse, or accept the risk.

   Once you know your answer, the call stops being frightening and the email stops sounding like begging.

Then send to the other nine the same week, so word doesn't travel ahead of you.

- "Get rid of tipping, but also..." → reframed as what you *used to* think.
- Single moms: from standalone → merged with Dee as *why* abolition failed.
- Cut: "I don't know," "The end I guess."
- Missing: what the 4% is a share of (tips? sales?). I left it vague. Worth confirming the Louisiana tip-pool rule before print. The closing two-line ask is mine, so swap it if it's not you.

## Rebuilt

**I Tried to Get Rid of Tipping. Here's What Actually Worked.**

Tipping in this country is broken, and everybody in the industry knows it.

My line cooks make $17 to $19 an hour. My servers, on a good Friday, walk out with $350 or more in tips. Same shift, same heat, same chaos. The guy plating your redfish makes a third of what the person carrying it makes. That's not fair, and I've been trying to fix it at Sauce Maman for years.

For a long time I thought the fix was obvious: get rid of tipping. So in 2022 we did. 20% service charge, no tipping.

Within two months, three of my five servers were gone. They could make more down the street, so they went. One of them, Dee, had been with us since day one. She told me straight: "You're asking me to take a pay cut so you can feel good."

She wasn't wrong. After four months we went back.

Here's what I learned. Servers in New Orleans are mostly women, and a lot of them are single moms. Tipping is how they make rent. When you talk about abolishing tips, you're talking about their rent. Anybody who wants to get rid of tipping should ask them first. I didn't, not really. Dee had to tell me.

And the other way to do it, paying everybody more and building it into the menu, means a $45 entree. Customers don't want that, and I don't blame them.

So I was stuck. Back of house needs more money. Front of house shouldn't lose money. Customers won't pay more. Every answer I tried broke one of those three.

Then last year we tried something smaller. Louisiana lets the kitchen share the tip pool, as long as no managers are in it. So now 4% goes to back of house.

Kitchen pay went up about $3.80 an hour. We lost one server, and she was leaving anyway.

That's it. No big announcement, no new menu prices. Just the people cooking your food getting a piece of what you leave for the meal.

It doesn't close the gap. My cooks still make less than my servers on a Friday. But it moved the number more than my big idea ever did, and it didn't run off my front of house.

So here's where I've landed after seven years and one failed experiment: the fight isn't tipping versus no tipping. That fight hurts the people it's supposed to help. The fight is over who the tips go to. For six of those seven years, at my own restaurant, the answer was "whoever carries the plate." It should be "whoever made the meal."

If you own a restaurant, look at your pool. If you eat out, ask who's in it.
