**Why we run it this way**
My dad, Ray, started Dalton in 1987 with one pickup truck and a simple rule: show up when you said you would, and charge what you said you would. We run 22 trucks now, and Ray still comes in on Fridays. Those guarantees up top are just his handshake, written down.
We treat every home like it's our own.
— [Your name], Dalton Air & Heat
*[Photo: Ray and you, current]*

oped-07__base.text:
## Short answer: don't cut it, and don't keep the one-liner either

The one-liner is actually the worst option. Cutting support entirely would be a lie of omission. "Growing pains we're ironing out" is worse, because your support team will read it as you minimizing something they flagged twice and got told to wait on. That's probably why your head of support went quiet.

The support data also makes the piece **more** credible. Every 4-day-week post online is a victory lap, and skeptics dismiss them for that reason. A founder who says "here's where it broke, here's why, and it was my call" is much harder to wave away.

A few other things before the draft:

- **The headline.** "We're never going back" doesn't hold up when CSAT dropped and a major customer shortened their renewal. I'd go with something like *"Six months of a 4-day week: what worked, what broke, and what I got wrong."*
- **The caveats.** It's a small sample over different seasons (Oct–Mar vs Apr–Sep), "focus" is self-reported, and hiring numbers depend on the market. Saying so up front builds trust.
- **The customer detail.** "9% of ARR" plus "enterprise" plus "renewal call" may let the customer recognize themselves. I've softened it below.
- **Talk to your head of support before publishing.** Show them the draft, and ask whether they're comfortable with you mentioning their hire requests.
- **Fill in the [brackets] with real commitments only.** Publicly promising fixes you don't follow through on would undo the whole point.

---

## Draft (~800 words)

**Six months of a 4-day week: what worked, what broke, and what I got wrong**

Six months ago we did something scary: we moved all 28 people at Faltwerk to a four-day week, with no pay cut and the same goals. I promised the team I'd write up the results publicly, including the parts that didn't go well. So here it is.

The short version: for most of the company, it worked better than I expected. For our support team, and for some of our customers, it didn't. The main reason it didn't was a decision I made.

**How we measured**

We compared the pilot (October–March) with the six months before it (April–September). We're a small company, the window is short, and the two periods fall in different seasons. Treat this as one company's honest experience, not a study.

**Engineering: same output, better focus**

We shipped 23 features during the pilot, compared with 21 in the six months before. Sprint velocity was essentially flat, up about 3%. In other words, we did the same amount of work in four days that we used to do in five.

The number that surprised me most was focus. Our engineers rated their ability to do deep, uninterrupted work at 8.0 out of 10, up from 6.2. [Add one or two concrete changes here, e.g. fewer meetings, no-meeting mornings, or tighter sprint planning. Readers will want to know *how*, not just *that*.]

**People: nobody left, and hiring got easier**

In the six months before the pilot, four people left voluntarily. During the pilot, nobody did. For a 28-person company, that's the difference between constantly backfilling and actually building.

Sick days dropped from 5.4 to 3.1 per person. Applications per open role went from 55 to 140. Part of that is surely the hiring market, but candidates told us the four-day week was why they applied.

**Support: where it broke**

Our support team is four people. To keep customers covered five days a week, they staggered their days off. That sounds reasonable until you do the math. With four people each working four days, you have an average of about 3.2 people on any given day instead of 4. That's 20% less coverage, every single day, not just on Fridays.

The results showed it:

- First-response time went from 2.1 hours to 6.8 hours.
- CSAT dropped from 4.6 to 4.1.
- Two of our enterprise customers raised slow support in their renewal conversations.
- One of our larger customers renewed for six months instead of twelve.

Here's the part I need to own. The support team saw this coming. They asked me twice during the pilot for a fifth hire, and both times I said we'd wait for the results. That was the wrong call. The coverage gap wasn't something the experiment needed to reveal; it was arithmetic, visible on day one. In practice, part of engineering's four-day week was paid for by the support team absorbing the gap, and by our customers waiting longer.

An earlier draft of this post called that "growing pains." It wasn't. It was a predictable staffing problem that I chose not to fix.

The broader lesson for anyone considering this: a four-day week works very differently for roles measured on output and roles measured on availability. Engineering can compress the same work into fewer days. Support's job is to be there when a customer needs help, and you can't compress being there. Coverage roles need their own plan: more headcount, a different schedule, or both.

**What we're doing now**

[Fill in only what's actually decided. For example:]
- [We've opened the fifth support role / hired for it as of ___.]
- [We're redesigning the support schedule with the team, rather than for them.]
- [We've reached out directly to the customers affected.]
- [Our target is first-response time back under ___ hours by ___, and we'll report back.]

We're keeping the four-day week. It made us a better place to work, and the engineering results speak for themselves. But I'm not going to claim it's a success until it works for everyone on the team and for the customers who depend on them.

**Should you try it?**

Yes, I think so, with some conditions:

- Measure your baseline before you start.
- Separate output roles from coverage roles, and plan for each differently.
- Budget for the coverage you'll need before the pilot, not after.
- When the people closest to your customers tell you something's wrong, believe them the first time.

Thank you to our support team, who kept our customers looked after through a gap I should have closed months earlier.

---

If you tell me what you've actually decided on the fifth hire and the schedule, I can tighten the "What we're doing now" section. I can also cut a shorter LinkedIn version, since 800 words is long for that format.

pitch-08__base.text:
Your mentor's right on both points, but you don't have to lose Lyon. The problem isn't the story, it's that the best line in the whole script ("I'll suffer quietly") is buried in the middle of a long sentence. Make that the thing people remember, and Lyon becomes the reason it's believable.

Here's a version at about 155 words (yours is about 230). Since 3:10 is a relaxed pace for you, this should land around 1:50, which leaves room for nerves or a laugh.

---

"When a K-drama character says 'I'm fine,' the subtitle says 'I'm fine.' But what they actually said is closer to: 'Don't worry about me. I'll suffer quietly.'

I'm Ji-woo, founder of Subtle. I learned this as a translator in Lyon, where my French friends were obsessed with K-dramas and kept asking me what characters *really* meant. I started an Instagram account explaining it. It grew to 40,000 followers.

Over 100 million people watch K-content. Lots of them want to learn Korean. But textbooks teach you how to order coffee, not how people actually talk.

So my co-founder Min-seok, an ML engineer, and I built Subtle. You pick the episode you just watched, we pull the scenes, and you practise the real lines with the nuance explained.

We launched in March. 210,000 downloads, mostly organic from TikTok. Day-30 retention is 31%, three times the category average. And 4.2% already pay.

We're raising 2.5 billion won to license content directly and add Japanese and Spanish.

Because 'I'm fine' almost never means fine. I'm Ji-woo, and this is Subtle."

---

**What changed and why**

- **Opened with the "I'm fine" line.** It's funny, instantly shows the problem, and needs no context. Lyon comes right after as *how you know this*, so it still opens your story.
- **Ended with a callback to it.** Repeating the hook at the end is what makes people remember it. Ideally someone at the drinks afterwards says "oh, the 'I'm fine' app."
- **Kept one strong number per idea.** 31% retention at 3x the category is your best stat, so I gave it room. Too many numbers in a row blur together.
- **Cut, but saved for Q&A or your deck:** the price (₩6,900), 5.3 lessons/week, top markets, where Min-seok worked, and how you met. These are good answers to questions; they just slow down the pitch.
- **Removed filler** like "We realised there was something bigger here." The story already shows that.

**Tips for the next 9 days**

- Time it out loud a few times. If you're still over, cut "mostly organic from TikTok" first, then "Lots of them want to learn Korean."
- Pause after "I'll suffer quietly." Let people laugh or react. That pause is worth more than any sentence you could fit in it.
- Put the numbers on a slide so you can say them slowly and the audience can see them too.
- If Min-seok's former company is a name people recognize (Naver, Kakao), say it. "An ML engineer from Naver" is only a couple of extra words and tells investors he can build.

The tone should still sound like you, short sentences and conversational. Change any phrase that doesn't feel natural in your mouth.

oped-10__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Fines failed at the one job they were supposed to do: without them more books came back, staff got hours back, and borrowers who had been driven away returned.

## The shape that clicked
```
BEFORE                              AFTER
Thesis: fines = class warfare       Spine: fines failed at their own job
  evidence: returns, costs,           ├ returns rose 91% → 94%  ← answers "accountability"
  rejoiners (proves something         ├ 9 hrs/week to collect €4,200
  else)                               ├ 340 back, mostly <18 / >65  ← fairness, earned
  objection: answered by rhetoric     └ €6, twelve years  ← the ending
```
I think this is what your editor meant. Your thesis is moral ("class warfare"), but every piece of evidence you have is practical. The figures prove that fines don't work, not that they're oppressive. The moral framing also tells the readers you most want to persuade, librarians and councils still charging fines, that they're defending a system built to keep the poor down. Your strongest answer to "accountability" is already in your data: returns went *up*.

## What moved
- Returns figure: middle → answer to the accountability objection, because it beats them on their own terms.
- Under-18/over-65 detail: passing mention → the fairness point, now grounded in evidence instead of assertion.
- The man and the €6: middle → ending, which solves your ending problem.
- Cut: "tax on the poor / class warfare" opening, "keep the poor in their place," "moral squeamishness." They argue the wrong thing and insult your audience.
- Softened: the Victorian history, reduced to one line.
- Missing: system-wide figures (critics will say "that's one branch"); the euro value of the staff time; a source if you keep the history line.

## Rebuilt

When Dublin's public libraries went fines-free in 2019, critics predicted chaos: books would vanish, shelves would empty, standards would collapse. The case for fines has always rested on one idea: without a penalty, people stop bringing things back.

At my own branch, the opposite happened. The share of items returned within six weeks went from 91% before the change to 94% after.

Meanwhile, we had been collecting about €4,200 a year in fines, and staff were spending an estimated nine hours a week processing them, chasing them and handling disputes at the desk. That's nearly 470 hours a year [worth roughly €X in staff time]: hours not spent helping the people in front of us.

And the fines had been keeping people away. In the first year, 340 lapsed borrowers rejoined, most of them under 18 or over 65. Those are the young and the old, exactly the readers a public library exists for.

Opponents will say that without fines there is no accountability. But accountability was what fines were meant to deliver, and on that measure they lost: more books came home without them. One branch is not a national study [add system-wide figures here if available], but nothing in our experience suggests the critics' chaos ever arrived.

Fines belong to an older idea of what a library is for. The question for any system still charging them is a practical one: what are they actually buying?

Here is what ours bought. One man in his seventies told me he had stayed away for twelve years over a €6 fine on a children's book his late wife had borrowed for their grandson. Twelve years of a reader lost, for six euro. Other library systems should ask how many people like him they aren't seeing at the desk.

academic-03__base.text:
## Short answer

Keep both, but not as parallel contributions. Your four results tell one story, and the disemployment result is what makes the informal wage result surprising. Once you frame it that way, the "stapled together" feel goes away, and each of you gets what you're arguing for.

## Why these aren't two papers

The canonical two-sector model (Welch 1974; Mincer 1976; Gramlich 1976) makes a joint prediction:

1. A binding minimum in the covered (formal) sector displaces some workers.
2. They move into the uncovered (informal) sector.
3. **The added labour supply pushes informal wages down.**

Your results confirm steps 1 and 2 almost exactly: formal employment down 1.8%, informal up 3.1%, total roughly flat. Then step 3 fails. Informal earnings rise 4.2% in the very sector absorbing the inflow.

That's the paper. The wage result isn't merely "a lighthouse effect exists," which Souza and Neri et al. already document. It's that the lighthouse effect is strong enough to overpower a supply shock that should have pushed wages the other way. You can only make that claim because you've shown the disemployment and reallocation. So the employment results aren't a second contribution. They're the setup that gives the wage result its bite.

## Who's right

**Your co-author is right that** the employment question is the entry point referees recognise and that dropping it would weaken the paper. A 1.8% decline from a 14% increase implies an elasticity around −0.13, which is unremarkable on its own but essential as the first half of the test.

**You're right that** leading with "we find modest disemployment" undersells the paper, because that finding alone is standard.

The resolution is to lead with the theory that links them. The first paragraph speaks to the classic minimum wage literature (your co-author's audience), and the payoff is the wage puzzle (your result).

## Sketch of paragraphs 1–2

> **P1.** In developing economies, minimum wages legally bind only part of the labour market. The canonical two-sector model (Welch 1974; Mincer 1976; Gramlich 1976) makes a sharp prediction about the rest: workers priced out of the covered formal sector move into the uncovered informal sector, where the added labour supply depresses wages. On this view, informality cushions employment but not earnings. Total employment may hold up, but the least-protected workers absorb the cost through lower pay. This prediction underlies a long-standing concern that minimum wages in economies with large informal sectors shift hardship rather than reduce it.

> **P2.** We test this prediction using a regional wage floor introduced in 2017 in three northeastern Brazilian states, set 14 percent above the national minimum. The first half of the prediction holds. Formal employment among low-wage workers fell 1.8 percent, informal employment in the same occupations rose 3.1 percent, and total employment was essentially unchanged. The second half does not. Average earnings of informal workers in affected occupations *rose* by 4.2 percent, although no law required informal employers to pay the floor. Informal wages moved toward the minimum at exactly the moment the model predicts they should have moved away from it.

Paragraph 3 then turns to mechanisms. The lighthouse literature (Souza 2011; Neri et al. 2015) enters here as a candidate explanation rather than a separate literature you're contributing to, alongside alternatives such as improved outside options or bargaining. You then state what your design can and can't distinguish. The contributions list follows naturally: (i) a direct test of the two-sector wage prediction, (ii) evidence that reference-point effects can dominate supply effects, (iii) implications for evaluating minimum wages where informality is high.

## The vulnerability this framing exposes

Making the wage result the centrepiece means referees will go straight for **composition**. If the workers displaced from formal jobs are more productive than incumbent informal workers, average informal earnings can rise mechanically with no lighthouse effect at all. Before committing to this framing, I'd want to see:

- Earnings of **incumbent** informal workers, using the PNAD Contínua rotating panel to follow individuals. If the effect holds for stayers, the composition story mostly dies.
- Hourly vs. monthly earnings, to rule out an hours response.
- Whether the "unchanged" total employment is a precisely estimated null or just an insignificant one. P2 leans on it.

If the effect survives these checks, it's a much stronger paper than "two findings." If it doesn't, your co-author's framing becomes the safer one, and the wage result moves to a section on spillovers.

## The conclusion

Once the intro is framed this way, the conclusion needs one core sentence rather than two parallel summaries. Something like: *"Informality absorbed the workers the minimum wage displaced, but not in the way standard theory predicts: the floor raised wages even where it had no legal force."* Everything else in the conclusion should elaborate that sentence.

positioning-08__base.text:
# My recommendation: none of the three as written. Lead with the 8% cap.

Your strongest positioning asset is sitting on page 6 of the T&Cs. Walk in Friday arguing for it, framed as a sharpened version of Route A so it lands as an evolution, not a hijack.

**Working line:** *"Your pet gets older. Your premium won't jump. Lifetime cover with increases capped at 8% a year."*

## Why this wins

**1. It answers the biggest problem in your own data.** Renewal hikes are the top frustration at 61%, more than three times slow claims (19%) and four times price at purchase (14%). The cap is a direct, contractual answer to the 61%. None of A, B or C addresses it.

**2. It targets a market that is actively moving.** 44% of owners with pets over 8 have switched or cancelled over a renewal increase. That's a large group in motion, already shopping, with a specific grievance you can name and solve.

**3. It's ownable and provable.** It's in the contract, not just in the advertising. Competitors can't match it without their own underwriter agreeing, which buys you time.

**4. It suits an 18-month-old challenger.** You need one sharp reason to choose you. "We won't punish you for your pet getting older" is simple, emotional and specific.

## Why not the three routes as briefed

**Route C (Fast Claims), the agency's pick.** It's the weakest of the three despite being the most "ad-friendly." It addresses a 19% concern, and two competitors already beat it with "same day." You'd be launching your first campaign on a claim where you're visibly in third place. Keep 48hr as a proof point in the customer journey, not the headline.

**Route A (Fair Price) as written, finance's pick.** You're mid-market, so you can't win a price fight on comparison sites, and only 14% name point-of-sale price as their main frustration. But the instinct is right: price fairness is what people care about. They care about it *over time*, not on day one. That's the bridge to the cap.

**Route B (Vet Designed), the founder's pick.** It's credible, but it doesn't solve a stated problem, and two vets on an advisory panel is thin to carry a whole brand. It does have a role: the 38% who are "unsure what's covered" are a real secondary audience. Vet-backed, plain-English cover explanations make good supporting content.

## How to bring each stakeholder with you

- **Finance:** "This *is* Fair Price, made defensible. We stop competing on day-one price, where we lose, and compete on lifetime cost, where we win. And it's a retention story, so it improves lifetime value, not just acquisition."
- **Founder:** "Vet expertise becomes our proof layer: vet-reviewed guides on what's covered, especially for older pets. It strengthens the cap story rather than competing with it."
- **Agency:** "You wanted a sharp, emotional claim. 'Your pet ages, your premium doesn't spike' is sharper than '48 hours' and nobody's beating us on it."

## Check these before Friday

Go in having already asked the hard questions, or the room will poke holes:

1. **Underwriter durability.** Is the cap guaranteed for new business going forward, and can it be withdrawn? You can't build a brand on something that might be pulled in 18 months.
2. **Adverse selection.** Marketing this will attract owners of older pets, who claim more. Your underwriter and finance need to be comfortable with that mix shift, ideally modelled.
3. **The "don't switch tier" condition.** Under FCA Consumer Duty and financial promotion rules, it must be prominent and clearly explained, not buried. Get compliance sign-off on wording early.
4. **The compounding maths.** 8% a year roughly doubles a premium over 9–10 years. That's still far better than the steep age-related jumps many owners report, but frame it honestly ("capped," "no shocks"), not as "your price stays the same." Build a simple illustration against typical market renewal increases for older pets if you can source fair comparison data.
5. **Stated versus actual behaviour.** People say renewal is their biggest pain but still often buy on day-one price. That's why this story is strongest with switchers and owners of pets aged 5+, and why your comparison-site listing should still make the cap visible.

## Your one-sentence argument

*"Our research says the market's biggest pain is renewal hikes as pets age, and we're the only one of these options that solves it in the contract, so let's stop hiding our best feature on page 6 and build the campaign around it."*

positioning-02__base.text:
## The short version

Your best content is buried at section 5. The results are the strongest thing you have, and the headline says nothing a competitor couldn't say. Move the proof to the top and rewrite the headline around the outcome: **getting paid faster.**

## New order

1. **Hero:** Outcome headline, one proof stat, a "Start free" button
2. **Results:** Your three stats, big numbers, minimal text
3. **How it works:** 3 steps: send invoice → Ojaa reminds them on WhatsApp → you get paid by transfer or card
4. **Customer story:** The Ikeja events company (₦4.2m) as a short story with a name and photo if they'll agree
5. **Pricing:** It's simple and free to start, so show it early
6. **All features:** Collapsed or "See all features." On mobile, an 8-item grid is a scroll wall.
7. **FAQ**

**Cut "Built for Africa."** Yes, it's a bit cringe, mostly because it's a claim instead of proof. Your users are in Nigeria; "Africa" is vaguer than your actual product. Keep the specifics (works offline, WhatsApp reminders, Naira payments) and put them in "How it works," where they show it rather than say it.

**Replace the current testimonials.** "Great app" does nothing. Message your best beta users and ask one question: *"What changed after you started using Ojaa?"* You want answers with numbers or feelings, like "I stopped calling customers to beg for money."

## Draft top section

**Headline options:**
- **Stop chasing customers for money.**
- **Get paid faster. Without the awkward calls.**
- **Your customers owe you. Ojaa reminds them on WhatsApp.**

**Subheadline:**
Send invoices in seconds. Ojaa sends polite WhatsApp and SMS reminders for you, so you get paid without the back-and-forth.

**Proof line (right under it):**
Businesses in our beta got paid in **19 days instead of 34.**

**Button:**
**Start free.** 10 invoices a month, no payment needed
*(only say "no card needed" if that's true)*

## Mobile bounce, quick wins

- **Match the ad.** If the Instagram ad says "get paid faster," the page must say that in the first line. A mismatch is a common cause of instant bounces.
- **Keep the headline, proof line, and button visible without scrolling** on a phone screen.
- **Check load speed on mobile data**, not office Wi-Fi. Heavy images on a slow connection kill pages before anyone reads a word.

## For the investors

The same page works, but label the results honestly as **"6-month beta, 140 businesses."** Investors respect that more than an unqualified claim, and it keeps your ad claims safe too. They'll likely ask about retention and how many beta users now pay, so have those numbers ready.

pitch-06__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Insider fraud that stays under every threshold is invisible to rule-based controls until the audit finds it; Vigia catches it by knowing what normal looks like for each employee.

## The shape that clicked

```
OLD:  Us -> Us -> Product -> Product -> [Proof] -> Product -> Terms
NEW:  Their blind spot -> Proof -> Their turn -> How it sees it -> Fit -> Terms
          (problem)       (Paraná)   (discussion)  (product)     (stack, LGPD, 6-8 wks)
```

Your strongest "them" material was buried at slide 5. The Paraná case already describes the CISO's nightmare: small changes, rules that never fired. Lead with that pattern, never name his incident, and he'll make the connection himself. Then hand the room to him and his analyst before you show any product.

## What moved
- **Case study**: slide 5 -> slide 3. It's the hook, not the evidence at the end.
- **Architecture + features**: reframed as "how Vigia saw the Paraná fraud" and "what your analyst gets."
- **LGPD masking**: pulled out of the features list into its own slide. Monitoring employees is a legal concern for a bank.
- **Integrations**: 40+ logos -> only the ones matching their stack.
- **About us**: two slides -> one, near the end.
- **Cut to appendix**: investors and awards, full integrations list.
- **Missing**: their core banking/AD/email systems, alert volume or false-positive data (the analyst *will* ask), a proposed first step, and whether Paraná can be named or used as a reference.

## Rebuilt
1. **Title**: "The fraud that never trips a rule." [Bank] + Vigia.
2. **The pattern**: The costliest insider fraud isn't one big move. It's many small ones, each under the threshold.
3. **A real case**: At a cooperative bank in Paraná, a back-office analyst was slowly changing beneficiary details on dormant accounts. Their SIEM rules never fired. Caught at R$ 2.3M; the bank estimates R$ 11M+ by the annual audit.
4. **Your turn**: "Where would a pattern like this surface in your environment today?" Let the CISO and analyst talk.
5. **How Vigia saw it**: It builds a behaviour baseline per employee from core banking logs, AD and email metadata, so it can spot drift rather than threshold breaches.
6. **What your analyst gets**: A real-time alert, a risk score and a case in case management, walked through on the Paraná pattern. [anonymized screen if permitted]
7. **Privacy built in**: LGPD-compliant data masking lets you watch behaviour without exposing employees. ISO 27001 certified.
8. **Fits your stack**: [the 5–8 integrations matching their systems]. Full list in appendix.
9. **Live in 6–8 weeks**: [week-by-week plan].
10. **Who we are**: Founded 2019, 60 people, São Paulo and Lisbon.
11. **Pricing and next step**: [the tier that fits them] + [proposed first step].
12. **Q&A**
**Appendix**: investors and awards, full integrations, all pricing tiers.

Spend roughly the first 10 minutes on slides 2–4. That's where the "them" happens.

oped-04__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Pell and Reyburn don't give English readers two versions of Maranhão but two different poets, one universal and one local; each is selectively faithful, each was rewarded by its market for the poet it built, and both silently remove the same thing.

## The shape that clicked
```
                Maranhão (Portuguese)
              /                       \
   PELL: "universal feeling"     REYBURN: "one particular coast"
   saudade -> 5 English words    saudade kept, no footnote
   regional words standardised   regional words kept
   BUT keeps her line breaks     BUT merges her lines
   NY press, sales, reading      Glasgow press, Brazilian grant,
   lists, "accessible"           "strange"
              \                       /
      BOTH drop the 11 dedications to her fisherman father
```
Your categories were parallel columns, so they could only produce a list. Every note is actually evidence for one claim: each translator builds the poet their introduction promises. Two notes break the pattern, and they give the essay its turns. Lineation shows neither translator is simply "the faithful one." The shared dropped dedications show where both projects stop.

## What moved
- Introductions: from one category among four to Section 1, because they state each translator's thesis about her.
- Saudade + regional words: merged into one section, since they are the same move at word level.
- Lineation: from first to Section 3, the complication that tests your own view that Reyburn "sounds more like her."
- Publishers, reviews, sales, reading lists: merged into one "market" section.
- Dedications: from a side note to the climax.
- Missing: a framework to name the poles (Venuti's domestication/foreignisation is the obvious candidate, but check it against your course reading). Side-by-side readings of at least one or two poems. What the 11 dedicated poems are about. Whether either translator explains dropping them. Whether Reyburn's line merging has a pattern. A source for Pell's sales. Exact review quotes.

## Rebuilt

**Intro (rewritten)**
Celeste Maranhão (1931–1989) remains under-translated in English. The two book-length translations that do exist, Dawn Pell's *Salt Hours* (1994) and Tomás Reyburn's *The Low Tide Notebooks* (2017), offer less two versions of her poetry than two different poets. Pell's introduction presents "a poet of universal feeling"; Reyburn's presents "a poet of one particular coast." This essay argues that each translation is built, choice by choice, to deliver the poet its introduction promises, and that each was received and rewarded for exactly that construction. Neither is straightforwardly the faithful one: Pell preserves Maranhão's lineation while standardising her vocabulary, and Reyburn preserves her vocabulary while merging her lines. On one point, though, they agree. Both remove the dedications to Maranhão's fisherman father that head eleven poems in the Portuguese. [Final claim to set once you've read the dedicated poems, e.g. that the universal and the local Maranhão are both produced by detaching her coast from the people on it.]

**Sections (about 4,000 words)**
1. **Two poets in the paratext** (~500). The introductions as competing theses about who Maranhão is.
2. **Building the poet word by word** (~900). Saudade dispersed vs. saudade withheld. Standardised vs. regional names for fish, nets and tools. Use close readings of [poems].
3. **Selective fidelity** (~600). Lineation reverses the pattern. Test "Reyburn sounds more like her": more like her in lexicon, less in form.
4. **Each poet finds her market** (~700). NY press vs. Glasgow press with a Brazilian grant. "Accessibility" vs. "strangeness" are the qualities each paratext promised. Pell is the Maranhão on reading lists, so her version largely *is* the poet in English.
5. **What both leave out** (~600). The eleven dedications. Pell's omission fits her universalising. Reyburn's sits uneasily with "one particular coast."
6. **Conclusion** (~300). What the anglophone Maranhão is, and what a future translation might restore.

life-decision-05__base.text:
## What your mentor meant by "backwards"

Your strongest material is buried in the middle, and your weakest material is at the start and end.

- **The opening** (childhood, rearranging your bedroom) is the generic "passionate since childhood" line that selection panels read constantly. It's also closer to interior design than UX.
- **The middle** (the report system) is excellent. You found a real problem, interviewed users, mapped the process, prototyped, tested in rounds, rolled it out, and measured the result. That *is* the UX process, done for real, with numbers.
- **The ending** falls back on adjectives ("organised, strong communicator, passion, empathy, dedication") that you've already *proven* with the project. Stating them afterwards weakens them.

So the fix is to flip it. Lead with the project, let it answer both "why UX" and "why you," and cut the claims the evidence already makes.

## Rewrite (~320 words, Australian spelling)

> Last year, I watched my colleagues lose around 11 hours a term to report writing, most of it spent copying the same data between three systems. Nobody had designed that process; it had simply accumulated. I wanted to understand why it was so painful, so I started asking.
>
> I interviewed 14 colleagues about where they got stuck and mapped the entire process on butcher's paper. The biggest drain wasn't the writing itself but the duplication. I built a prototype in Google Sheets with dropdowns and auto-filled comment banks, then tested it with the Year 3–6 team over three rounds, refining it each time. After rollout to all 60 staff, average report time fell to about 6.5 hours, a saving of more than 40 per cent. The principal has since asked me to present it to two other schools in our network.
>
> That project is why I want to work in UX. I loved every stage of it: listening for the real problem behind the complaints, testing ideas with the people who would use them, and seeing a practical design change give teachers back hours of their term.
>
> Teaching prepared me for this work more than I expected. Every day I adapt lessons for 28 Year 5 students who each learn differently. That means constantly observing, adjusting and checking whether something actually works for the person in front of me, not just whether it works in theory.
>
> Since then, I've completed the Google UX Certificate and I'm currently learning Figma. But self-directed learning only takes me so far. What I need now is structured training, critique from experienced designers and the chance to work on real products with real users, which is exactly what Brightline offers. [Add one sentence on something specific about Brightline: a partner organisation, its approach, or the placement model.]
>
> I've seen what good design can do for 60 teachers. Now I want to learn to do it for many more people.

## A few things to check before you submit

1. **Make the reflection yours.** The "I loved every stage" sentence is my guess at how you felt. Swap in what actually hooked you, because that's the part a panel will remember.
2. **Fill in the Brightline sentence.** Right now nothing in the statement explains why *this* fellowship rather than any UX course. One specific detail shows you've done your homework.
3. **Optional stat:** 4.5 hours saved × 60 staff is roughly 270 hours a term across the school. If that holds up (i.e., the 11-hour figure applied to most staff), it's a strong line to add.
4. **Spelling** is already Australian ("organised", "per cent"). Just keep it consistent if you edit.

pitch-04__base.text:
## The core problem

The deck is organized by **topic** (team, market, tech, competitors...) rather than by **argument**. Each slide is fine alone, but nothing builds on the previous one. And your strongest material, the pilot and the pipeline, sits at slides 7 and 9, after the investor has sat through generic context they heard in meeting one.

It's a second meeting, and they told you what they care about: **install speed** and **contract stickiness / who signs**. Right now the install-speed story is split across slides 4, 6, and 7, and the contract story across 8, 9, and 10. They'd have to reassemble your argument themselves.

## Specific issues

- **3 and 5 are one idea split in two.** Building stock without ETS2 is just a big number. ETS2 without the building stock is just policy. Together they're "why now."
- **4, 6, and 7 are one argument: why you're fast.** The tech explains the speed, competitors explain why others are slow (custom engineering), and the pilot proves it. Merge them or keep them adjacent.
- **8 and 10 belong together.** Grants covering 30-50% of capex are a core part of your unit economics, not a standalone "bonus" slide.
- **The contract slide is thin for what they asked.** "12 yr contracts" doesn't answer who signs (board? members' assembly vote?), what happens on early termination, who owns the equipment, or how payment is secured. This is the gap they flagged, so it needs its own slide.
- **Energy-as-a-service means you carry the capex.** They'll ask how €4M funds installs at scale. Is it equity for the company with project finance or a debt facility for the units? If the deck doesn't address this, it'll come up anyway.
- **No unit economics.** Contract value per building, margin, payback, and how grants change it. Climate funds will want this before anything else in the business model.
- **LOIs need context.** 27 cooperatives and ~1,900 buildings is strong, but investors discount LOIs heavily. Show who signed them, what converts an LOI into a contract, and how long that takes.
- **The 41% saving is vs. coal.** Your market slide also says "old district heating." If a big share of the addressable market is on district heating, expect "what's the saving there?" Either have the number or narrow the market claim.
- **Double-check the 1.6M figure** and its source. Then show the addressable slice: buildings with a boiler room you can retrofit, not already on modern district heating. A smaller, defensible number beats a big one they can poke holes in.
- **Roadmap (CZ/SK 2026) works against you.** With 3 pilots done and 1,900 buildings in the domestic pipeline, expansion abroad reads as unfocused. Cut it to one line on the ask slide or move it to the appendix.
- **The ask has no use of funds or milestones.** €4M should be tied to concrete outcomes, e.g. "convert X LOIs, install Y buildings, reach Z ARR by [date]."
- **The team slide doesn't connect to anything.** Your team is actually perfect for the risks here (Tomasz = scaling installs, Marta = the tech, you = industry and channel). Make that link explicit and move the slide later.

## Suggested order

1. **Title + one-line pitch**
2. **Pilot results** – lead with proof: 212 flats, 41% cost drop, 9 days vs 6-8 weeks
3. **Why we're fast** – modular tech + why competitors need custom engineering *(merge 4 + 6)*
4. **Why now / market** – ETS2 + addressable building stock *(merge 3 + 5)*
5. **Contract structure** – who signs, decision process, term, termination, ownership, stickiness *(new, answers their question)*
6. **Business model & unit economics** – EaaS, per-building economics, grants' effect on capex, how installs get financed *(merge 8 + 10)*
7. **Pipeline** – 27 LOIs, who signed, conversion path and timeline
8. **Team** – each person mapped to a key risk
9. **Ask** – €4M, use of funds, milestones; one line on CZ/SK as a later option

**Appendix:** competitor detail, grant program specifics, expansion plan, pilot data breakdown.

The logic: *it works → here's why it's hard to copy → why the market opens now → how the money flows and why it sticks → demand is already there → this team can execute → here's what €4M buys.* Each slide answers the question the previous one raises.

team-03__base.text:
You can tell one story, and it's stronger than either draft alone. The data supports a causal chain rather than two competing explanations:

**Vacancies create the gaps. ShiftGrid decides how those gaps land on nurses, and it's landing them in the most damaging way possible.**

Staffing is the root cause. Scheduling is the amplifier, and it's the lever you can pull before April. That framing leads with the top finding (so no cherry-picking), gives your director the headline they want, and still gets you a decision leadership can make next week.

## Why the data supports a combined story

**The two issues are entangled, not separate.** When nurses say "workload," some of that is being called in on a day off or moved to another unit with a day's notice. A nurse who's had six last-minute changes this month will experience that as workload. The 44% and 31% almost certainly overlap heavily, and the comment counts (241 vs. 208) are close enough that many comments probably mention both.

**Overtime up 22% fits both stories.** Gaps have to be filled by someone, and the platform's auto-fill logic determines who and how abruptly.

**The scheduling evidence is your most specific finding.** "Burnout is high and we have vacancies" is what leadership has heard a hundred times. "Last-minute changes nearly doubled, from 3.1 to 5.8 per nurse per month, after we changed one system" is new, concrete, and points at something you control.

## Where each draft is vulnerable

**Draft A (40 FTEs):**
- Budget is frozen, so the ask has no near-term path to yes. You'd spend 15 minutes on a request that can't be approved.
- Be ready to show where 40 comes from. If it's derived from the 17% med-surg vacancy, show the math.
- Hiring takes months even after funding, so it does nothing for the nurses filling out this survey.

**Draft B (ShiftGrid):**
- **The biggest risk is a confound.** If vacancies also rose over the same 14 months, more gaps alone would produce more last-minute changes, whatever platform you used. Someone in the room may ask this. Pull the vacancy trend before the meeting.
- **The manual-units comparison is suggestive but fragile.** It's two small units, and small units differ in team cohesion, census volatility, and possibly vacancy rates. Present it as "consistent with" rather than proof. One useful detail: 52% is almost exactly the 2022 network baseline of 54%, which is a nice way to frame it.
- Verify that "reconfigure within a quarter at low cost" holds up. Talk to IT or the vendor about what auto-fill is actually doing (pulling scheduled staff to cover gaps? ignoring seniority or preference rules? floating across units?) and whether changing it is a settings change or a contract change.

## Checks worth doing before the meeting

1. **Vacancy rate over the past 14 months.** If it was flat, your ShiftGrid case gets much stronger. If it rose, the combined framing becomes essential.
2. **Burnout by number of last-minute changes.** If nurses with 6+ changes report much higher burnout than those with 0–2, that's your best evidence. It's within-network and doesn't depend on the two manual units.
3. **Overlap between "workload" and "schedule" respondents and comments.** This demonstrates the entanglement directly.
4. **Vacancy rates on the two manual units.** If they're similar to network average, the comparison holds up better.

## A possible 15-minute structure

1. **The headline (2 min):** Burnout went from 54% to 71%. Workload is the top reason nurses consider leaving. Lead with this.
2. **What's driving workload (4 min):** Vacancies (17% med-surg) create gaps; overtime is up 22%. Then show how the gaps reach nurses: last-minute changes nearly doubled after ShiftGrid, and 63% had a change with under 48 hours' notice last month.
3. **The supporting signal (2 min):** Manual-scheduling units sit near the 2022 baseline, with appropriate caveats.
4. **Two-track recommendation (5 min):**
   - **Now, within the freeze:** Approve a ShiftGrid reconfiguration (name the specific auto-fill rules) and commit to measuring it. Track last-minute changes per nurse monthly and run a short burnout pulse at 90 days.
   - **For April:** Direct HR and nursing leadership to bring a costed staffing proposal, informed by what the reconfiguration fixes and what it doesn't.
5. **The ask (2 min):** Two decisions, one cheap and immediate, one deferred with a date.

The sequencing helps you too. If the ShiftGrid fix reduces changes and burnout moves, you've shown leadership that you deliver results, and the April staffing request arrives with credibility. If burnout doesn't move, you've ruled out the scheduling explanation, and the case for more staff is cleaner than it is now.

For the line about your director's view: "Staffing is the underlying problem, and we'll bring you the case for it in April. But we're currently making the shortage feel worse than it has to, and that part we can fix this quarter."

## The spine
The work you did this summer saved the project; the way I let it happen was wrong; August is me refusing to repeat it.

## The shape that clicked
```
OLD:   Apology  <-- "at the same time" -->  Defense

NEW:   The work  -> saved the project     (credit: theirs)

```
Don't cut the "not wasted" part. Change what it's about. Right now it defends the *push*, so it reads as "sorry, but." If it credits the *people's work*, and the apology covers *your planning*, the two halves stop competing. Your producer is right: the team stays visible. You are also right: you stop sounding defensive.

## What moved
- **The news:** from the middle to the top, with publisher and budget, so nobody reads the rest anxious about their job.
- **"Not wasted":** reframed as credit to the team, placed before the apology. The "At the same time" hinge is cut, because that phrase turned the defense into a rebuttal.
- **The apology:** made specific. It now names the planning failure, so the two new rules read as the direct fix for it.
- **The new rules:** set as a short list so they read as commitments.
- **Missing:** the public announcement date. Also how people can respond (Q&A, open door). And please confirm the slice milestone really was agreed without lead input. The rebuild assumes it.

## Rebuilt
Hi everyone,

Before we announce it publicly [date], I want you to hear it from me first: Ashfall is moving from March to August. Northgate has agreed, and the budget is covered through the extension.

Here's why. After the vertical slice review, it became clear that the open-world traversal system needs a rebuild. It also became clear that the scope we committed to couldn't be done by March without sustained crunch through winter. I wasn't willing to ask that of you again.

Which brings me to the summer. Many of you worked 55–60 hour weeks for nearly ten weeks to hit the slice. What you built is the reason we still have a project. Without it, Northgate would likely have pulled funding. Several of you have told me you were proud of what we showed at the review, and you should be.

But the hours it took were not okay, and they are my responsibility. We agreed to a milestone without asking the people doing the work whether it was feasible. I'm sorry.

So two things change, starting now:
- No milestone will be agreed with Northgate without sign-off from department leads on feasibility.
- Overtime beyond 45 hours will require my personal approval.

I know trust has to be earned back, not announced. [How people can raise questions or concerns.]

Bartek

proposal-01__base.text:
**Statement of Need and Impact**

In Kisumu County, many women still give birth at home, not because they reject facility care but because reaching a facility in labour is costly, slow, or impossible at night. [Insert county maternal mortality ratio and/or home-birth rate, with source, e.g., KDHS 2022.] When complications arise, distance can decide whether a mother survives.

Mama Salama Trust has shown that this barrier can be removed quickly and affordably.

**What we did**
In 2022 we added two low-cost tools to our established network of 41 community health promoters across 19 sub-locations:

- **A mobile-money transport voucher** (KES 600 per trip) so that a woman in labour can reach a facility by boda boda at any hour, without needing cash on hand.
- **A danger-signs checklist**, used by promoters at 32 and 36 weeks, to flag high-risk pregnancies before labour begins.

**What changed**
Between January 2022 and December 2023:

- Facility births among enrolled women rose from **54% to 88%**, a 34-point increase.
- In comparable sub-locations without vouchers, facility births rose only from **51% to 59%**.
- Among 1,312 enrolled women, we recorded **zero maternal deaths**. In the comparison area (approximately 1,100 women), there were four.

Early uptake was slowed by mobile network failures. We identified the problem, switched providers, and redemptions rose. [Optional: add redemption figures.]

**Why it works**
The voucher succeeds because it builds on more than a decade of community trust. Mama Salama was founded in 2011 by retired midwives offering home visits in three villages. Our promoters respect local birthing traditions while connecting women to facility care, so when a promoter says it is time to go, women go. Since 2019 we have worked in formal partnership with the County Department of Health.

**Why now**
The County has asked us to expand into Nyando sub-county. This request endorses our results and creates an opportunity to grow: the government partnership, promoter model, and voucher system are already proven and ready to scale.

**Our request**
We request **KES 18.4 million over two years** to:

1. Extend the program to 12 additional sub-locations [in Nyando sub-county], reaching approximately [X] more women;
2. Sustain stipends for the community health promoters at the heart of the model; and
3. Commission an independent external evaluation to rigorously test our results and build the evidence for county-wide adoption.

---

**What I changed (about 420 words, leaving room to fill placeholders):**

- **Reordered around the argument:** problem, then solution, results, why it works, why now, and the ask. Your history moved from the opening to "Why it works," where it explains *why* the voucher succeeds rather than reading as background.
- **Added the "need" itself.** The original had no problem statement. I've left a placeholder rather than inventing figures. One credible county statistic will strengthen this considerably.
- **Turned the network problem into a strength.** It now shows adaptive management instead of reading as an apology.
- **Framed the evaluation as confidence**, not a gap.

**Two things to check:**

- **Be careful with the maternal deaths comparison.** Zero vs. four is striking, but the numbers are small and the groups weren't randomised. I kept it factual ("we recorded") rather than claiming the program *prevented* deaths. I'd avoid stronger wording, since a careful reviewer may push back.
- **Confirm whether the 12 new sub-locations are in Nyando.** If they are, saying so explicitly ties the ask directly to the county's request. If you can add a cost-per-woman figure, funders tend to find that very persuasive.

## The spine

Your homepage should speak to the older patients who already are your business, and sport should get its own page, because sports patients arrive through Instagram and the GAA club, and those can link straight to it.

## The shape that clicked

```
OLD: one promise, two audiences, nobody first
              "every body"
             /            \
     rugby pitch        garden
   (27%, 4.1 sess.)   (58%, 9.6 sess.)

NEW: one homepage, plus a separate sports page
   GP / word of mouth ──> HOMEPAGE: older patients
                            "patient, explains everything,
                             parking at the door"
   Instagram / GAA ─────> /sport: "back for the season"
```

The current page tries to greet everyone equally, so it says nothing your reviews actually praise. The question that settles it isn't "which audience do we love?" It's "who lands on the homepage without a link pointing them somewhere more specific?" On your numbers, that's mostly the over-60s.

## What moved

- **Over-60s**: from one of two pictures to the homepage lead, because they're 58% of new patients and about five times the sessions (per 100 new patients, roughly 557 sessions vs 111).
- **Sport**: from a homepage half to its own page, because its channels can deep-link and "back for the season" is a different promise.
- **Ciarán's expertise**: from a competing audience to the method. The strength class *is* training, so his rehab background strengthens the older-patient offer instead of fighting it.
- **Cut**: "Move Better, Live Better" and "every body", because they could be any clinic.
- **Missing**:
  - Price or revenue per session by group. You need this to test the "premium" claim, since visit counts alone don't settle it.
  - Homepage analytics.
  - Who the other 15% are.
  - Whether the strength class can expand. It already has a waiting list of 22.

## Rebuilt

**Option A: One page, one shared promise**
> **Get strong enough for what's next.**
> Whether it's the stairs, the garden or the season, Canal Physio in Rathmines builds you back with strength-based rehab and explains every step. Parking at the door.
> [Recovering from surgery, a fall or ongoing pain →] [Getting back to sport →]

*Risk:* it's still split, just more honestly. This is the best option if Ciarán won't accept a secondary page.

**Option B: Two pages (recommended)**
> *Homepage:*
> **Physio that takes its time.**
> At Canal Physio in Rathmines we explain everything, go at your pace, and help you get stronger after a hip replacement, a fall or years of aches. Parking right at the door.
> [Book an assessment] [Join the strength class waiting list]

> *Sports page (linked from Instagram and the GAA club):*
> **Back for the season.**
> ACL rehab, running gait analysis and return-to-play programmes, led by a physio with a master's in sports rehab.
> [Book a sports assessment]

**Option C: One clear focus**
> **Stronger, steadier, and back to the things you love.**
> [Option B homepage text], with sport reduced to one line in the services list.

*Risk:* your Instagram and GAA traffic lands on a page that isn't talking to them, and Ciarán's specialism disappears.

**Decision rule for you and Ciarán:** the homepage belongs to whoever arrives without a more specific link. Every other group gets a page their channel can point to. Two checks before March:

1. Compare revenue per patient by group. If sport really is premium, Option B still holds; the sports page then just deserves more marketing spend.
2. Decide whether you can add strength-class capacity. Otherwise a better homepage just grows the waiting list.

oped-04__base.text:
Your supervisor is right, but the good news is that your notes already contain an argument. You've just filed it under "lineation, vocabulary, paratext, reception" instead of stating it.

## What your notes are actually saying

Most of your observations line up on one axis:

| | Pell (1994) | Reyburn (2017) |
|---|---|---|
| Intro frames M as | "universal feeling" | "one particular coast" |
| Regional vocabulary | standardised | kept |
| *Saudade* | translated (5 ways) | left in Portuguese |
| Press | big New York commercial | small Glasgow, Brazilian grant |
| Reviews praise | "accessibility" | "strangeness" |

This is close to Venuti's domestication/foreignization distinction (*The Translator's Invisibility*, 1995, a year after Pell). On its own, though, "Pell domesticates, Reyburn foreignizes, Reyburn is better" is a description with a verdict attached, and a fairly predictable one. Three things in your notes complicate it, and the complications are where your argument is.

1. **The dedications.** Both translators drop the dedications to her fisherman father. That's the most important note on your list. Reyburn keeps the names of the fish, nets and tools of that coast but removes the fisherman. His "particularity" preserves the landscape and its vocabulary while erasing the person, the labour and the family relationship behind it.

2. ***Saudade* without a footnote.** *Saudade* is the stock "untranslatable" Brazilian/Portuguese word, the one English readers already half-know as a token of Lusophone soulfulness. Leaving it untranslated every time can be read as resistance, or as a recognisable badge of Brazilianness. Pell's five renderings might, conversely, show close contextual attention rather than flattening. This is your best close-reading site, because it can cut either way.

3. **The market.** "Accessibility" and "strangeness" are both selling points. Pell's Maranhão is packaged for a mass Anglophone readership that values universal feeling. Reyburn's is packaged for a niche world-literature readership that values local texture, and it's partly funded by a national cultural body with its own interest in projecting a certain Brazil.

## A possible thesis

> *Pell's* Salt Hours *and Reyburn's* The Low Tide Notebooks *are usually read, and present themselves, as opposites: one universalising Maranhão for a mass readership, the other preserving her regional particularity. This essay argues that Reyburn's foreignizing approach is better understood as a different market positioning than as a recovery of the "real" Maranhão. His particularity is selective: it retains the coast's lexicon and the emblematic* saudade *as markers of difference while, like Pell, omitting the dedications to the poet's fisherman father. The shared omission suggests that both translations, for different audiences, make Maranhão's local world available as texture while removing its social and biographical specificity.*

That is something a reader could disagree with, which is the test of whether you have an argument. Your notes support it, and it still gives Reyburn real credit (he does sound more like her, you think).

**Alternatives, if that doesn't feel like yours:**
- *A defence of Pell:* her "domestication" is the reason Maranhão has any English presence at all (sales, reading lists), and Reyburn's strangeness addresses a readership that was never going to need persuading.
- *A reception argument:* because Pell's version is the one on reading lists, the academy's Maranhão is the "universal" one. The essay then asks what that framing has cost her reputation.

## Suggested structure (~4,000 words)

Order the sections by the steps of the argument, not by category. Each section should move it forward.

1. **Introduction (~400).** Under-translation, the two books, the apparent opposition, your thesis.

2. **Two Maranhãos: the frame (~600).** Start with the paratexts ("universal" vs "one particular coast"). The translators state the opposition themselves, so you can set it up in their words before you test it. Genette on paratext is useful here.

3. **The opposition in the texts (~900).** Regional vocabulary and lineation. Show that the difference is real: Pell's standardising, Reyburn's retention, and what each does to rhythm and image. Berman's "destruction of vernacular networks *or their exoticization*" (one of his deforming tendencies) is almost tailor-made for this section, because it names both translators' risks at once.

4. **The hinge: *saudade* (~700).** Close-read a few instances. Pell's five choices may be more careful than "domestication" suggests, and Reyburn's untranslated, unglossed *saudade* may be more of a gesture than it first appears. This is where the simple binary starts to wobble. Emily Apter (*Against World Literature*) on untranslatability would be useful.

5. **Markets of difference (~600).** Presses, the grant, and the reviews' "accessibility" vs "strangeness." Present both as forms of commodification. Casanova or work on the world-literature market could anchor this.

6. **The shared omission (~500).** The dedications. This is your climax: the one thing neither translation can accommodate, and what that tells you about both.

7. **Conclusion (~300).** Return to the reading lists. What does it mean that the "universal" Maranhão is the one being taught, and what would a translation that kept the father look like?

## Two practical checks before you commit

- **Verify the dedications.** Check which Portuguese edition(s) each translator worked from. If the edition they used lacked the dedications, section 6 becomes an argument about editions and source choice rather than translator decisions. That's still interesting, but different. Look for translator's notes, acknowledgements, and copyright-page details. (I also can't independently verify details about Maranhão or these two books, so treat the scholarly framing as something to test against your sources rather than as established fact.)
- **Make "sounds more like her" concrete.** If you keep that judgement, it needs evidence: sound patterning, line length, syntax. The lineation material is probably where you can show it.

Would it help if I drafted a revised intro paragraph around the thesis, or worked through one of the *saudade* passages with you if you paste the Portuguese and both translations?
