## Rebuilt
1. **Title + agenda**: "Last time you asked about install speed and contracts. Here's both."
2. **Pilot results**: 3 buildings, 212 flats, -41% vs. prior coal boiler room, 9 days vs. 6-8 weeks.
3. **Why it's 9 days**: modular cascade, existing boiler room, no facade work. Big brands do single-family, and large systems need custom engineering.
4. **The contract**: who signs, approval process, 12-yr EaaS, what makes it sticky. Grants 30-50% capex. [signing process], [exit terms], [who funds hardware]

proposal-08__base.text:
The case *is* strong. The problem is that the letter makes it in the wrong order. Your most persuasive argument is sitting at the bottom under "For your reference," unconnected, while the top of the letter reads as a morale complaint. Administrators often read staffing requests as cost requests. Your numbers show this one may be **closer to a cost saving**, but the letter never says so.

## Why it's not landing

1. **The financial case is never stated.** You listed the numbers but didn't do the math for them:
   - Overtime: P1.86M in 6 months ≈ **P3.72M/year** (annualized)
   - Turnover: 4 × P180,000 = **P720,000/year**
   - That's roughly **P4.4M/year** in costs linked to understaffing, against a request of **P2.1M**.
   - Even if new hires eliminated only *half* the overtime and *half* the resignations, that's about P2.2M saved, enough to cover the cost.
2. **Diversions aren't priced.** 17 diverted patients is lost revenue. Get the average ICU admission revenue from billing and multiply. This could be your single biggest number.
3. **The ask is buried** in the middle, with no explanation of what 4 nurses would change.
4. **"Writing again" plus exhaustion and low morale** reads as frustration. It's justified, but it makes it easier to file as a complaint than a proposal.
5. **No fallback.** It's yes/no, and they've said no twice.

## Before you send version 3

- **Ask the CNO directly what "justification" would satisfy them.** Cost data? Benchmarks? Incident rates? This 5-minute conversation may be worth more than any rewrite.
- **Check the diversions.** At 91% occupancy, were patients diverted because beds were full or because beds couldn't be staffed? If no physical beds were available, more nurses won't fix it, and management may already know that. Only claim the staffing-related ones.
- **Normalize the incident data.** "9 of 13 on nights" is stronger if you show nights are, say, 50% of patient-hours but 69% of incidents.
- **Cite a source for the 1:1–1:2 standard** (DOH, PNA, or your accreditation body). An unsourced standard is easy to dismiss.
- **Show what 4 nurses buy.** Remember that one extra nurse on every shift 24/7 takes about 4.5–5 FTEs. Calculate the resulting night ratio (e.g., 1:3.6 → 1:2.8) so they see a concrete outcome.
- **Ask for a meeting with Finance present**, not just another letter.

## Float pool vs. dedicated staff

Your colleague is right that it's politically easier, and you're right about the risk. ER volume is unpredictable and visible, so float nurses often get absorbed there. There's also a hidden cost: float nurses must be **ICU-competent** (ventilators, drips, codes), which means cross-training time and money.

My suggestion: **keep the dedicated ICU request as your primary ask, and offer a protected float pool as a fallback**, with written conditions:
- Float nurses are ICU-trained.
- The ICU has a minimum staffing floor, and float staff can't be pulled below it.
- Each nurse has a "home unit."
- Deployment is tracked and reviewed monthly.

Note also that a 6-nurse float pool needs ER and step-down data you don't currently have, so it isn't a quick switch.

## Rewritten letter

> **Subject: ICU Staffing Proposal – 4 Staff Nurses (estimated cost-neutral within 12 months)**
>
> Dear [CNO name] and [Administrator name],
>
> Thank you for reviewing my earlier requests. I have revised this proposal to show the financial and risk case more clearly.
>
> **Request:** Approval to hire 4 additional ICU staff nurses (est. P2.1M/year including benefits), assigned primarily to night shift.
>
> **Summary:** The ICU is currently spending more on overtime and turnover than these positions would cost. The hires are expected to largely pay for themselves while reducing patient safety and liability risk.
>
> **1. Financial impact (annualized from Jan–Jun data)**
>
> | Item | Annual cost |
> |---|---|
> | ICU overtime (P1.86M × 2) | ~P3.72M |
> | Turnover (4 resignations × P180,000) | ~P0.72M |
> | Lost revenue from 17 diversions (~34/year × P[avg ICU revenue]) | ~P[X]M |
> | **Total cost of current understaffing** | **~P4.44M + diversions** |
> | **Cost of 4 additional nurses** | **P2.1M** |
>
> Even if the new hires reduce overtime and resignations by only half, the savings (~P2.2M) would cover the full cost, before counting recovered diversion revenue.
>
> **2. Patient safety and liability**
> - Night shift ratio averaged 1:3.6 (Jan–Jun), against a recommended ICU standard of 1:1 to 1:2 [source].
> - 9 of 13 reportable ICU incidents this year (69%) occurred on night shift.
> - On 14 March, with 11 patients and 3 nurses, a ventilated patient self-extubated while his nurse was responding to a code. He was reintubated without harm, but a similar event with a worse outcome would expose the hospital to significant liability and regulatory scrutiny.
>
> **3. Retention**
> We lost 4 ICU nurses in 12 months, and 2 more are currently applying abroad. Each departure increases overtime for those who remain, which drives further resignations. Experienced ICU nurses are difficult and costly to replace.
>
> **4. Expected outcome**
> Four additional nurses would improve the night ratio from 1:3.6 to approximately 1:[X]. I will report overtime, incidents, resignations, and diversions to you at 3 and 6 months so the results can be verified.
>
> **5. Alternatives, if full approval is not possible**
> - **Phased:** 2 nurses now, 2 after a 6-month review of results.
> - **Protected float pool:** ICU-trained float nurses with a guaranteed ICU minimum staffing level.
>
> I would appreciate 20 minutes with you and Finance to review these figures together.
>
> Respectfully,
> [Name]
> ICU Nurse Manager

**Final tips:** Keep it to one page, attach your raw data separately, and if possible have someone in Finance check your numbers before sending. A figure Finance has already verified is much harder to reject. If you can, deliver it in person rather than by email. Good luck. Your team is lucky to have a manager building this case for them.

strategy-10__base.text:
## Short answer: your data is arguing against your recommendation

The email isn't clicking because the evidence supports a different plan, the one buried in your last line ("expand credit, improve same-day coverage, launch the app"). Your instinct is picking up on that.

Look at what your numbers say:

- **Contribution margin is positive only where you have same-day delivery, and that's 40% of your zone.** So in 60% of your current market, you lose money on each order.
- **Monterrey means building that model from scratch**: new warehouse, new suppliers, new team. You'd be copying a model that isn't yet profitable in most of your home market, which multiplies the problem rather than solving it.
- **Your two strongest levers are underused.** Credit drives 2.8x order volume with 2.9% defaults but covers only 4 alcaldías. Same-day lifts frequency 35% and is the difference between losing and making money.
- **The cost is large relative to your size.** At MXN 14M GMV and 6.5% take rate, net revenue is about MXN 910K/month. The MXN 6M warehouse alone is roughly 6–7 months of total revenue, before the sales team of 8.
- **The competitive threat may be smaller than it feels.** ConstruYa has about 200 contractors in Monterrey after ~9 months. That's an early foothold, not a locked-up market.

So it's mostly that the strategy, as your own data frames it, points to fixing the core first. The email is also structured backwards: a big claim up front, then evidence that doesn't connect to it.

## When Monterrey *could* be right

To be fair to the original idea, it could still win if:
- Supplier or contractor relationships in Monterrey get locked up early, so arriving late means you can't get in at any price.
- You have enough capital to do both without starving CDMX.
- ConstruYa is growing much faster there than ~200 contractors suggests.

If you don't know these, say so in the email. That reads as rigor, not weakness.

## Framing it for Ricardo

Don't make it "Monterrey vs. CDMX." Make it **"how we beat ConstruYa."** The pitch: we win the north by arriving with a model that makes money on every order, while competitors burn cash on unprofitable expansion. Fixing the core is the competitive strategy, not a retreat from competing. Then give him a concrete Monterrey milestone so it doesn't feel like "never."

## Restructured draft

> **Subject: 2025 plan: make CDMX profitable, then take Monterrey from a position of strength**
>
> Ricardo,
>
> My recommendation: in H1, we put our capital into the two levers that make our model profitable (same-day coverage and credit), and we prepare a Monterrey entry for H2 with a proven playbook. I think this is how we beat ConstruYa, not just how we match them.
>
> **Why the core first:**
> - Contribution margin is positive only in zones with same-day delivery, which is 40% of our CDMX zone. In the other 60% we lose money per order.
> - Where we offer same-day, order frequency is 35% higher.
> - Contractors using credit order 2.8x more per month, with 2.9% defaults, but credit is live in only 4 alcaldías.
> - The business is healthy: MXN 14M GMV/month, 62% from repeat contractors. We have a loyal base to grow into.
>
> **Why not Monterrey in Q1:** Entering requires ~MXN 6M for a warehouse, a sales team of 8, and new suppliers. If we go before our unit economics work, we'd be replicating a model that loses money in most of our current zone, in a market where we have no supplier relationships yet.
>
> **On ConstruYa:** They have ~200 contractors in Monterrey after about 9 months. That's a foothold, not a locked market. If they're expanding on weak economics, time works in our favor. We arrive with a profitable model, credit as a differentiator, and the app.
>
> **Proposed plan:**
> - **Q1–Q2:** Expand same-day coverage from 40% to [X]% (warehouse capacity in CDMX/Edomex); roll credit out to [N] more alcaldías; launch the contractor app.
> - **In parallel, low cost:** Start Monterrey groundwork: supplier conversations, market sizing, and tracking ConstruYa's traction.
> - **H2 decision point:** Go/no-go on Monterrey based on [specific triggers, e.g., contribution margin positive across X% of CDMX, credit defaults stable].
>
> Happy to walk through the numbers. I'd especially like your read on the Monterrey timing.

## Before you send, check these

1. **Credit selection bias.** Contractors who choose credit may already be your biggest buyers, so the 2.8x may not all be caused by credit. Know your answer if Ricardo asks.
2. **Default maturity.** Is 2.9% measured on loans that have fully come due, or is it early? Defaults often rise as books age.
3. **Fill in the brackets.** A specific same-day target and H2 trigger make this a plan rather than a deferral.
4. **Cost of the CDMX plan.** You're asking him to skip a MXN 6M spend, so show roughly what the alternative costs and returns.

Happy to translate this into Spanish or tighten it further if Ricardo prefers short emails.

business-decision-03__base.text:
**Recommendation:** Take Option B, but renegotiate two terms first. Bring the lead angel in through a smaller, separate arrangement rather than taking his full note. The one exception: if both contract-stage cooperatives fall through, switch to A.

## What you may not be seeing

**1. Your base case doesn't need either deal. This is an insurance decision.**
At 6-8% monthly growth, you go from USD 35k to 70k MRR in about 9-12 months. You reach break-even around month 10-11. Your runway is 14 months. So on current trajectory you hit both break-even and your Series A threshold with a few months to spare and no new money.

Your tables keep coming out even because they compare the options in the base case, where neither matters much. The real question is which instrument protects you best, at the lowest cost, if things go wrong: the pipeline stalls, growth slows to 3-4%, or the Series A slips by six months.

**2. Your RBF repayment estimate looks too optimistic, and that changes the picture.**
7% of USD 35k growing at 7% a month reaches 1.4x (USD 420k) in about 38 months, or about 35 months at 8%. Hitting 26-30 months would take roughly 10-12% monthly growth. Please check this against the fund's model, but the implications are:
- **The skim before break-even is small.** Cumulative repayments through month 11 are only about USD 39k, roughly USD 2.5-5k a month. "The skim hurts while we're burning" is not the real cost.
- **The real cost comes later.** The obligation will still be outstanding at your Series A. Series A investors often dislike a senior claim on revenue and may ask you to pay it off from the round, which means using equity dollars to repay debt at 1.4x.

**3. The cost comparison isn't actually close.**
- **A:** at a USD 6M cap, USD 400k converts to roughly 6-7% of the company. A Series A at 70k MRR in East Africa plausibly prices around USD 6-10M pre-money, so the cap will likely bind or nearly bind. You'd be giving up equity worth about USD 400-650k at Series A prices, and far more at exit.
- **B:** costs USD 120k in cash, spread over about three years, and flexes down automatically if revenue falls.

For an insurance policy you probably won't need to claim on, B is several times cheaper. Your cap-anchoring worry is overstated: Series A funds price on your metrics. The real cost of A is dilution, not anchoring.

**4. The angel's value is separable from his money.**
Your chair's argument for A is the relationships, and SACCO access genuinely matters for your input-credit linkage. But you don't need USD 400k at a 6M cap to get it. Offer him:
- a smaller note (USD 100-150k) at a higher cap, perhaps USD 8M, which is justified by being near break-even, or
- an advisor role with equity, or
- a committed allocation in your Series A.

If he only wants in at the full ticket and low cap, that tells you how he values the relationship versus the deal.

**5. The swing variable resolves soon, and you're deciding before it does.**
The two contract-stage cooperatives matter more than any term in either offer. If they sign, you're close to break-even and the case for raising at all weakens. If they fall through, A's extra runway and lack of repayment become worth the dilution.

## What to do

1. **Renegotiate B before signing.** Ask for:
   - a prepayment discount, e.g. settle at 1.25x if repaid within 18 months, so you can clear it cleanly at Series A
   - confirmation of no covenants, minimum payments, or personal guarantees
2. **Restructure the angel's involvement** into one of the smaller forms above.
3. **Decision rule:** if both pipeline deals collapse before you close B, take A instead. Equity is the better instrument when the timeline gets uncertain. Accept that A may be repriced by then, which is the cost of waiting.
4. **Set a deadline.** Six weeks is long enough that one or both offers may lapse or harden, which would make the decision for you.

Your CFO is right on the economics and your chair is right that the angel matters. The mistake was treating those as the same decision.

talk-03__base.text:
Your instinct is right, and it's sharper than you think. Most of your findings point the same direction. The main fix is the framing.

## Reframe "performance vs. communication"

At a sociolinguistics conference, "it's performance, not communication" will get pushback. Performance *is* communication, and the binary can sound like you're calling the kids' language use fake. What you're actually seeing is that **the heritage language isn't carrying referential content. It's carrying social meaning.** English does the propositional work; heritage words do relational work (intimacy, play, in-group membership).

A possible one-sentence claim:

> In these group chats, heritage-language words function less as a code for saying things than as a peer-owned resource for signaling closeness and play, used regardless of speaker competence and suppressed when outsiders are present.

Adjust the wording, but you should be able to say something like this in one breath. That's what your supervisor was asking for.

## Sorting your findings

**Core evidence (these carry the argument):**

| Finding | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Categories: food, family, teasing, exclamations | These are emblematic, affective domains, not propositional ones. The words index belonging rather than carry information. |
| Teasing switches get 3.1 vs 1.2 reacts | Peers *ratify* it. The switch is doing visible social work and getting uptake. |
| ~70% drop when an aunt joins | Audience design (Bell 1984). The code is calibrated to who's listening. This is your "when it's just us" quote in numbers. |
| 7/15 "can't really speak it" | Use is decoupled from competence. This is the puzzle your whole talk answers. |
| Cross-borrowing ("aiyah," "walao") | Possibly your most interesting finding. It suggests these words have become *peer-group* property, not just ethnic-heritage property. Look at Rampton's work on **crossing** (*Crossing*, 1995) and Derek Denis's work on Multicultural Toronto English, which is literally your city. |
| "When it's funny" / "when it's just us" | Participants' own metalinguistic framing. Great for opening or closing. |

**Context (brief, supports the frame):**

- **82% English matrix.** This sets up the core observation: English is the frame, heritage words are inserted into it. One slide early on.
- **Spelling variation.** It fits if you frame it lightly: these words are learned orally and used as emblems, not as a written language with norms. One bullet, not a section. (Don't overclaim that "kayn" is stylized unless you've analyzed that.)

**Needs checking before it goes in:**

- **Late-night 2.3x.** It *could* fit as another "who's in the room" effect: late night means a smaller, closer subset of participants and less monitoring, so it's more backstage. But first check whether the rate is normalized per message (not just "more messages at night") and whether fewer people are active late. If late-night activity really is the inner circle, it slots right next to the aunt finding. If you can't check, move it to a backup slide for Q&A.

**Not part of the claim:**

- **Anonymization methods.** I know it took forever. Give it one slide within methods, framed as ethics ("here's how I handled minors' private chats," which audiences do care about). The full procedure could be a separate methods paper or poster. It deserves its own venue rather than eating your talk.

## Suggested structure (aim for ~15–16 min of talking)

1. **Hook: the puzzle (1.5 min).** An anonymized example message plus the stat: "7 of 15 say they can't really speak their heritage language. They use it constantly. So what is it doing?"
2. **Claim and framing (1 min).** Your one-sentence claim, plus a nod to the literature you're in conversation with.
3. **Data and methods (2 min).** Corpus, participants, interviews, one ethics/anonymization slide.
4. **English is the frame (1 min).** 82% matrix, insertional switching.
5. **What gets switched (2 min).** The categories: social, affective, emblematic. Spelling as a brief aside.
6. **How it lands (1.5 min).** Teasing and reactions. Peers ratify it.
7. **Who's listening (2.5 min).** The aunt drop (flag n=2 and the topic shift to event planning as a confound yourself, before someone else does), plus late night if it holds up.
8. **Who it belongs to (2 min).** Crossing. These words circulate as shared peer resources.
9. **Back to the puzzle (1.5 min).** Competence doesn't matter because competence isn't the point. Close with "when it's just us."
10. **Implications (1 min).** For example, this challenges deficit framings of heritage speakers. Symbolic use may be a meaningful form of attachment and maintenance, not just loss.

Each section answers a question about the claim: *what* is used, *how* it lands, *when*, *by whom*. That's what makes it a talk instead of a list of findings.

If you want, send me your current slide titles and I can help map them onto this, or we can draft the hook and claim slides together.

positioning-08__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Back a sharpened Route A: not "cheap today" but "fair as your pet gets older." It is built on the 8% renewal cap, the one asset you have that answers owners' biggest frustration.

## The shape that clicked
```
Owner frustration             %    What answers it
Renewal jumps with age       61    8% cap (T&Cs p.6, unused)
  (44% of 8+ owners left)
Unsure what's covered        38    B, indirectly
Slow claims                  19    C, but beaten by 'same day'
Price at point of buying     14    A as written, but we're mid-market
```
As briefed, all three routes compete for the bottom three rows of your own research. The top row, the frustration that drives switching, is answered by a feature buried on page 6. Route A was close: its territory is price, but it was aimed at the wrong price moment.

## What moved
- **8% cap:** page 6 → the headline. It is the only asset matched to the 61% and the 44%.
- **Route A:** price at purchase → price over the pet's lifetime. Finance keeps a price story without fighting on a price you don't win.
- **Route C:** lead → proof point. It is true, but it addresses 19%, and "48 hours" loses next to "same day."
- **Route B:** lead → the trust layer. The vets help answer "what's covered."
- **Cut:** "comparison-site friendly" as the goal. Mid-market prices make it a fight you lose.
- **Missing:** see "Before Friday" below.

## Rebuilt: the case to walk in with

**1. Our research says owners leave over renewals.** 61% name premium jumps as their top frustration, and 44% of owners with a pet over 8 have switched or cancelled because of one. Price at purchase is the frustration least mentioned (14%), and slow claims are 19%.

**2. We already have the answer, and nobody knows.** Our lifetime policies cap annual increases at 8% for as long as the policy is held, regardless of age, as long as you stay on your tier. Marketing has never used it.

**3. So the route is "Fair Price," redefined: fair for the whole of your pet's life.** Working territory: *[Your premium can't rise more than 8% a year, however old your pet gets]*. The agency writes the line. The tier condition stays visible.

**4. Why not the others as the lead:**
- **C (Fast Claims):** "48 hours" invites a comparison we lose to "same day." It becomes a supporting fact.
- **B (Vet Designed):** credible, but it doesn't answer a top-ranked frustration on its own. It becomes the reason to trust the policy, and our clearest way to address "what's covered" (38%).
- **A as briefed:** we're mid-market, so we can't win on cheapest.

**5. Objections, housed:**
- *Agency:* "C is simpler." C is simple but second place, while the cap is simple and ours. *[Confirm whether any competitor offers a comparable cap.]*
- *Finance:* "We need price." This is a price story, and one we can win.
- *Founder:* the vets anchor credibility in every execution.
- *Risk:* 8% a year still compounds, so we must never imply flat premiums. Honesty about this is part of the "fair" claim.

**6. Before Friday, get or flag:**
- Underwriter confirmation that the cap holds at campaign-level volumes, and for how long.
- Compliance and ASA view on the claim wording, including the tier condition.
- *[Our own renewal and retention data for pets 8+, if available.]*

proposal-02__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Support a pilot CBD cordon charge to cut congestion and emissions, and recycle its revenue into outer-suburban buses, sized for the fact that revenue will fall as the charge works.

## The shape that clicked
```
OLD:   Recommendation
        ├─ Revenue ──> funds OSBU          ┐ success on one
        └─ Fewer entries ──> less CO2      ┘ shrinks the other

NEW:   PURPOSE: fewer CBD entries (congestion, CO2)
              │
        $11 charge
              │
        revenue  (declines as entries fall 22–40%)
              │
        recycled ──> OSBU (equity)
        rule: commit OSBU against the declining trajectory, not year one
```
You're right that both stories belong in the memo. The problem is presenting them as two equal purposes. They pull against each other: every car the charge removes is revenue lost to OSBU. Your own numbers show this (entries down 22–30%, up to 40% by 2032). "Revenue volatility" is sitting in Risks as a footnote, but it is the core tension. Your director is asking whether this is a funding tool or a demand tool. Pick one as the purpose and make the other its consequence. Then no content is lost.

## What moved
- Emissions/entries: second point → the purpose, because it is the charge's actual mechanism.
- Revenue/OSBU: co-equal rationale → "what the revenue does," with a sizing rule.
- Revenue volatility: Risks footnote → part of the design.
- EV line: rising EV share *reduces* the emissions saved per avoided entry, so as written it argues the wrong way. Now qualified.
- Missing: the year and entry level the $310m assumes, the revenue trajectory to 2032, whether the "improved PT" in the 40% modelling includes OSBU, and a fallback if revenue drops.

If the department's real driver is closing the OSBU funding gap, flip the order and lead with revenue. Then you must show the revenue holds up, and your entry-reduction figures become the case against you. I'd lead with demand management.

## Rebuilt

**Recommendation:** The Department should support a pilot cordon charge for the Melbourne CBD at $11 per weekday entry, commencing July 2026, to reduce congestion and emissions in the CBD. Net revenue would be recycled to fund the Outer Suburban Bus Uplift (OSBU).

**What the charge does**
- Expected to reduce CBD vehicle entries by 22–30%, consistent with international experience. This cuts transport emissions in the cordon by approx. 140kt CO2-e per year.
- Modelling suggests entries could fall by up to 40% by 2032 if the charge is paired with improved PT. [Confirm whether this modelling's "improved PT" includes OSBU.]
- Over time, mode shift increases the emissions benefit, while rising EV share reduces the emissions saved per avoided entry. [Net trajectory from modelling.]

**What the revenue does**
- Estimated $310m annually in net revenue [year/entry-reduction assumption], hypothecated to OSBU, currently unfunded beyond 2025-26.
- OSBU would extend frequent service to 14 growth-area corridors where 38% of households have no access to a 15-minute-frequency service.
- Because the charge is designed to reduce entries, revenue will decline as it succeeds: [revenue trajectory to 2032]. OSBU commitments should be sized to [projected floor], with [fallback funding source / service scaling rule] if revenue falls below it.

**Equity**
- Lower-income outer-suburban residents are less likely to drive into the CBD (only 6% of trips from bottom-quintile postcodes). The charge is therefore mildly progressive, and more so with revenue recycled to OSBU.

**Risks**
- Revenue decline and volatility: expected by design; managed through the OSBU sizing rule above.
- Business opposition (CBD retail).
- Tight legislative timeline.

positioning-06__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

The tagline isn't the problem: the donate page is written for a renter in crisis and never shows a donor what their money does. Pick B, and use the page to prove it.

## The shape that clicked

```
NOW                                   REBUILT
Reader: tenant in crisis              Reader: donor (50+, homeowner, local biz)
N12? Rent hike? -> Call us            B: Know your rights. Keep your home.
         |                                     |
"Donate today" (one line)            Proof: 64% vs ~40% kept tenancy

```

Neither tagline felt like a fix because the page beneath it talks to the wrong person. Your donors mostly own their homes, so "Facing an N12?" isn't their question. A is true but generic; any housing charity could say it. B is a claim your own numbers back up, so it can lead to proof and then to a price.

## What moved

- **Tagline B**: from a slogan aimed at tenants to the headline of a donor page, with evidence underneath.
- **2023 numbers**: from the annual report to the middle of the page, as proof.
- **$35 per call**: from a buried stat to the donate button.
- **Hotline details**: from the main body to one line for tenants who land on the page.
- **Cut**: tagline A, because it can't point to anything specific you do.
- **Missing**:
  - Why online giving fell from $14,900 to $11,200. Don't promise the board that a tagline will reverse it.
  - Your partner clinic's OK to cite its ~40% estimate.
  - A caller story, shared with permission.

## It's neither. Your data points to reseller onboarding.

You have a built-in control group: customers older than 12 months got the **same price increase and the same support delays**, and churned at 1.4%, basically normal. If price or support were the main driver, you'd see it there too. You don't.

What the data does show:
- **61 of 94** churned accounts (65%) onboarded in the last 9 months
- **55 of those 61** came through MedPraxis Digital, which is **58% of all Q3 churn from one channel**
- Top exit reason by far: **"didn't use it enough / never got set up properly" (16 of 38)**, more than price (9) and support (7) combined
- Reseller onboarding is done by the partner, and **you have zero visibility into it**

So the story is: *a cohort of customers came in through a channel we don't control, many were never properly set up, and they're leaving.* Price and support likely acted as **accelerants**. A clinic that never got value out of the product is the one that looks at a 12% increase or a 7h response time and decides to cancel. But they're not the root cause.

That's a single, clear headline, not a cop-out. "Multiple factors" becomes "one primary cause, two aggravating factors."

## Check before Monday (if you can)

These turn a strong story into a bulletproof one:

1. **Reseller cohort churn rate.** How many customers came through MedPraxis in total? 55 churned out of how many? That's your killer number.
2. **Direct-onboarded recent customers.** Only 6 of the 61 new churners were direct. What's their churn *rate*? If it's near normal, you've isolated the channel, not just "new customers churn more."
3. **Historical new-customer churn.** First-year customers always churn more. Show that Q3's new-customer churn is above what you've seen before, so nobody can dismiss it as normal.
4. **Exit survey by cohort.** Do the "never got set up" answers come mostly from reseller accounts? I'd bet yes.
5. **Activation/usage data**, if you have it: logins, appointments booked, calendars connected. If reseller accounts show low activation from day one, that's proof of the onboarding gap without needing MedPraxis's notes.

## Suggested deck structure

1. **Headline:** Q3 churn spike is concentrated in reseller-onboarded customers; tenured customers are stable
2. **The control group slide:** tenured churn 1.4% despite the same price and support conditions. This is the slide that ends the price-vs-support debate.
3. **Where churn came from:** 55/94 from MedPraxis, plus the exit survey reasons
4. **Price & support as accelerants:** acknowledge they matter, especially for at-risk accounts
5. **What we don't know:** no visibility into partner onboarding (this is itself a finding)
6. **Recommendations:**
   - Health check / re-onboarding outreach for remaining MedPraxis accounts *now*, before Q4
   - Onboarding standards + reporting requirements for the partner (checklists, activation metrics)
   - Support coverage plan for leave periods (this gives Aylin something legit)

## The politics

- **Give Jens and Aylin a heads-up before Monday.** Neither should be surprised in the room. You can frame it to both as: "the data doesn't support either single story, here's what it does show."
- **Aylin still gets something.** Doubled response times plausibly hurt struggling accounts, and a re-onboarding push for the reseller cohort will need CS capacity. Her headcount case may actually get *stronger*, just for a different reason.
- **Find out who owns the MedPraxis partnership** and talk to them first. This finding lands on them, and you want them as an ally in fixing it, not blindsided in front of leadership.

You've done the hard part; the answer's already in your numbers. Good luck Monday.

## What moved

- **"Nobody is losing their job"**: kept right after the change, aimed at Platform.
- **Growth and survey findings**: intro → the "why" section.

- **The 11-days stat**: keep it. It's your clearest reason, and leaving it out makes the move look arbitrary. Team,

Starting 1 November, the Platform team will no longer be a standalone group. Each of our four product domains (Payments, Lending, Onboarding and Risk) will own its own infrastructure, and Platform's 14 engineers will join those domains, three or four per domain. A small Developer Experience group of 3, led by Joost, will stay central and look after shared tooling and CI. [Clarify whether these 3 are part of the 14.]

proposal-04__base.text:
Your note at the end matters a lot. The overlap between your sites and your volunteer network is probably the strongest argument you have. Right now it's described as a practical convenience. It could be the design principle of the whole proposal.

## The central question is already in your data

Look at what WP1 and WP2 imply together:

- WP1: Less frequent mowing makes margins much more attractive for nesting (2.3x).
- WP2: Bees nesting at farm sites carry pesticide residues in 68% of samples.

Put those side by side and you get a sharp, policy-relevant question:

> **Do well-managed field margins act as refuges for wild bees, or as ecological traps that attract them into pesticide exposure?**

An ecological trap is a habitat that looks high-quality to an animal but lowers its fitness. If agri-environment schemes improve margins and draw bees to nest beside sprayed crops, the schemes could be less beneficial than assumed, or beneficial only under certain spraying conditions. That is a single question that needs habitat data, exposure data, and outcome data. Your three WPs become three necessary parts of one answer rather than three projects.

A possible retitle: *"Refuge or trap? Margin management and pesticide exposure as joint drivers of wild bee persistence in agricultural landscapes."*

## How each WP serves the question

**WP1: Habitat quality (does management attract bees?)**
Largely as is. Mowing regime is now one axis of the design.

**WP2: Exposure (what are bees exposed to in those margins?)**
The 18 shared sites become the core of the design, not a side effect. Consider two additions:
- **Pollen identification (palynology or metabarcoding) of the Osmia loads.** This tells you whether residues come from crop pollen or from margin flowers contaminated by drift. That distinction is central to the trap question and to scheme design (e.g., margin width, buffer distances).
- **Residue sampling in margin soil or flowers at WP1 sites.** Your WP1 bees are ground-nesters and WP2 uses a cavity-nester. A reviewer will notice that Osmia is a proxy. Measuring exposure in the nesting substrate of the WP1 bees makes the link explicit.

**WP3: Landscape-scale outcomes and management data (what happens to populations, and why?)**
This is where reframing matters most. As written, WP3's deliverable is an app, which is why it reads as separate. Reframe it so the app is a *method*, not the goal:
- Volunteers generate bumblebee occurrence and diversity data across the same districts. That is your response variable at a scale the trap nests and transects can't cover.
- Many volunteers are farmers or farm neighbours. **They can provide management records**: actual mowing dates and spray timing. Those data are notoriously hard to get, and they would let you link exposure to specific events. This is a strong integrating argument, and it's currently hidden in a footnote.
- Farmer-volunteers become co-designers of the scheme recommendations. That turns "public engagement" into a credible route to impact.

## Should you cut one?

WP1 and WP2 are the core, so keep both. WP3 is the honest question. You have two good options:

1. **Integrate it as above**, with the app development shrunk to a task and most of the WP's effort going to data collection, management records, and co-design. This is my recommendation if you can make the volunteer data analytically meaningful.
2. **Demote it** to a knowledge-exchange or impact component rather than a full WP. This is better if the app is mostly about engagement and the data won't feed the analysis.

What a panel will not fund is a three-year junior project where one-third of the effort produces a tool that doesn't answer the research question. Also note that 81% accuracy on 9 species will raise questions. Bumblebees include cryptic groups (e.g., *B. terrestris/lucorum*), so state how you will handle species that can't be separated from images, and how expert verification works.

## Things to check before you commit to this framing

- **Confounding at the 18 shared sites.** They were chosen for practical reasons. Do they span both mowing regimes and a range of pesticide intensity, or do they cluster? If well-mown margins happen to sit next to organic or low-input fields, you can't separate the effects. If the overlap is unbalanced, redesign the site selection for the full study as a deliberate crossing of mowing regime × exposure gradient, and say so.
- **Foraging scale.** Osmia forages over a few hundred metres, so pollen residues reflect the surrounding landscape, not just the margin. Acknowledge this and use land-cover data around each site as a covariate.
- **Fitness, not just presence.** A trap is defined by reduced fitness. If you can measure any reproductive outcome (Osmia brood cells, offspring number or mass, sex ratio), the trap hypothesis becomes testable rather than speculative. Trap nests make this relatively cheap.

## For the resubmission itself

- Open with the central question and two or three explicit hypotheses (e.g., H1: reduced mowing increases nesting; H2: margin-nesting bees experience residue exposure that varies with adjacent crop management; H3: the net effect on populations depends on the interaction).
- Include a figure showing the shared sites, districts, and data flows between WPs. Panels respond well to seeing integration rather than being told about it.
- Make dependencies visible in the timeline. WP3 management records feed WP2 analysis, and WP1 and WP2 combine in a joint final analysis.
- In the response to reviewers, address the comment directly: *"The panel asked for the central question. The revised proposal is organised around a single question, whether field margins act as refuges or ecological traps, and the three work packages now share sites, data and a joint analysis."*

If you can tell me how the 18 shared sites are distributed across mowing regimes, I can help you judge whether the existing data already support the trap framing or whether you need to redesign the site selection.

oped-01__base.text:
Your partner's right, and the fix is mostly reordering rather than rewriting. Your strongest material is the exit interviews and the agency-cost comparison, and right now it's buried in paragraph four. The first two paragraphs are warm-up: general grumbling and concessions to the Trust. Those can shrink to a couple of sentences and move later, where they make you sound fair rather than hesitant.

Here's a reworked version using your own sentences wherever possible:

---

Four of the nine nurses who left my ward this year mentioned parking in their exit interviews. Our ward manager told me that covering those four posts with agency staff has cost more than the Trust made from raising staff parking charges across the whole hospital. I asked her to double-check. She did.

I've worked at Eastgate General for eleven years. Since April, a staff permit costs £58 a month, up from £22. For a band 5 nurse on nights, that's [a big chunk of a shift's / X hours'] take-home pay every month just to park at the place you work. Buses don't run from my estate before 6am or after 11pm, so for most of us on nights there is no other option.

The Trust says the charges pay for maintenance and security, and I'm sure some of that is true. Car parks cost money, and I've grumbled along with everyone else about the card machines, the sticking barriers and the overflow car park by the laundry block that floods every November. Nobody is saying parking should be free for visitors forever, and I understand the Trust is under pressure from all sides.

But staff are a different story. We're not here for an hour's appointment. We're here at 3am because the ward needs us.

I think the Trust should reverse the increase for night staff at minimum, and look again at whether it makes sense for anyone on a clinical rota. I love my job and I love this hospital. I just don't want to keep saying goodbye to colleagues over a car park.

---

**What changed**
- The opening is now your most surprising fact: the increase may be costing the Trust money. That's what makes an editor and a reader keep going.
- "I asked her to double-check. She did." now lands in the first paragraph. It's the best line in the piece.
- The grumbling about machines and flooding is kept but folded into the concession, so it shows you're reasonable without delaying the point.
- I added two short sentences ("We're not here for an hour's appointment..."). Cut or change them if they don't sound like you.

**Worth checking before Friday**
1. **The "full shift" figure.** £58 might be less than a full night's take-home for a band 5, even with enhancements. Editors and the Trust's press office will check numbers like this, so it's worth working out the real figure from your payslip and using that. "Most of a shift" or "five hours' pay" can still hit hard.
2. **The agency-cost claim.** It's your strongest point, so make sure your manager is comfortable with it appearing in print, even unnamed. Ask her whether the figure is something the Trust could confirm or dispute.
3. **Trust media policy.** Many NHS trusts ask staff to notify comms before writing for the press, even in a personal capacity. It's worth a quick look so the piece doesn't cause you trouble.

You're at about 340 words, so you have room if the Gazette wants closer to 600. The best use of that space would be one specific story, such as a colleague's last shift or a night when you sat in the car park doing the maths. More argument wouldn't help as much. Happy to help with that if you want to add one.

NEW:   School signs --> Teachers adopt (board-aligned content, dashboard)

- **Schools**: from rival bet to acquisition channel.
- **CAC and churn**: from unsaid to stated, because they are the honest reason to change.
- **Vernacular**: from a 2025 commitment to next in line, because the team can do one restructuring a year.

## Rebuilt

**Where Padhai is going in 2025**

What's changed is how parents find us. Reaching them directly costs nearly twice what it did: CAC has gone from ₹410 to ₹780 in 18 months, and about 9% of paid subscribers leave each month. Meanwhile, 31% of our paid subscribers came to us because their school uses Padhai. A school is the most trusted recommendation a parent gets. It also pays: our 140 partner schools bring ₹3.4 crore ARR at 81% gross margin, on annual contracts, with near-zero CAC once a chain signs.

**So in 2025 we grow the consumer business through schools.**

1. **Content:** our one big restructuring this year is state-board alignment, because that's what teachers need to adopt Padhai. Vernacular content (Kannada, Tamil, Hindi) is next in line [timing to confirm with content team].
2. **Teachers:** we build the teacher dashboard.
3. **Parents:** progress reports become the bridge. What the teacher sees, the parent sees. Every school student's family is a parent we reach without paying ₹780.
4. **Pricing:** we test the ₹199/month tier with families at partner schools first, before a wider Tier-2 launch.

**What we're not doing:** splitting our energy between two businesses. This is one business with one funnel, from school to student to parent.

**How we'll know it's working:** the share of new paid subscribers who come through schools, and [retention of school-acquired vs. direct subscribers].

oped-02__base.text:
It's one post, not two. You just buried the thesis in paragraph four.

The org chart point is the argument. The cost and latency numbers are the evidence. Right now the draft presents the numbers as the point and then says "actually, it wasn't microservices," which reads like you're contradicting yourself. Flip the order and the contradiction disappears: *the problem was a mismatch between architecture and team size, and here's what happened when we fixed it.*

That framing is also better for HN. "Monolith good" starts the same flamewar for the 400th time. "We had 14 services and 9 engineers" is a specific, slightly embarrassing, relatable story, and the numbers hit harder when they're proof of an idea rather than the idea itself.

## Suggested structure

**Title:** something like *"We had 14 microservices and 9 engineers"* or *"Our architecture was mirroring an org chart we didn't have"*

1. **Hook: the mismatch.** Open with 14 services and 9 engineers. That one ratio tells the whole story.
2. **What it was actually like.** Services owned by nobody, 6 hops per request, 7-8 week onboarding, on-call misery. Make the pain concrete before the fix.
3. **What we did.** Merged back into one Rails app. Briefly cover how, since people will want to know.
4. **Results.** Cost, latency, onboarding, pages. All your numbers stay; they just move here.
5. **The real lesson.** Architecture should match the team you have, not the team you imagine having. Microservices weren't wrong; they were wrong *for us at that size*.
6. **Lessons learned.** Concrete, not "it depends."

## Things to fix

**Cut "Probably! Unless you shouldn't. It depends on your team."** It undercuts everything. You already know what it depends on, so say it. Something like:

> The question isn't "monolith or microservices." It's "does every service have a team that owns it, gets paged for it, and would notice if it got worse?" If the answer is no for most of your services, you have more architecture than organization.

**Soften the former CTO line.** Naming a past leader's decision as the cause reads as blame, and it's a hiring post. Try: *"We split early, planning for a scale we didn't end up reaching."* Same information, no finger-pointing, and it makes Tallowbird look reflective instead of messy.

**Check the burnout detail.** At 40 engineers, "two engineers who told me they were burned out" might be identifiable. Ask them first, or generalize it to something like "people who'd been struggling with the codebase started enjoying it again."

**Minor:** "its" → "it's," "tho" → "though" (unless your blog voice is that casual).

## Possible opening

> In early 2023 we had 14 microservices and 9 engineers. Every service had an owner on paper and nobody in practice. Last March we folded them all back into a single Rails app.
>
> Six months later, our AWS bill is down 60%, booking latency is down by more than half, and new hires ship their first real PR in two weeks instead of eight. But the lesson we took away isn't "microservices are bad." It's that our architecture was mirroring an org chart we didn't have.

## Lessons learned (drafts to replace the todos)

- **Count owners, not services.** If a service doesn't have someone who'd notice it degrading, it's a liability.
- **Network hops are a tax on every request.** Six hops cost us over 500ms at p95.
- **Onboarding time is an architecture metric.** If it takes two months to ship a first PR, your system is too hard to hold in your head.
- **Split when the team forces you to, not before.** Separate services make sense when separate teams are stepping on each other, not when you're predicting they someday might.

This version also works for your hiring push: "we noticed something wasn't working, fixed it, and engineers are happier" is exactly what candidates want to read.

academic-04__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

The trial found a modest, imprecise effect that does not rule out no effect; the interviews suggest several possible pathways, the most novel being that official messages gave women leverage with mothers-in-law, which is worth testing directly.

## The shape that clicked

```
NOW                                   REBUILT
Policy: scale + target MILs           Implication: test the pathways
        ▲                                        ▲
"The mechanism" (1 quote)            Authority   Memory   More ASHA
        ▲                              (MIL)               contact
"Improved ANC" (p = 0.09)                  └────────┼────────┘
                                                     ▲
 [memory, ASHA visits: orphaned]       Modest, imprecise effect
```

Your instinct is right. The draft is a tower: each floor is narrower than the one it rests on. The base doesn't establish an effect (the CI crosses 1). A single quote then becomes "the mechanism" of that effect, and the policy advice rests on top of it. Meanwhile, your strongest rival explanation (ASHAs visited more often) sits in an aside. Laid side by side, the pathways make the qualitative work *more* interesting, because the mother-in-law finding is presented as a credible hypothesis instead of an overclaim a reviewer will attack.

## What moved

- "Improved uptake" → "consistent with a modest benefit, but includes no effect," because 95% CI 0.96–1.74.
- Mother-in-law quote: "the mechanism… primarily" → the most novel of three candidate pathways, because the interviews are intervention-arm only and give no comparison.
- More ASHA visits: aside → interpretation and limitations, because it may be the active ingredient.
- MIL-addressed messages: recommendation → something to test.
- Cut: "Policymakers should consider scaling," because the result doesn't support it yet.
- Missing: how many of the 18 described each pathway; whether ASHA visits were measured in both arms; your powered effect size.

## Rebuilt

ANC4+ completion was six percentage points higher in intervention than control villages (47% vs 41%; adjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.96–1.74). This estimate is consistent with a modest benefit, but the confidence interval includes no effect, so the trial does not establish that SMS reminders delivered through ASHAs increased antenatal care uptake. [The study was powered to detect X.]

Interviews with 18 women in intervention villages point to several pathways through which the intervention could have acted. [N] women described reminders helping them remember appointment dates. Several noted that ASHAs visited more often during the study period, which raises the possibility that increased ASHA contact, rather than the messages themselves, drove any difference. The most novel account concerned household negotiation: "When the message came, I showed it to my mother-in-law, and she could not say no because it was from the government." For [some] women, a message perceived as official seemed to provide an external authority to invoke with senior family members.

This account fits prior work documenting the influence of mothers-in-law on care-seeking (Kumar 2012; Rao & Singh 2017). It also suggests that official communication might counterbalance that influence. Because interviews were conducted only in intervention villages, we cannot compare these accounts with those of women who received no messages, or judge how common each pathway was. They are best read as hypotheses rather than evidence of mechanism.

A larger trial would show whether the effect is real. Designs that separate message content from ASHA contact could identify which component matters. Messages addressed explicitly to mothers-in-law are a promising variant to test directly.

*Add to limitations:* Beyond [representativeness of the two districts], the effect estimate was imprecise. Qualitative data came from intervention villages only. ASHA visit frequency [was not measured / differed between arms], so we cannot separate the effect of the messages from that of increased contact.

## The spine
Your arithmetic is fine, but 59% of the plan rests on one non-committal sentence from Achieng, and your own non-solicitation clause may stop you acting on it. The question isn't "do the numbers work?" but "does the firm survive if Tarvo doesn't come, or comes late?"

## The shape that clicked
```
   12-month non-solicit ──┐
                          ▼
 "we'd definitely   ──► TARVO 9.6M (59%) ──► breakeven ──► profit by month 4
  consider"               │
                          ▼
            Without Tarvo: 6.7M/yr ≈ 558K/month
            vs 555K/month of costs before your draw
```
Your list makes the revenue look diversified, with the risks filed as "other things." They aren't side notes. Most of them point at the same client.

## What moved
- **Non-solicit clause**: from side note to the centre, because it likely covers your biggest revenue line.
- **Achieng's quote**: from revenue to untested assumption. "Would consider" isn't a commitment, and she may not be the final decision-maker.
- **Savings**: from cushion to the plan's real runway, and it's household money.
- **Partnership track**: from aside to your strongest reason to go. It's stalled.
- **The two ex-partners**: from anecdote to your best source of evidence.
- **Missing**: a written legal opinion on the clause; one-off setup costs (deposit, fit-out, equipment); how fast your clients actually pay; whether Kilima and Gathoni are also firm clients; working capital separate from household savings.

## Rebuilt

**Your wife isn't just being risk averse.** She has spotted that your largest number rests on your least certain fact. That's not a reason to stay. It's a reason to de-risk before March.

**Stress test, using only your figures** (costs 955K/month):

| Scenario | Annual | Monthly | vs costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| As planned | 16.3M | ~1.36M | +~400K |
| Tarvo moves half its work | 11.5M | ~958K | roughly breakeven |
| No Tarvo | 6.7M | ~558K | −~397K; covers costs only if you draw nothing |
| No Tarvo, no new business | 4.7M | ~392K | −~563K |

**Timing.** If billing takes three months to catch up, as you assume, you need about 2.9M before meaningful cash arrives, plus setup costs. That would come from savings meant to cover your household for six months.

**The trap.** The obvious way to firm up Tarvo is to ask them directly. While you're still employed, that conversation may itself be what the clause prohibits. So the legal opinion comes first, not a friend's "hard to enforce." Ask specifically whether a client who chooses to follow you, without being approached, is caught by the wording, and what you can safely say before you leave.

**Before resigning:**
1. Get the written opinion on the clause.
2. Redesign the plan to survive 12 months without Tarvo. For example, hire the associate only once a second client is paying, set a lower starting draw, and ring-fence firm working capital from household savings.
3. Ask both former partners what made the difference between thriving and closing at 18 months.

**Decision rule.** Go in March if (a) the opinion says you can take Tarvo if they come to you, and (b) the no-Tarvo version survives 12 months on a draw your household can live with. If either fails, move the date and fix it. Don't abandon the plan.

Bonjour! Your English is very clear, and writing like this was a good idea. Here is what I see in your text. I think you are right that it goes in circles, and I think I can see why.

**1. Both options end in the same word.**
"Excitement, then tired." "Proud, then tired." Then: "I am tired of being tired." You are asking *Montreal or bistro?*, but your own feelings give the same answer to both: another 70-80 hours a week. Montreal is the old life in a new city. The bistro is the old life with debt and admin added. The first feeling (excitement, pride) is about your ambition. The second feeling (tired) is about your body and your life right now. The second one sounds more honest.

**2. Your daughter comes last in the text, but she decides a lot.**
You write that Montreal makes your weekends with her "impossible." That is not a small problem. It is a big change in your relationship with a 9-year-old. The bistro makes it "difficult," and in the first two years, when you work every day, "difficult" can quietly become "rarely." Is she the main question, written at the end because it is the hardest part?

**3. You dismissed the third option with someone else's judgment.**
Look at École Ferrand on paper. It is the only option that:
- gives normal hours (35 instead of 75),
- protects your back,
- keeps you in Lyon with your daughter,
- needs no debt.

The salary is also not bad. Roughly calculated, Montreal pays maybe €13-14 *gross* per hour. École Ferrand pays about €22 *net* per hour.

But you said no to it with the phrase "this is for people who are finished as chefs." Is that true, or is it an old kitchen belief? Many very good chefs teach. They pass on 20 years of knowledge, and some return to cooking later, rested and with a clearer idea of what they want. Teaching for two or three years does not make you "finished." It can also be a pause before something else, like a bistro later, on your terms, with savings instead of debt.

**4. The real question may not be "Montreal or bistro."**
It may be something like: *"Can I accept that I need a different rhythm, without feeling that I have failed?"*

Some questions to ask yourself:
- If nobody would ever judge you, would you take the teaching job?
- In five years, what do you want your life with your daughter to look like?
- What does your back need? Can it survive another 10 years on the line?
- With the bistro: is there a version with fewer opening days, or with Théo responsible for more? Or is it only attractive because it means "my own boss"?

I can't decide for you. You know things about yourself, Théo, and your family that are not in this text. But if I just read what you wrote, you are not describing a choice between two dreams. You are describing a tired man looking for permission to stop running. It might be worth calling École Ferrand and asking more questions before the end of the month, not to say yes, but to see the option clearly, without the word "finished."

Bon courage. If you want, tell me more about your daughter or about Théo, and we can think through it further.
